Ryco performance research: cold boot and first use

Commit f1be4abc7 · 2026-10-11 · 263 findings across 17 scenarios, each re-checked by an adversarial verifier · no source changes

The biggest single lever is idle time, not code size. React 19's 300 ms Suspense reveal throttle fires on every lazy boundary. On a cold loopback load the composer appears at 764 ms, and ~500 ms of that the main thread is idle. Patching the throttle out (A/B) brought it to 412 ms, and first opens of Settings, Projects and Statistics drop from ~320 ms to ~40 ms. Route-level code splitting removes it.

On the desktop, the backend dominates real-world launch time. In your own logs (430 launches), the backend needs p50 1.6 s and p90 12.3 s from spawn to listening. Everything waits on it: the renderer cannot load app code until then, and the server does provider probing (15 processes, ~1.9 GB peak RSS), triple read-model loads and git identity probes on the boot path.

The research found real reliability bugs along the way. Requests made during server startup are never answered. Shutdown waits up to 20 s whenever a WebSocket is open, so every desktop quit ends in a SIGKILL. A per-turn prefix breaks Claude /compact and slash commands. Statistics are silently truncated, and its Activity tab stalls the whole server for seconds. See Reliability bugs.

Start with the 22 prioritized themes and the 31 quick wins (mostly S effort). Every claim links to a verified finding with file:line references, evidence, a proposal and the verifier's corrections.

Priorities

These themes consolidate overlapping findings across scenarios (several problems were found independently by 2–4 investigations). They are ordered by user-visible impact relative to effort. Effort is S (hours to a day), M (days), L (a week or more).

1

Remove the 300 ms React Suspense reveal delay from every navigation

Expected gain
Composer −390 ms (803 → 412 ms, measured A/B); sidebar −220 ms; first open of Settings/Projects/Statistics/PRs 313–391 ms → 36–125 ms
Effort
M
Evidence
Measured A/B + code-verified

React 19.2 holds back any Suspense content commit until 300 ms after the most recent fallback was shown. RootAppShell and every route body use hand-rolled React.lazy inside <Suspense>, so a cold boot pays the delay twice (shell, then thread route) and every first page open pays it once, even when the chunk is already cached. Settings is idle-preloaded and still takes 336 ms. The main thread is idle throughout.

What to do

  • Switch route components to TanStack route-level splitting (lazyRouteComponent, .lazy.tsx or autoCodeSplitting) so the router awaits the chunk before it commits. No fallback is shown, so the throttle never starts.
  • Import RootAppShell inside root beforeLoad (authenticated/hosted-static only, never on /pair) and render the resolved module directly.
  • Add one shared preloadableLazy helper for SettingsPage, HostedHubRoot, CommandPaletteDialog and ThreadWorkspacePanel, then enable defaultPreload: 'intent'.
  • Add a browser test asserting that the time from chunk-resolved to commit stays under 50 ms.

The gain is smaller on bandwidth-bound links, where the throttle overlaps downloads. Desktop loopback gets the full benefit. The A/B removed nested lazy boundaries too, so treat −390 ms as an upper bound.

5 underlying findings
  • Web bootstrap waterfall: React 19 Suspense reveal throttle adds ~250-300 ms idle to boot, the first thread and every first page open
  • Live browser measurements: React's 300 ms Suspense reveal delay adds ~250-300 ms idle per lazy boundary: twice on every boot and once on every first page open
  • New thread, open, switch: React 19's 300 ms Suspense reveal delay adds ~300 ms to the first thread/draft open in every document
  • Statistics, Projects, Settings, PRs: Dedicated pages use React.lazy inside the component: no intent/idle preload and no loader-started data, so the chunk and data load in sequence
  • Live browser measurements: The idle SettingsPage prefetch has no measurable benefit and competes with the critical path on slow links
2

Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain
Indefinite hangs → ≤280 ms wait; readiness pollers +0.9–1.8 s → +3–19 ms (prototype measured: 0 of 118 early requests hung)
Effort
S
Evidence
Root-caused, reproduced 190/190, fix prototyped

The HTTP port is bound when HttpServerLive is built at the bottom of the layer graph, but Node's request/upgrade handlers are attached only when HttpRouter.serve runs. That happens after migrations, engine hydration and the provider registry. A request in that window is emitted to zero listeners and is never answered or closed (sockets were held 330 s in testing). Clients set no fetch deadline on descriptor/session/ws-token requests or on the WebSocket URL provider, so a reconnect that lands in the window stalls indefinitely.

What to do

  • Add an httpStartupGate through the server factory NodeHttpServer.layer already accepts. It holds early requests and upgrades (bounded), replays them once the real handler attaches, and answers 503 + Retry-After on overflow. Report the drop upstream to Effect.
  • Add a shared fetchWithDeadline (5 s) for primaryAuth, primaryContext and remoteApi, and wrap the WS URL provider in Effect.timeout so reconnect retries keep advancing.
  • Send a structured readiness frame over the existing fd 3/4 pipe instead of parsing the 'Listening on' log line, and make markHttpListening depend on serve.
  • Lower the SSH remote readiness probe timeout; every SSH cold launch currently pays ~0.9 s.
8 underlying findings
  • Startup request black hole: The HTTP port is bound ~150-280 ms before any request/upgrade handler exists; requests accepted in that window are dropped and never answered or closed
  • Server process boot: Port is bound 70–305 ms before any request handler exists; requests in that window hang forever
  • Startup request black hole: Client descriptor/session/ws-token fetches and the WS URL provider have no timeout; one request in the window stalls reconnects indefinitely, and saved-env connects pile onto the hung attempt
  • Web bootstrap waterfall: Bootstrap and ws-token fetches have no timeout: a request that is never answered hangs boot or WS reconnect forever (reliability)
  • Startup request black hole: Every SSH remote cold launch pays ~0.9 s: the 100 ms / 1 s readiness poller always puts one probe into the dead window
  • Startup request black hole: Desktop readiness depends on parsing the INFO log line 'Listening on http://'; when it is missing, the HTTP fallback costs +0.9 s on every boot
  • Desktop cold boot: Readiness depends on a stdout log substring plus a 100 ms HTTP poll that lands in the server's pre-listen dead window
  • Startup request black hole: markHttpListening is signalled by a layer built concurrently with HttpRouter.serve, so 'http listener ready', the ready event and pairing output can come before handlers are attached
3

Bound shutdown and crash handling

Expected gain
Desktop quit/relaunch/update: no more SIGKILL after 2 s with a window open; CLI Ctrl-C 20.4 s → ~1 s; an endless splash on fatal errors becomes an actionable error
Effort
S
Evidence
Measured + code-verified

Effect's NodeHttpServer awaits server.close() before it interrupts WebSocket fibers. Any open WebSocket therefore makes graceful shutdown wait the full 20 s timeout (measured 20.4 s, against 1.0–1.5 s with no clients). The desktop always holds a WebSocket and sends SIGKILL after 2 s, so every quit, relaunch and update skips runtime finalizers: restart-continuation hints and the SQLite close. Separately, deterministic startup failures such as 'schema newer than binary' are retried forever while the window sits on the splash (145 respawns across 6 app runs on Oct 5–6 in your logs).

What to do

  • Immediately: pass gracefulShutdownTimeout ≈ 750 ms. Then patch @effect/platform-node so the per-request scope closes before server.close().
  • Bound the analytics shutdown flush (300 ms).
  • Use distinct exit codes for fatal and retryable startup errors. Desktop stops restarting after a fatal exit or 3 pre-listen failures and shows an error page.
  • After a backend crash-restart, reconnect instead of reloading the renderer to '/'.
4 underlying findings
  • Startup request black hole: Graceful shutdown waits the full 20 s gracefulShutdownTimeout whenever a WebSocket (or hung request) is open; desktop sends SIGKILL after 2 s, skipping later finalizers
  • Startup request black hole: With no clients, graceful shutdown still takes 1.0-1.5 s (1.7-2.8 s right after boot), close to desktop's 2 s SIGKILL; the analytics finalizer does an unbounded network POST
  • Desktop cold boot: Deterministic backend start failures are retried forever while the window stays on the splash (reliability bug)
  • Startup request black hole: After a backend crash-restart, desktop navigates the renderer back to the backend root (full app reload); this currently hides stuck reconnects
4

Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain
Your launches: p90 12.5 s to backend listening. Removes ~15 child processes, ~1.5 GB of transient RSS and ~4 cores × 1.5 s of CPU from every boot
Effort
M–L
Evidence
Measured; real-world stall root cause still open

In your real launch logs, launch → backend listening is p50 1.8 s and p90 12.5 s, and 17 of the last 30 sessions took more than 5 s. The listener waits behind the whole layer graph (migrations, engine hydration, provider registry, hub identity), so any stall shows up as splash time. After listening, every enabled provider is probed cold on every boot, because results are never treated as fresh across restarts. Measured: 15 child processes, 1.87 GB peak process-tree RSS and 423% CPU while the UI is loading. That includes opencode serve (739 MiB) and a Claude probe (250 MiB) that also starts the user's MCP servers. The desktop never reads the on-disk provider status cache, so the model picker is empty until the probes finish.

What to do

  • Persist probe results with freshness (binary path + version + settings hash). At boot, run only cheap checks. Run rich probes on demand, or staggered after the first snapshot, and never during desktop boot.
  • Run the Claude probe with no MCP servers (strict empty MCP config), and stop background probes from refreshing Claude Code's OAuth token.
  • Seed providersRef from the status cache in every mode, and defer registry construction in web/headless mode as desktop already does.
  • Make boot listener-first: answer static assets and the descriptor while engine hydration runs behind an engine-ready Deferred (combine with the startup gate).
  • Instrument the first 30 s (event-loop delay plus a threadpool canary) to pin down the 3–15 s stalls; they are not root-caused yet.
8 underlying findings
  • Server process boot: Every boot runs cold capability probes for every enabled provider: 15 child processes, ~1.9 GB peak process-tree RSS, and Claude Code credential refresh
  • Desktop cold boot: Real-world boot is dominated by 3–15 s backend stalls before 'Listening'; the listener waits behind provider creation and migrations
  • Server process boot: Desktop mode never reads the on-disk provider status cache at boot, so providers and models are missing until each cold probe finishes
  • Server process boot: In web/headless mode, provider driver construction blocks HTTP listen (desktop already defers it)
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: Routes are served only after engine hydration and projector catch-up, while the socket is already bound
  • Startup request black hole: Serve the static shell from bind time and let desktop start loading the renderer while the 150-280 ms runtime graph builds
  • Server process boot: Hub connector identity runtime (sequential store loads plus keychain) is built before the router attaches
  • Startup request black hole: HubConnectorLive (process lock plus identity runtime with ≥12 sequential file/keychain awaits) is built between listen() and handler attachment, widening the dead window for hub-enabled nodes
5

Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain
On large DBs: −0.4–2 s before routes are served and −0.5–1.4 s before the command gate; the first connect no longer triggers 2P+1 full shell snapshots
Effort
S–M
Evidence
Measured on a copy-scale synthetic DB and read-only on your DB

Boot loads the full command read model three times: engine init, a workspace.validate whose result is thrown away when the workspace is not restricted, and orphan-session reconcile. One of its queries filters activities by kind, which no index leads with, so it scans every row. On your 9.27 GB state.sqlite (563k activity rows, 470 matching) that takes 0.24 s warm and ~2 s cold on synchronous node:sqlite. The first subscribeShell forks reconcileAllWorktrees, which builds 2×P+1 full shell snapshots (53 for your 26 project roots). Every shell snapshot waits on 2 git spawns per project root (1-minute TTL). A new projector replays the entire event log one transaction per event: 50k events took 29 s before routes were served.

What to do

  • Add a migration with a kind-leading index on projection_thread_activities and drop the redundant prefix index, plus an EXPLAIN guard test. A partial index was used by the planner in one experiment and ignored in another, so confirm with EXPLAIN.
  • Check isRestricted before loading anything. Expose the engine's in-memory read model to reconcile and restart continuation.
  • Load rows once in reconcileAllWorktrees (narrow per-project queries), skip chat projects, and run it after the first snapshot has been served.
  • Persist repository identity in projection_projects with a .git/config fingerprint so snapshots become pure SQL. Use a targeted pending-goal query at startup.
  • Batch projector catch-up and filter by event type. Tune PRAGMAs (mmap, cache) only after a repeated A/B.
13 underlying findings
  • Server process boot: getCommandReadModel runs 3× per boot, and its actionable-activity query full-scans the activity table (0.24–2 s each on a real 9 GB DB, synchronous)
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: Boot loads the full command read model 3 times before the command gate (and once per page afterwards), although the engine already holds it in memory
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: No index leads with projection_thread_activities.kind: hydration, boot checkpoint-revert recovery and statistics full-scan the largest projection table
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: The first subscribeShell after boot forks reconcileAllWorktrees, which builds 2×P+1 full shell snapshots (P = projects and chats whose folders exist)
  • Loading projects: First subscribeShell starts a worktree reconciliation that loads 2 full shell snapshots per project (2P+1 total) plus 4 git spawns per project
  • Connection and state sync: First shell subscription forks worktree reconciliation that loads the full shell snapshot 1+2P times and spawns git per project
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: Repository identity (2 git spawns per project, 1-minute TTL, 1 s budget, chats included) blocks every shell snapshot, including the one built at boot
  • Loading projects: Repository identity is recomputed with 2 git spawns per project (60 s TTL) inside every shell snapshot and project lookup. A 1 s timeout silently nulls it and flips sidebar grouping
  • Server process boot: Startup reactors call getShellSnapshot, which spawns 2 git processes per project root (up to a 1 s budget) before the command gate opens
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: Projector catch-up replays one event per transaction and decodes every event even when no lagging projector consumes it: 50k events took 29 s before routes served
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: SQLite runs with default page cache (2 MB), no mmap, file temp store and no PRAGMA optimize on a database that grows to hundreds of MB
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: One synchronous connection on the main thread: heavy reads block the event loop and queue behind writes, and busy_timeout=5000 can freeze the loop for 5 s
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: getShellSnapshot is used as a generic lookup by about 30 server-internal call sites, each paying the full build plus git probes
6

Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain
−250–320 ms per launch from spawning earlier; −110 ms backend and −30 ms main from a V8 compile cache (measured on the installed app); fewer launches with cold renderer caches
Effort
S–M
Evidence
Measured on the installed 0.1.31 app + your logs

desktopEntry synchronously requires the 2.27 MB desktopMain.cjs (~175 ms). It contains the whole Hub/E2EE stack, the contracts barrel, effect and electron-updater. Next come menus, protocols, the updater, a port probe, IPC and computer-use; then the window is created, and only after that is the backend spawned, ~320 ms after process start. Neither main nor the backend uses a V8 compile cache, whereas T3 Code Nightly does. The renderer origin follows the first free port from 3773, which is also T3 Code's default. About 5.6% of launches flip origin: they start with cold HTTP and V8 caches, and drafts seem to vanish because localStorage is origin-scoped.

What to do

  • Move a dependency-free backend launcher into desktopEntry and spawn before requiring desktopMain. The trivial first step, spawning before new BrowserWindow, saves ~37 ms.
  • Call module.enableCompileCache in desktopEntry. Pass --require compileCache.cjs (or set NODE_COMPILE_CACHE) for the backend and the MCP/stdio children, and call flushCompileCache after startup.
  • Persist the last bound port and use a Ryco-specific default port. Longer term, load from the registered ryco:// origin so renderer work overlaps backend boot.
  • Lazy-load the Hub/E2EE and updater modules in main. Make the shell-env cache stale-while-revalidate: the current 7-day TTL blocks the spawn once a week and can drop PATH when capture fails.
9 underlying findings
  • Desktop cold boot: Backend spawns ~320 ms after process start; spawn it from desktopEntry before loading the 2.27 MB main bundle
  • Desktop cold boot: No V8 compile cache for the Electron main process or the backend child (T3 Code ships one)
  • Desktop cold boot: Electron main eagerly loads the whole Hub/E2EE/relay stack, the contracts barrel, effect and electron-updater before 'ready'
  • Desktop cold boot: Renderer origin follows the first free port from 3773, which T3 Code also uses; origin flips split caches and localStorage
  • Desktop cold boot: Renderer cannot fetch or parse any app JS until the backend listens; the ryco:// origin with codeCache is registered but unused
  • Desktop cold boot: Shell-env cache has a hard 7-day TTL with a blocking refresh before backend spawn
  • Desktop cold boot: Sync main-thread work before the window and spawn: duplicate dock icon, LaunchServices write, PlistBuddy, sync log sink
  • Desktop cold boot: Main window uses the default v8CacheOptions; after each update, code cache kicks in only on the 3rd launch
  • Desktop cold boot: Synchronous IPC for local environment bootstrap on every node HTTP URL and in ChatView render
7

Server cold start: compilation, imports and the login shell

Expected gain
−160–200 ms per web/CLI boot (sync login shell); −60–84 ms (compile cache); −50 ms (@pierre/diffs subpath); −28 ms and −25 MiB (lazy sharp); −50 MiB idle RSS
Effort
S
Evidence
Measured (CPU profiles, A/B runs)

In web/CLI/headless mode, fixPath runs execFileSync of an interactive login shell before any layer is built. That takes 160–200 ms with a light .zshrc and ~0.6 s more with a slow one. Interactive zsh ignores SIGTERM, so the 5 s timeout cannot stop a hanging rc file (measured 8 s). About 800 modules (16.9 MiB) are compiled on every boot without a cache. Diffs.ts imports the @pierre/diffs root (263 modules including shiki) for a single parser, and sharp is loaded eagerly for avatars. Idle RSS is 340–360 MiB, ~50 MiB of which is an inflated young generation.

What to do

  • Reuse the desktop's shell-environment cache and worker (SIGKILL, 1.5 s, cwd = home) on the server. Apply the cached PATH synchronously and refresh after listen.
  • Ship a tiny bin.mjs shim that enables the compile cache before importing the real module graph.
  • Import @pierre/diffs/utils/parsePatchFiles and lazy-load sharp. Put Codex/ACP schemas, computer use, hub E2EE, source-control providers and CLI admin commands behind dynamic imports.
  • Drop the unused CJS build (10 MiB). Strip JSDoc and escape non-ASCII, because bin.mjs is currently held as a 15.9 MiB two-byte string. Pass --max-semi-space-size=16.
8 underlying findings
  • Server process boot: Synchronous interactive login shell blocks the event loop at every web/CLI boot, and its timeout cannot stop a hanging .zshrc
  • Server process boot: Enable the V8 compile cache for the backend (desktop and CLI)
  • Server process boot: `@pierre/diffs` root import pulls shiki/oniguruma/hast (263 modules) into boot for a single parser
  • Server process boot: sharp (native libvips) loads at every boot but is only used for avatars and thumbnails
  • Server process boot: About 4.7 MiB of the 8.1 MiB bin.mjs is feature or protocol code evaluated at boot (Codex/ACP schemas, computer use, hub E2EE, source-control providers)
  • Server process boot: Server build: bundle effect and pure-JS deps, strip JSDoc/escape non-ASCII, stop emitting the unused CJS build
  • Server process boot: Idle RSS of 340–360 MiB: V8 young generation grows to 128 MiB during boot and never shrinks
  • Desktop cold boot: app.asar ships an unused CJS server build and duplicate helper binaries (~45 MiB)
8

New thread and the first turn

Expected gain
Claude first token −2.0–2.3 s with a warm session (estimate); title/branch generation −4 CPU-s and −1.1 GiB each; checkpoint capture 820 → 118 ms (measured); −35–120 ms per turn from listSessions
Effort
S–L
Evidence
Measured (CLI cold starts, checkpoint bench, real trace)

'New thread' awaits a full getConfig (85–131 KB) and then project preferences before it navigates. On Send, a cold Claude session pays for the CLI boot (2.30–2.38 s with your setting sources, 0.30 s without) before the prompt is consumed. Sessions are reaped after 5 minutes idle, so returning threads go cold again. The first turn forks title and branch-name generation as full-config CLIs (MCP servers, plugins, tools; ~1.3 GiB peak each) right next to the session boot. The first-turn checkpoint baseline builds a fresh temp index with no stat data, so git add -A rehashes every file (1.36 s of a 1.49 s capture in your trace). sendTurn does not wait for that baseline, which is a correctness race. ProviderService.listSessions runs 1+N queries over all 701 historical bindings, about 6× per turn start.

What to do

  • Navigate first using the cached per-environment config, and apply project preferences when they arrive (keep the hosted-node freshness guard).
  • Run text generation in the existing side-question light mode, merge title and branch into one call, and start it after the first delta.
  • Seed the checkpoint temp index from the real index (clear assume-unchanged/skip-worktree on the copy). Create or join the baseline before sendTurn, and use a per-thread checkpoint worker.
  • Use a targeted getSessionForThread instead of listSessions, and targeted thread queries in CheckpointReactor.
  • For pre-warming, first keep the open thread's session alive past the reaper. Full speculative pre-warm is L effort and costs memory.
  • Stop invalidating the source-control discovery cache on every composer mount; it re-runs gh/glab auth checks (0.8–1.5 s).
11 underlying findings
  • New thread, open, switch: 'New thread' waits for a full getConfig (85–131 KB) and then getProjectPreferences before it navigates
  • Send → first token: Pre-warm the provider session (Claude CLI / Codex thread) before Send, with an idle TTL
  • Send → first token: Title and branch-name generation spawn full-config provider CLIs alongside the session boot
  • Send → first token: Seed the checkpoint temp index from the real index instead of `read-tree HEAD` (7x faster capture)
  • Send → first token: sendTurn does not wait for the pre-turn baseline (correctness), and the CheckpointReactor is one global serial queue
  • Send → first token: ProviderService.listSessions scans every historical binding (1 + N queries) and runs ≥6 times per turn start
  • Send → first token: CheckpointReactor loads the full thread detail 3x per turn start (plus a fully redundant turn.started path) and enqueues streaming deltas into its global queue
  • Send → first token: Worktree-mode first send: full-remote fetch, worktree add, client RPCs and dispatches run serially before the turn exists
  • New thread, open, switch: Composer mount triggers source-control discovery, and the server's 'discover' RPC discards its cache and re-runs gh/glab auth checks (network)
  • New thread, open, switch: Branch list is fetched twice on first mount and again on every thread switch (~7 git processes each)
  • Send → first token: Per-turn attachment-instructions prefix turns '/compact' and every Claude slash command into a plain prompt
9

Statistics: memoize, aggregate incrementally, never block the server

Expected gain
Usage tab 2.5–8.2 s per open → <100 ms on reopen; Activity tab whole-server stall of 2.6–8.5 s → milliseconds; SQL fix −1.4 s warm / −1.8 s cold
Effort
S–L
Evidence
Measured on your real data (read-only)

getUsageSummary rebuilds everything on every open. It synchronously parses and decodes a 22 MB scan cache. If pricing is older than 24 h, it blocks on a 2.75 MB LiteLLM download, which is retried on every open while offline (up to 10 s). It scans sources one after another, re-prices all 228.7k records, and rewrites the full 22 MB cache. The Activity tab runs six synchronous queries inside a transaction on the only DB connection: 2.6 s warm / 8.5 s cold on your DB, stalling provider ingestion and every client. Its NOT EXISTS lookup cannot use its expression index because of type affinity. Correctness problems: cached records count toward the 100k scan limit, so Codex 90d/all is already silently truncated and Claude 30d (the default view) is close. Loading /statistics directly shows 'No usage environments are connected' forever.

What to do

Sidebar and projects: stop running the full VCS pipeline per row

Expected gain
First sidebar render with ~30 visible folders: ~1,000–1,300 child processes → ~0–30; project icons: ~0.9 s of child processes per connect → ~0
Effort
M–L
Evidence
Spawn counts measured by emulation and code trace

Every visible thread row with a branch subscribes to the full VCS status stream for its folder, only to show a branch name and a PR badge. The local status alone is ~20 git spawns. The remote status then runs a network git fetch (even with polling at its default of 0), a second full local status, config reads and a heavy gh pr list. That is ≈40 processes per feature-branch folder. Base-branch resolution runs twice per status. Project icons spawn one Node/Electron child per project per connection, with no server cache. There is no process-wide concurrency limit. Background git status runs without GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0, so it takes .git/index.lock while agents run git in the same worktree (a reliability problem).

What to do

  • Add a lean sidebar summary stream {refName, pr, provider}: read HEAD from the gitdir, and take the PR from persisted worktree links or a single lean PR index per repo.
  • Add a RepoFacts cache per gitCommonDir. Serve remote status from tracking refs, and fetch in the background only for the focused thread.
  • Cache icons on the server, keyed by root + mtimes (keep the kill-able child for cloud files), and put an iconRevision in the shell.
  • Add a ProcessGovernor with interactive and background lanes, set GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 on all read paths, and use one combined rev-parse for repo detection.

  • Loading projects: Local status resolves the base branch twice and does one spawn per config/ref lookup; remote status recomputes the whole local status

  • Live browser measurements: Each project icon spawns a new Node child process and is resolved twice per load (HTTP fallback before config, then RPC)
  • Loading projects: No process-wide concurrency limit or priority for git/gh/glab child processes
  • Loading projects: Background `git status` reads run without GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0, so they rewrite `.git/index` and take `index.lock` while agents run git in the same worktree
  • Loading projects: VCS repository detection runs three sequential `git rev-parse` processes and caches the result for only 2 s

Measured pure derivations; end-to-end trace pending

The Sidebar subscribes to the whole environmentStateById, which gets a new identity on every WebSocket event, and builds a new grouping-settings object on every render (the React Compiler does not compile Sidebar). Every commit therefore re-runs grouping, sorting and composeSidebarTree for every project, plus the inbox model.   • Compose the tree in a single pass and render only the active sidebar mode (or use <Activity mode="hidden">). Fix the React Compiler bailouts (render-time ref writes) and make useSettings subscribe per selector.

Expected gain

Evidence
Measured (CDP frames) + code-verified

The WebSocket connect starts in a passive effect after the lazy RootAppShell graph (533 KiB gzip) has loaded and committed, even though the connection code is already in the boot graph. ServerConfig (113–130 KB) is sent twice at boot (subscription snapshot plus a parallel getConfig) and fetched again by Statistics, Projects and New thread. A second /ws/device socket runs device.list on every connect (xcode-select, xcodebuild, simctl ×2).   • Open the device channel lazily on the first device surface, cache iOS availability, and dedupe the simctl calls.
  • Make server pipelines chunk-preserving (Stream.mapArrayEffect) with a per-chunk byte cap; the client applies one array per commit.
  • Shell snapshot: drop the redundant whole-snapshot decode and page it (the 4 MiB relay limit is hit at ≈3,200 threads).

S–M
Evidence
Measured switch timings; window sizes from your DB

Split panes key each pane by thread, so every switch remounts the whole ChatView (Lexical, LegendList, header). That also disabled the older useDeferredValue timeline deferral. A thread's history is requested only from a passive effect after mount, and until it arrives existing threads render the new-thread hero. Up to 6 sibling windows are requested before the active thread's own window. Windows carry full activity payloads (80–95% of bytes; up to 5 MiB on your DB), which exceeds the 4 MiB hosted relay cap and then falls back permanently to the unbounded legacy subscription. Each subscription polls Codex history every 30 s, spawning codex app-server and loading the full thread detail.

What to do

  • Use a stable pane key when the layout is not split. Quick win: useDeferredValue(threadId, null).
  • Retain the detail subscription at navigation intent or in a route loader, and show the hero only once detail has loaded.
  • Schedule sibling prefetch at idle, after the active window has landed.
  • Bound windows by bytes, with activity previews and an on-demand payload RPC. Never fall back to the legacy subscription on size errors.
  • Make history recovery event-driven with backoff, check cheap preconditions before loading detail, and use a pooled app-server.
  • Fix the retained-bytes estimate that never decays (one busy thread evicts every idle cached thread).

Side panels: terminal, diff, files

Expected gain
Non-diff panels stop spawning 3 workers (~6.6 MB); −608 KiB of dead WASM per worker; −432 KB of WebSocket traffic per connect per running terminal; terminal prompt ~1,058 → ~650–700 ms
Effort
S–M
Evidence
Measured (Playwright, worker heap via CDP)

LazyRightPanel wraps every mode in DiffWorkerPoolProvider, so opening the terminal or the files tab spawns 3 diff workers. They are torn down 360 ms after close, so grammars are cold on every reopen. The worker is built as an IIFE with an inlined Oniguruma WASM (608 KiB) that is never used, because the JS regex engine is selected. subscribeTerminalEvents replays the full scrollback of every running terminal on every connect (75% of boot WebSocket bytes measured). Those replays reopen closed drawers, and combined histories over 4 MiB cause a deterministic resync loop every 250 ms. The PTY spawns only after chunk load, reveal and xterm fit, and every reopen downloads the history again. While any shell is alive, the server runs ps over the whole process table every second.

What to do

  • Provide the worker pool only for review and PRs, as an app-lifetime ref-counted pool with an idle grace period. Set worker.format: 'es', and optionally switch to the WASM engine.
  • Make replay snapshots metadata-only and mark them as replay, add backoff for resync errors, and keep xterm instances in a small LRU.
  • Start terminal.open on click or shortcut, before the chunk resolves (not on hover until the replay handling is fixed).
  • Detect foreground processes instead of polling ps, and persist history append-only.

  • Terminal, diff, files panels: Every connect and reconnect streams the full scrollback of every running terminal, then terminal.open sends it again
  • Terminal, diff, files panels: Initial terminal snapshots share the 4 MiB subscriber byte budget, so large combined histories cause a deterministic resync loop every 250 ms
  • Terminal, diff, files panels: Connect-time snapshot replay is treated as a fresh terminal start: it reopens closed drawers and switches the active terminal on every connect or reconnect
  • Terminal, diff, files panels: PTY spawn waits for chunk load, reveal and xterm fit, so shell rc startup is serialized after all client work
  • Terminal, diff, files panels: Closing the drawer or switching panel tabs disposes xterm; every reopen re-downloads and re-parses the whole scrollback
  • Terminal, diff, files panels: No intent or idle preload for panel chunks or data; with modulePreload off, the chunk graph is a 3-level waterfall
  • Terminal, diff, files panels: Terminal server spawns `ps` over the whole system every second and rewrites the full history file every 40 ms under output
  • Terminal, diff, files panels: Client checkpoint-diff store keeps every viewed patch forever (keepAlive atoms, no eviction at refCount 0)

Expected gain

Effort
S–M
Evidence
Measured with the real WorkspaceEntries layer

The workspace file index lives in a cache with a 15 s TTL counted from build time and no stale-while-revalidate, and it is invalidated after every turn. Most '@' lookups therefore block on a rebuild: 3 rev-parse calls, ls-files, K sequential check-ignore chunks and ~100 ms of synchronous JS at 60k files. The 25k cap is applied after an alphabetical sort, so in a 60k-file repo ~66% of files cannot be found. A bare '@' sends nothing and says 'No matching files'. The '#' picker requests the heaviest PR field set plus a stack-summary GraphQL call.

What to do

  • Use a stale-while-revalidate index store with single-flight rebuilds and in-place patches on writes. Replace check-ignore with a parallel ls-files -ci.
  • Separate the corpus cap from the payload cap, and show truncated in the menu.
  • Prewarm on '@' with an empty query, and show indexing and error states.
  • Use a lean field set for the picker and one canonical list per (cwd, state), and scope the post-turn invalidation to the affected cwd.

  • Composer @ and # menus: Index build pipes every listed path through sequential `git check-ignore` chunks; one parallel `ls-files -ci` gives the identical set
  • Composer @ and # menus: The 25,000-entry cap is applied after an alphabetical sort, so most files in large repos can never be found (correctness)

  • Composer @ and # menus: Every turn completion force-refetches the last '@' query of each mounted composer (all environments), so the server rebuilds the file index even when the menu is closed

Connecting to a Hub

Expected gain
−1 RTT per cold start/resume (session + directory in parallel); HostedHubRoot load removed from the connect path (est. 150–400 ms on phones); one establishment per relay drop instead of two (−200–550 ms)
Effort
M–L
Evidence
Code trace + micro-benchmarks (no hosted build measured live)

A hosted cold start takes ~9–10 sequential browser↔Hub round trips plus 3–4 Hub↔node round trips (≈0.9 s at 50 ms RTT, ≈2.4 s at 150 ms on a phone; estimates). Session restore and the directory fetch run serially. The relay connect is started from effects in the 570 KiB-gzip HostedHubRoot chunk, which loads only after bootstrap. A separate ticket POST precedes every connect. On every relay drop the transport reconnects and then the client is rebuilt, costing a second ticket, handshake and full snapshot. All E2EE crypto is pure-JS noble on the main thread (~25 ms cold on desktop); on the node, node:crypto would be 6–30× faster. On black-holed networks, the boot gate can hold the loading surface for 30–60 s.

What to do

  • Inside the single lifecycle owner: fetch listNodes in parallel with restoreSession, prefetch HostedHubRoot during bootstrap, and start the orchestrator/coordinator from the boot gate.
  • Adopt the reconnected channel instead of rebuilding the client, or let only the controller reconnect.
  • Add Hub-session protocol v2 so tickets are minted on the socket. Use short boot-phase deadlines and a 5 s liveness probe on foreground/online.
  • Prewarm noble or add a WebCrypto fast path (needs crypto review), use node-native AEAD on the server, and consider compress-then-encrypt only after a security review.

Several of these touch the hosted lifecycle boundaries in AGENTS.md and need owner/security sign-off.

13 underlying findings
  • Connecting to a Hub: Every in-session relay drop establishes the relay twice (probe reconnect, then full client rebuild)
  • Connecting to a Hub: Session restore and directory fetch run serially on every cold start and every foreground resume; the Hub-session socket opens only afterwards
  • Connecting to a Hub: Relay connect waits for the 570 KiB-gzip HostedHubRoot chunk graph, which starts loading only after bootstrap finishes
  • Connecting to a Hub: Every connect and reconnect needs a separate HTTP ticket round trip although the Hub-session socket is already authenticated
  • Connecting to a Hub: Client NX handshake runs cold, pure-JS noble X25519/Ed25519 on the main thread, about 25 ms on desktop V8 for the first connect
  • Connecting to a Hub: Server/desktop relay E2EE uses noble where node:crypto is 6-30x faster for the identical algorithms
  • Connecting to a Hub: No payload compression on the relay; E2EE makes transport-level deflate useless
  • Connecting to a Hub: Boot gate can hold the loading surface for 30-60 s on a stalled network (30 s deadline, directory awaited)
  • Connecting to a Hub: A silently dead Hub-session socket takes up to 45 s to detect; foreground and online signals skip 'healthy' states
  • Connecting to a Hub: SW install precaches ~7.3 MiB gzip at boot, refetches everything on every deploy, and the PWA boot document has no boot shell
  • Connecting to a Hub: Hosted connections never use shell-sequence resume, so every reconnect or resume re-downloads the full shell
  • Connecting to a Hub: Connects to nodes that send no E2EE carrier pay a fixed 1.5 s T_ADV wait before any RPC flows, on every connect and reconnect
  • Web bootstrap waterfall: Hosted Hub boot: three sequential dynamic imports, then 2 Hub RTTs, then the 1.8 MiB HostedHubRoot download, then the reveal throttle

Mobile app cold start

Expected gain
−6,094 of 8,557 eagerly evaluated modules (−71%) from Tabler deep imports; direct-only users skip a Ryco Cloud round trip (30 s worst case); hosted gate −1 RTT
Effort
S–M
Evidence
Static graph analysis; not measured on a device

Metro runs with Expo's defaults (no inline requires, no tree shaking), so every static import is evaluated before the first frame. That is 8,557 modules, 6,189 of them Tabler icons pulled in through the root barrel for 91 icons in use. All screens, the shiki grammars (~0.8 MB of JSON.parse) and the E2EE stack are eager as well. The access gate waits for both planes: direct-only users wait for a Hub bootstrap-status probe, and hosted users also wait for listNodes. HomeScreen rebuilds the inbox and projects models ~30× per second while scrolling.

What to do

  • Use deep icon imports plus a lint rule, and split AppSymbol per platform.
  • Unlock the gate as soon as either plane grants access, skip the Hub probe when no token is stored, and unlock the hosted plane on authenticated.
  • Add a lazyScreen helper, load shiki grammars lazily, enable the React Compiler, memoize home data and keep the scroll offset in a ref.
  • Skip snapshot capture when the persisted slices are unchanged (Hermes uses a pure-JS TextEncoder polyfill).
10 underlying findings
  • Mobile cold start: Root-barrel Tabler imports evaluate 6,185 icon modules at startup to use 91 icons
  • Mobile cold start: Direct-only users cannot see their workspace until a Ryco Cloud bootstrap-status request finishes (up to 30 s)
  • Mobile cold start: Hosted users see a logo until restoreSession AND listNodes finish; offline launches show sign-in instead of the cached workspace
  • Mobile cold start: HomeScreen rebuilds inbox+projects models and re-renders all rows on every scroll event and every store change
  • Mobile cold start: All 25+ screens (and the locked-stack identity/camera/webview screens) are statically imported and evaluated at launch
  • Mobile cold start: Shiki core, JS regex engine and 7 grammars (~0.8 MB JSON.parse) are evaluated at startup
  • Mobile cold start: Every projection change triggers a full-environment JSON.stringify + double UTF-8 encode + SQLite write 500 ms later
  • Mobile cold start: React Compiler is enabled for web but not for the mobile app, leaving hand-written memoization fragile
  • Mobile cold start: Relay E2EE stack (noble curves/ciphers/hashes, cborg, relayE2ee*) is pulled into the pre-first-frame graph by the authorization barrel, partly just for a 5-line account-id validator
  • Mobile cold start: Every direct cold connect pays a GET /api/auth/session RTT (and up to 3 keychain reads) before requesting the ws-token

Background I/O: logs and traces

Expected gain
Provider logs defaulting to lifecycle/off: −486 MB/day of disk writes and ~4 GB freed; canonical log −43% typically / −90% in workflow bursts; trace file −75% (SQL text spans)
Effort
S–M
Evidence
Measured on your install (read-only)

Every provider event is written twice (native + canonical), with no off switch and no total budget: 4.1 GB in 689 files on your install, and none old enough for the 30-day sweep. The canonical stream embeds the full native message in every derived event, so during workflow bursts rotation keeps only ~5 minutes of history. Each record costs an open/write/close. Under load the server trace file writes ~1 GB/h, 75% of it sql.execute spans with the full query text. Expected failures are logged as full stack traces in hot retry loops: 26k history-recovery warnings, and 1.7k stacks from deleted worktree directories that are never marked removed. Diagnostics tails two files that nothing writes.

What to do

  • Add a providerEventLogs setting (default 'lifecycle' in packaged builds), an hourly byte-budget sweep, and gzip for rotated files.
  • Drop raw.payload from derived events, coalesce native deltas, and use a held file handle with batched writev.
  • Sample or normalize SQL spans, add log-once helpers, and mark missing checkouts removed once.
10 underlying findings
  • Logs and traces: Provider event logging is always on, has no off switch and no total-size budget, and nothing in the app reads it (4.1 GB on disk; Diagnostics reads a file that never exists)
  • Logs and traces: Canonical log embeds the full native message in every runtime event (11x the native bytes; 87-95% of the canonical file is a copy of the native log)
  • Logs and traces: AsyncRotatingFileSink opens, writes and closes the file once per record, and records are awaited one by one (12-29x more main-thread time than a held handle)
  • Logs and traces: Expected failures in hot retry loops are logged as full stack traces and dominate server-child.log and desktop-main.log
  • Logs and traces: Worktrees whose checkout directory was deleted outside Ryco are never marked removed, so every source-control refresh re-probes them and logs a ~2.8 KB stack trace
  • Desktop cold boot: The desktop backend's local trace file writes ~280 KB/s under agent load, 75% of it full SQL text spans
  • Logs and traces: Native log writes one ~700 B envelope per streaming delta that carries ~9 B of content (1.2% useful); deltas are 14-58% of native bytes
  • Logs and traces: Shared native and canonical loggers are never closed: the last batch is lost on quit, writers are never evicted, and the queue bound counts records instead of bytes
  • Logs and traces: Electron main writes backend stdout/stderr and its own console with synchronous appendFileSync (3 sync writes per console chunk)
  • SQLite and snapshots at boot: Small boot and runtime overheads: N+1 orphan-chat sweep, and every SQL statement exported as a roughly 1 KB trace span

Make startup measurable

Expected gain
Turns today's blind spots (main-module load, time to a usable shell, snapshot decode, paint) into per-launch numbers and CI budgets
Effort

Evidence
Code-verified

Desktop startup timing starts after desktopMain's requires and stops at did-finish-load, before the app's own JS has run. Renderer marks are collected only behind an env flag, and primary-shell-usable is marked before render and paint. Even so, the always-on desktop logs were enough to reconstruct p50/p90 for 430 real launches.

What to do

  • Add desktop.entry.start and shell-usable marks reported through preload, and send server startup phases over fd 4.
  • Add a perf:boot-report script that reads user logs (the parsers already exist in .perf-research/desktop-boot/).
  • Use a realistic 30-project / 2,000-thread fixture, dist-based bundle budgets, and React Profiler commit-count tests.
3 underlying findings
  • Desktop cold boot: Startup timing misses main-module load and time-to-usable-shell; proposed measurement plan
  • Main-thread CPU at boot: Startup marks miss decode and paint; no reproducible boot or streaming CPU benchmark at realistic scale
  • Web bootstrap waterfall: Bundle guard only greps route source text; transitive regressions (+32% boot, +50% ChatRightPanel) went unnoticed

A. Cold boot

Desktop cold boot 17 findings · 3 high · 5 medium · 9 low

Everything runs in sequence. The backend is spawned ~320 ms after process start, the renderer cannot load app code until the backend listens, and in your real launches the backend needs p50 1.6 s / p90 12.3 s to listen.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

Packaged desktop cold boot today runs strictly in sequence. desktopEntry.ts synchronously requires the 2.27 MB desktopMain.cjs, which pulls in the effect barrel, rpc, undici, electron-updater, the full @ryco/contracts barrel and the whole Hub/E2EE/relay stack. I measured about 175 ms for this in the installed 0.1.31 binary, and none of it shows up in startup timing. After ready, main builds the menu and protocols, sets up the updater, probes the port through an Effect runtime, registers IPC and starts the computer-use bridge. Only then does it create the window, which loads the boot shell (desktop-boot.html over file://) and is revealed at p50 195 ms. After that it reads the shell-env cache and spawns the backend (process.execPath bin.mjs --bootstrap-fd 3, ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE, no compile cache). The spawn happens about 320 ms after the main script starts. Readiness comes from matching "Listening on http://" in stdout, raced against a 100 ms HTTP poll. Once the backend is ready, the window navigates cross-site to http://127.0.0.1:PORT. Only at that point does the renderer start fetching and parsing the 2 MB boot graph and the RootAppShell. Hosted-identity/Hub resume also starts only after the backend is ready.

I parsed the user's real logs (~/.ryco/userdata/logs, 430 single-spawn launches since Sep 5 and 417 backend sessions). Almost all of the time is spent in the backend before it listens. Launch to backend listening is p50 1.8 s and p90 12.5 s; app did-finish-load is p50 1.9 s and p90 14.6 s. 17 of the last 30 sessions took more than 5 s. In those sessions the four drivers that run resolveProviderMaintenanceCapabilitiesEffect (sync PATH stat plus async realpath) all finish within about 30 ms of each other after 3–15 s, while copilot and opencode finish in about 50 ms. That pattern points to a shared stall (libuv threadpool or event loop); Dropbox-backed project roots timing out git at the same time support that. Migrations also took 9.5 s and 27 s on two boots against the 9.27 GB state.sqlite. One more thing came up: a deterministic "schema newer than binary" failure caused 266 backend respawns in one day while the window sat on the splash.

Desktop-only wins: spawn the backend before loading the main bundle (−250–320 ms), add a V8 compile cache for backend and main (measured −110 ms and −30 ms), keep the renderer origin stable (port 3773 collides with T3 Code; three origins are already in the caches and localStorage), lazy-load the Hub/E2EE graph, stop the fatal crash loop, start Hub resume in parallel, and replace stdout readiness matching with a structured signal over fd 4. The structural option is to load the app from the already-registered ryco:// origin so renderer work overlaps backend boot. The biggest real-world lever is still server-side: the listener should not wait behind provider and migration stalls.

Part of Priority 3: Bound shutdown and crash handling

Expected gain

Turns an infinite splash plus 266 futile respawns per day into an immediate, actionable error; ~0.4 s CPU saved per avoided respawn

What happens today

Every exit before readiness calls scheduleBackendRestart, with backoff of 500 ms doubling to 10 s and no attempt cap. The readiness failure is only written to the log (main.ts:1484), so the boot shell spins indefinitely. The server exits with code 1 for every error (bin.ts:51), so the desktop cannot tell fatal from transient. Real logs: 291 'exited before logging readiness (code=1)'; 266 on 2026-10-06 alone, all 'Database schema 77 is newer than this binary supports (76)'. That error is deterministic after a downgrade, and each retry costs ~400 ms of module load plus opening a 9.27 GB DB.

Proposal

Server: exit with distinct codes, e.g. 78 (EX_CONFIG) for non-retryable startup errors such as schema-too-new or invalid config and 75 for retryable ones. Also write {type:'fatal',code,message} on the fd-4 duplex before exiting. Desktop: stop restarting on fatal codes or after 3 consecutive pre-listen failures, and show an error state in the boot window (load an error page or pass the message to desktop-boot.html) with Retry / Open logs / Quit. Keep the backoff only for crashes that happen after readiness.

Verifier (Confirmed)

The code is as described. Every pre-listen exit calls scheduleBackendRestart (main.ts:2754-2774 → 2622-2632). The backoff is 500 ms doubling to a 10 s cap with no attempt limit (main.ts:443-446, backendRestartBackoff.ts:27-38), and it resets only after successful readiness (main.ts:1378). The failure is only logged (1484-1487). bin.ts:49-52 exits 1 for every expected error, and the schema-too-new message is at Migrations.ts:567. The counts need correcting. Each exit writes 'exited before logging readiness' twice (the writeDesktopLogHeader at 1484 plus the console.warn at 1487, captured to the same log), so the 290 lines are 145 actual respawns: 133 on 2026-10-06 and 12 on 10-05, across 6 app runs, 117 of them at the 10 s cap. server-child.log.1 has 145 'Database schema 77 is newer than this binary supports (76)' lines. main.ts:620-622 already documents an earlier restart loop of the same kind (VITE_DEV_SERVER_URL), so this class of failure recurs.

Part of Priority 6: Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain

~250–320 ms off every launch's time-to-app (p50 1.92 s, ~15%); ~37 ms from the spawn-before-createWindow reorder alone

What happens today

Today's order: require(desktopMain.cjs) (~175 ms measured) → top-level eval → ready (p50 76 ms after the launch mark) → whenReady sync steps (p50 24 ms) → await port probe → exposure → registerIpcHandlers → await computerUseRuntime.start() → createWindow (window.create→spawn p50 37 / p90 60 ms) → shell-env cache → spawn (ready→spawn p50 69 / p90 107 ms). The backend is the critical path (spawn→listening p50 1.59 s), yet it starts about 175+76+69 ≈ 320 ms after the main script starts. None of its inputs need Electron 'ready': port probe (net), token (crypto), settings and shell-env cache (fs), spawn(process.execPath). Only the envelope's computerUseBridge binding (main.ts:2695) depends on later work. The server reads the envelope with a 1000 ms timeout, starting after its ~550 ms module load.

Proposal

Move a dependency-free backend launcher (node:net/child_process/fs/crypto only) into desktopEntry.ts. It reads desktop-settings plus the shell-env cache, resolves the port (persisted port first), spawns process.execPath [--require compileCache.cjs] bin.mjs --bootstrap-fd 3 with fd3 left open, then requires desktopMain and hands it {child, port, token}. desktopMain writes the envelope once the computer-use bridge is listening, or the bridge binding moves out of the envelope into a control-token call. Raise readBootstrapEnvelope's timeout to ~10 s when --bootstrap-fd is explicit, so a late envelope can never fall back to a non-desktop boot. In whenReady, create the boot window before menu/protocol/updater/computer-use. Do the trivial part now: spawn before new BrowserWindow (saves window.create→spawn p50 37 ms on its own). Also move requestSingleInstanceLock into desktopEntry so refused second instances exit before loading 2.27 MB.

Verifier (Confirmed)

The order checks out. desktopEntry.ts:30 synchronously requires desktopMain.cjs (2,269,362 bytes in the installed asar). bootstrap() at main.ts:4027-4116 then runs port probe → applyDesktopServerExposureMode → registerIpcHandlers → await computerUseRuntime.start() (4094) → ensurePackagedBootstrapWindowOpen (4104) → shell env (4106) → startBackend (4107). The log stats reproduce: ready p50 76, bootstrap.start 101, window.create 109, backend.spawn 145 ms, all measured from the desktop.launch mark. On the latest launch window.create→spawn was 31 ms. I re-measured the desktopMain require with main-load-cost.cjs at 373–422 ms (load avg ≈10 on 18 cores); the investigator got 172–185 ms on a quieter machine. So the saving is at least the claimed 250–320 ms, and more on a busy machine. The envelope inputs really are Electron-independent: applyDesktopServerExposureMode (main.ts:1094-1135) only uses OS.networkInterfaces and settings, and only computerUseRuntime.backendBinding() (2695) needs later work. Risks: readBootstrapEnvelope defaults to a 1000 ms timeout (bootstrap.ts:26), and two places would own the spawn args, so put them in one shared launcher module. Moving requestSingleInstanceLock up needs app.setPath('userData') to go first (main.ts:3971-3992).

Prior work

none. Commit 099bea0bd added the boot shell but kept backend spawn after window creation and computer-use start.

Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

p90 time-to-app ~14.6 s → ~2 s if stalls stop gating the listener; p50 ~1.9 s → ~1.2–1.4 s with listener-first boot (estimate)

What happens today

MEASURED from the user's installed app logs. Launch→backend.listening is p50 1808 / p90 12545 ms and app did-finish-load p50 1920 / p90 14618 ms (n=430). 17 of the last 30 backend sessions took >5 s to listen. In 47 of 417 sessions a provider registry entry took >5 s (p90: codex 8082, claudeAgent 8210, cursor 7425, grok 7533, against copilot 76 and opencode 515 ms). In slow sessions grok/cursor/codex/claude complete within ~30 ms of each other after 3–15 s (2026-10-10: 12129–12167 ms) while copilot/opencode finished at ~50 ms. Exactly those four drivers call resolveProviderMaintenanceCapabilitiesEffect during create(). That function does a sync resolveCommandPath (statSync+accessSync across 41 PATH entries) and then an async fileSystem.realPath on the libuv threadpool. The simultaneous release points to a shared queue (a 4-thread libuv pool saturated by stuck fs or DNS work, or an event-loop block). In the same window on 2026-10-06, git on Dropbox-backed project roots timed out after 5000 ms and there was a 12 s gap before 'Agent Control MCP listener started'. Other stalls: migrations took 9.5 s and 27.4 s (pr_terminal_at repair) on a 9.27 GB state.sqlite with 1.6M events. The HTTP listener only binds after the whole layer graph, including the initial provider reconcile, so the window shows the splash for the entire stall.

Proposal

(1) Desktop, S: in backendChildEnv set UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=32 when unset, so a few stuck File-Provider fs calls or DNS lookups cannot starve all async fs. (2) Server, M: never await PATH/realpath probing in driver.create(). Compute maintenance capabilities lazily inside the provider-check fiber and make resolveCommandPath async with a timeout. (3) Server, M/L: bind the HTTP listener (static assets, auth/session, health) before the provider registry reconcile and other heavy layers, keeping RPC/WS behind the existing startup command gate. This first needs the EVIDENCE 'request hangs before Listening' bug fixed, so early requests are queued instead of dropped. (4) Run one-time repairs or migrations that scan big tables after listen, behind a visible 'upgrading data' state. (5) Instrument the first 30 s: perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay plus a threadpool canary (fs.stat(os.tmpdir()) every 100 ms), logging 'startup stall' with the phase in flight, to confirm the root cause.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

I re-ran the investigator's parse-server-boot.mjs on server-child.log{,.1,.2} and the distribution reproduces: 400 sessions, listen p50 1689 / p90 13849 ms, 47 sessions with a provider over 5 s, and 17 of the last 30 sessions over 5 s. On 2026-10-10T16:01 grok/cursor/codex/claudeAgent finished at 12129/12156/12152/12167 ms while copilot and opencode took 50/54 ms. Migration stalls are also real (9889 ms on 10-02, 27442 ms on 10-04). The listener does sit behind the layer graph: in the server log 'startup command gate ready' appears at 18:01:37.781 and 'Listening on' at 37.827 (server.ts:599-606 httpListeningLayer, serverRuntimeStartup.ts:1031). The root-cause attribution is wrong, though. OpenCodeDriver.ts:124 also calls resolveProviderMaintenanceCapabilitiesEffect during create(), and which opencode resolves ~/.opencode/bin/opencode, so it pays the same sync PATH stat and async realPath. It still finishes in about 42 ms in the same slow sessions. So the PATH/realpath probe is not what separates the four slow drivers, and proposals (1) UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE and (2) async resolveCommandPath are speculative. What does set the four slow drivers apart is that they yield ChildProcessSpawner in create(); opencode and copilot do not. That is also unproven. Not every stall is provider-related either: on 2026-10-06T06:24 reconcile finished at 863 ms but listen came at 13170 ms. Only (3) listener-first and (5) stall instrumentation are well-founded. Effort is L for listener-first. This overlaps the server-boot dimension.

Prior work

EVIDENCE measured reconcile ≈70 ms and listen ≈775 ms on a scratch DB; real installs are 2–17× slower. The Aug hardening made provider refresh single-flight but did not take provider creation or PATH probing off the listener path. The server-side root cause overlaps the server-boot dimension; the desktop threadpool mitigation and the real-world distribution are new.

Part of Priority 6: Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain

Avoids fully cold renderer caches (2–3.7 MB refetch and recompile) on every launch where another 3773 app started first; prevents apparent loss of drafts and UI state (correctness)

What happens today

DEFAULT_DESKTOP_BACKEND_PORT=3773 is identical to T3 Code's default (seen in its main.cjs). Right now lsof shows Ryco on :3773 and T3 Code on :3774; whichever app starts first wins. The app document is loaded from backendHttpUrl, so the renderer origin changes with the port. On this machine the Local Storage leveldb holds origins :3773, :3774 and :3775. Code Cache (10,671 files, 310 MB) and the HTTP cache (14,676 files, 890 MB) hold entries for 3 ports. On a flipped launch the immutable asset cache and V8 code cache are cold, so the boot graph and RootAppShell are refetched from the still-busy backend and recompiled. Origin-scoped state (composer drafts, uiStateStore, theme, terminal state) appears lost.

Proposal

Persist the last successfully bound port in desktop-settings.json and probe it first. Move to a Ryco-specific default port. Scan upward only when the persisted port is taken, and log the flip as a warning. Long term, decouple the origin from the port entirely (see renderer-serialized-behind-backend).

Verifier (Confirmed)

backendPort.ts:4 sets 3773 and 74-78 scans upward. T3 main.cjs also has DEFAULT_DESKTOP_BACKEND_PORT = 3773. lsof right now shows Ryco on :3773 and T3 Code on :3774. Frequency from the desktop logs: of 427 sequential-scan selections, 403 got 3773, 15 got 3774 and 9 got 3775, so about 5.6% of launches flip. The Local Storage leveldb has keys for _http://127.0.0.1:3773, :3774 and :3775. Composer drafts persist through a localStorage-bound store (client-runtime draftStore.ts:845-865), so a flipped launch really does hide drafts; that is a correctness problem. Code Cache is 310 MB and HTTP Cache 890 MB. Persisting the last port alone does not help when T3 starts first and takes it. A Ryco-specific default port, or decoupling the origin from the port, is the real fix.

desktopMain.cjs (2,269,362 bytes) is required synchronously before ready. Loading it with all externals took 172–185 ms (303 CJS modules), all of it before the launch mark. Proposal

(a) Put Hub/E2EE/workspace/SSH/computer-use/appSnap/cuaDriverHost modules behind await import() (tsdown emits CJS chunks), triggered from the existing lazyAsyncResource factories and IPC handlers. Register those IPC handlers eagerly with a stub that awaits the chunk. (b) In main, use narrow contracts subpaths or type-only imports instead of the barrel. (c) Lazy-require electron-updater in configureAutoUpdater or at the first check. (d) Replace the Effect port probe with plain net.createServer().listen()/close(). (e) Add a guard test similar to webBundleSplitting.test.ts that fails if the desktopMain eager graph grows.

Part of Priority 6: Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain

Overlaps ~0.2–0.5 s (estimate) of renderer fetch/parse/execute plus the process swap with the backend's 1.6 s+ boot; lets the shell paint cached state through 3–15 s stalls; also fixes the port-dependent origin

What happens today

The window shows desktop-boot.html (file://). Only after 'Listening' (p50 1.8 s, p90 12.5 s) does it loadURL(http://127.0.0.1:PORT). Only then are the boot graph (75 files, 2,023 KiB raw / 638 KiB gzip) and RootAppShell (+1,681 KiB) fetched, parsed and executed, from a backend that is still finishing startup. The file:// → http:// navigation is cross-site, so Chromium swaps in a fresh renderer process and re-runs preload. Meanwhile the ryco:// scheme is already privileged (standard, secure, supportFetchAPI, corsEnabled, codeCache) with a static handler serving the same bundled client from the asar. The web app already gets its backend URLs from desktopBridge.getLocalEnvironmentBootstrap() rather than location.origin.

Proposal

Behind a flag, load the packaged app from ryco://app/ as soon as the window is created: one navigation, a stable origin independent of the port, assets read from the asar, V8 code cache via the scheme privilege. The client runtime's connection supervision then connects once the backend is ready, and the shell renders persisted state while 'connecting'. Prerequisites: allow the ryco://app origin in the server's browserApiCorsLayer and WS upgrade check, and use bearer/DPoP for the desktop primary environment (client-runtime already supports bearer mode), because cookies to 127.0.0.1 are third-party from ryco://. Migrate origin-scoped localStorage once. Measure with the new shell-usable mark.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code is as described. The boot page loads via loadFile (main.ts:3925-3932). loadURL(backendHttpUrl) happens only in the readiness .then (1469-1478 → 1442-1460). ryco:// is registered as privileged with codeCache (300-313), and its static handler (1807-1845) uses the deprecated protocol.registerFileProtocol. web target.ts:113-134 takes its URLs from desktopBridge. listening→app did-finish-load is p50 64 ms, but that excludes the dynamically imported main and RootAppShell, so the 0.2–0.5 s overlap is unmeasured. The benefit is overstated for long stalls. No persisted local-environment shell snapshot exists (the only read caches are hosted: hostedHub/threadReadCache.ts, hostedReadCache), so during a 3–15 s stall the shell could paint chrome but not real data without new caching work. It also needs CORS/WS origin allowlisting, bearer auth for the primary environment, a localStorage migration, and a move to protocol.handle. The impact estimate is speculative; I downgraded it to medium.

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

Removes 10–150 wasted probes per boot and a latent 1 s-per-probe failure mode; makes readiness robust to logging changes

What happens today

Ready = the substring 'Listening on http://' in backend stdout (414/427 launches), raced with a GET /.well-known/ryco/environment poll started at spawn: every 100 ms, 1 s per-request timeout, 60 s budget. Before bind, each probe gets ECONNREFUSED. Per EVIDENCE, a request that connects 0–180 ms before the Listening log never gets a response, so with 100 ms polling a probe typically hangs in that window until its 1 s timeout. That is harmless only because the stdout match wins and aborts it. Any change to log format, level or routing would turn readiness into repeated 1 s hangs. fd 4 is already a duplex pipe with a line reader in main that today only accepts {type:'sample'}.

Proposal

The server writes {type:'listening',port} on fd 4 once the request handler is installed (after the dead window), and later {type:'ready'} when the command gate opens. Desktop resolves readiness from fd 4, keeps the stdout match as a fallback, and starts the HTTP poll only after ~3 s as a last resort. The same channel can carry the startup phase timings and the fatal exit reason.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Part of Priority 6: Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain

Removes a 135–580 ms (up to 2 s) block from the backend critical path about once a week per user, and from the first-ever launch if the env goes through the envelope

What happens today

A cache older than 7 days is a miss, and bootstrap then awaits a fresh capture (worker runs the login shell; 1.5 s exec timeout, 2 s overall) before spawning the backend. Historic captures on this machine took 134–580 ms (p50 ≈165 ms), and 13 hit ETIMEDOUT at 1.5 s. The current cache is from 2026-10-04T20:46Z, so the first launch after 2026-10-11T20:46Z will block the spawn. Earlier builds refreshed in the background after a hit (332 'deferred-refresh' entries); current code does not, so a hit can be up to 7 days stale. The server already skips fixPath in desktop mode (os-jank.ts:38), so this is the only login-shell cost on the desktop path.

Proposal

Use stale-while-revalidate. Accept any parseable cache regardless of age (still invalidate on shell, platform or version change), spawn the backend immediately, and refresh in the worker after the backend listens, writing the cache for the next launch. Only a launch with no cache at all should wait. Even then, spawn the backend in parallel and deliver PATH etc. through the bootstrap envelope, applied to process.env before layers build.

Verifier (Confirmed)

The TTL and the blocking path are confirmed (shellEnvironmentCache.ts:7, 112-116; main.ts:663-679, 4106-4107), and nothing refreshes after a hit (synchronizeDesktopShellEnvironment is only called from the miss path, main.ts:678). Measured stale-miss blocks from cache.miss → backend.spawn: 194 ms (09-20), 364 ms (09-27), 302 ms (10-04). The cache file mtime is Oct 4 22:46 local, so the next stale launch will be the first one after 2026-10-11T20:46Z. This is also a reliability bug the investigator did not mention. On a stale miss the old PATH is discarded. If the capture then fails or times out (1.5 s per exec in shellEnvironmentWorker.ts:25, 2 s overall in captureShellEnvironment.ts:37; a 'spawnSync /bin/zsh ETIMEDOUT' is logged on 2026-09-09), synchronizeDesktopShellEnvironment returns without applying anything (main.ts:639-642). The backend then inherits the GUI launchd PATH, and the server skips fixPath in desktop mode (os-jank.ts:36-38), so CLIs under /opt/homebrew/bin and ~/.local/bin go missing for that session. Stale-while-revalidate fixes both problems.

Part of Priority 6: Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain

Eliminates one sync IPC per node HTTP URL and per ChatView render (~0.1 ms when main is idle, up to main's busy time under load)

What happens today

getLocalEnvironmentBootstrap is ipcRenderer.sendSync, which blocks the renderer main thread until Electron main replies. readPrimaryEnvironmentTarget calls it for every resolvePrimaryEnvironmentHttpUrl (all node HTTP routes via webEndpoint, auth bootstrap, client tracing). ChatView's render body also calls it whenever desktopWorkspace.localEnvironmentId is null. The values are fixed for a renderer's lifetime: port and token are created once, and exposure-mode changes relaunch the app (main.ts:3023-3029). Whenever main is busy (sync log appends, module loading, IPC bursts), each call stalls the renderer.

Proposal

Read the bootstrap once in preload (one sendSync at preload time, or pass it via webPreferences.additionalArguments) and return a cached frozen object. In web, memoize readPrimaryEnvironmentTarget per page load and remove the call from ChatView's render path.

Verifier (Confirmed)

preload.ts:164-170 uses ipcRenderer.sendSync. The main handler (main.ts:2858-2866) returns values that only change at bootstrap (backendHttpUrl is set only at 1125). readPrimaryEnvironmentTarget → resolveDesktopPrimaryTarget → getDesktopLocalEnvironmentBootstrap (target.ts:12-14, 113-114, 166-170) re-issues the sync IPC on every call, and ChatView.tsx:1104-1106 calls it in render when localEnvironmentId is null. The cost is small while main is idle, and caching it in preload is safe.

Part of Priority 6: Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain

~25–60 ms earlier first reveal and backend spawn; fewer main-thread stalls during backend log bursts

What happens today

Real launches: ready→bootstrap.start p50 24 / p90 36 ms; window.create→spawn p50 37 / p90 60 ms. configureAppIdentity runs twice (module scope and whenReady). On packaged macOS each run decodes the 512×512 prod-resources/icon.png for app.dock.setIcon, although the bundle .icns is already the dock icon. app.setAsDefaultProtocolClient writes to LaunchServices on every launch even though electron-builder registers the scheme in Info.plist. configureAutoUpdater constructs MacUpdater. The DesktopComputerBeta constructor runs execFileSync('/usr/libexec/PlistBuddy') (≈3 ms measured) to read CFBundleIdentifier, which equals the build constant appId 'com.laurinfrank.ryco'. computerUseRuntime.start() is awaited before the window. Every backend stdout chunk and captured console write goes through the synchronous RotatingFileSink (appendFileSync; 3 sync appends per console write) on Electron main, while AsyncRotatingFileSink already exists in the same module.

Proposal

In whenReady: spawn the backend, create the boot window, then do menu, protocol, updater and computer-use. Call configureAppIdentity once and skip dock.setIcon on packaged macOS. Call setAsDefaultProtocolClient only when !app.isDefaultProtocolClient(scheme), and defer it. Use the appId build constant (or an fs read of Info.plist) instead of spawning PlistBuddy. Use AsyncRotatingFileSink for backendLogSink and coalesce writeDesktopStreamChunk into a single write.

Verifier (Confirmed)

All items verified. configureAppIdentity runs twice (main.ts:3973 and 4153) and calls dock.setIcon (2063-2068). setAsDefaultProtocolClient runs on every launch (2071-2075) although the installed Info.plist already has CFBundleURLSchemes ['ryco']. The DesktopComputerBeta constructor runs execFileSync PlistBuddy (computerUse/beta.ts:97-108), reached through DesktopComputerUseRuntime (runtime.ts:79) inside bootstrap before the window (main.ts:4074-4094). The desktop and backend log sinks are the sync RotatingFileSink (main.ts:1553-1562, logging.ts:36-57), and writeDesktopStreamChunk does 3 sync writes (1498-1512). The gain estimate is a little high: ready→bootstrap.start p50 is ≈25 ms and bootstrap.start→window.create is 8–37 ms, so about 20–40 ms. Check visually before dropping dock.setIcon, since the PNG may intentionally differ from the icns.

Part of Priority 6: Desktop: start the backend first, cache compiled code, keep a stable origin

Expected gain

Code-cache hits one launch earlier after every update (~30–80 ms of compile for ~3.7 MB boot+shell JS, estimate); bounded cache directories

What happens today

webPreferences sets no v8CacheOptions. With the default 'code', Chromium produces a code cache for a script only once it has been seen as hot, so the first two launches after an update compile cold. Ryco updates often (nightly channel) and every build changes all chunk hashes. Code Cache already holds 310 MB / 10,671 entries and the HTTP cache 890 MB, largely stale builds and ports.

Proposal

Set webPreferences.v8CacheOptions='bypassHeatCheck' for the main window, so the first execution of each script or module produces a cache. Consider 'bypassHeatCheckAndEagerCompile' only after measuring. On version change, prune the old caches with session.clearCodeCaches({}) and clearCache() so disk use stays bounded.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed that the main window's webPreferences (main.ts:3777-3783) set no v8CacheOptions, and that Code Cache is 310 MB and Cache 890 MB. The 'cache kicks in on the 3rd launch after an update' claim is Chromium's documented heat heuristic and was not measured in Ryco. Neither was the 30–80 ms gain. bypassHeatCheck also writes cache for every executed script, including rarely used chunks, so measure it before adopting.

Part of Priority 7: Server cold start: compilation, imports and the login shell

Expected gain

≈−45 MiB uncompressed app.asar (≈23%); smaller downloads and updates; does not affect boot time

What happens today

In the installed 0.1.31 app.asar (194 MB), apps/server/dist ships ESM (11.0 MiB, 32 files) and CJS (10.2 MiB, 32 files), but desktop only launches bin.mjs. apps/desktop/prod-resources inside the asar is 35.1 MiB, including cua-driver 32.9 MB, ryco-computer-use-helper 1.6 MB and ryco-computer-ui-helper 0.9 MB. These binaries are also shipped as extraResources, which is what runtime uses (process.resourcesPath); binaries inside an asar cannot be executed anyway.

Proposal

Exclude apps/server/dist/*.cjs from DESKTOP_BUILD_FILES, or stop emitting CJS if nothing consumes it. Exclude the prod-resources binaries that are delivered via extraResources (keep the icons). Re-measure with measure:desktop-stage.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Listing the installed asar header shows 32 apps/server/dist/*.cjs files totalling 10,720,792 bytes. apps/server/package.json has only bin → dist/bin.mjs, with no main or exports, and the only bin.cjs reference is a test fixture (scripts/lib/validate-runtime-dependencies.test.ts:113). Inside apps/desktop/prod-resources in the asar are cua-driver (32,938,320 bytes), ryco-computer-use-helper (1,660,416) and ryco-computer-ui-helper (945,248). The same binaries also sit in Contents/Resources through the mac extraResources at build-desktop-artifact.ts:974-975, and runtime uses process.resourcesPath (main.ts:4082, beta.ts:109/192). The copy at 1324 exists for AppImage icons, so any exclusion must keep icon.*. Stopping CJS emission for the server would also shorten server builds. Size only; no effect on boot time.

Expected gain

~500–600 ms less latency and CPU per ACP session start and per external MCP bridge launch; tens of MB less transient RSS (estimate)

What happens today

Cursor/ACP sessions get an MCP server process.execPath bin.mjs __agent-control-stdio-proxy, and external clients run bin.mjs mcp serve. bin.ts dispatches these only after its static imports of cli.ts and the full server graph have evaluated. That graph takes 665 ms median (554 ms with compile cache) to load in packaged Electron node mode before the proxy handles a byte. The historic desktop log has 1,223 'second instance refused' entries in batches of 4 (until 2026-09-11) from such launches hitting the GUI entry.

Proposal

Add dedicated tiny tsdown entries (dist/agentControlStdioProxy.mjs, dist/mcpBridge.mjs) that import only the proxy and bridge modules, and point proxyEntryPoint and externalBridgeLaunchArgs at them. Turn bin.ts into a thin dispatcher that loads cli.ts with dynamic import().

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The mechanism is real. bin.ts:10-17 statically imports cli.ts and the full graph before the dispatch at 84-85, and the proxy command is execPath plus argv[1] (CursorAdapter.ts:603-604, ProviderInjection.ts:278-281). It is not on the default path, though. AgentControlSettings.enabled defaults to false (contracts settings.ts:494-496), and the user's settings.json has no agentControl key, so ACP sessions do not spawn the proxy by default. The external MCP bridge only runs for paired integrations. The proxy's load also overlaps the ACP agent's own startup. The 'second instance refused' count is 3,806 across the rotated desktop logs, not 1,223, and the last one was on 2026-09-11, so it is historical and already fixed by the desktopEntry bridge dispatch. None of this is cold boot.
