Server process boot 14 findings · 4 high · 8 medium · 2 low

~775 ms to listen in web/CLI mode (~545 ms desktop): ~200 ms ESM compile, ~180 ms synchronous login shell (web/CLI only), then the layer graph. After listening, every enabled provider is probed cold: 15 child processes and 1.9 GB peak process-tree RSS.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

Ryco server boot (production node apps/server/dist/bin.mjs, Node 24.21, macOS arm64, warm scratch DB). In web/CLI/headless mode the median is about 600 ms to the first log line and 775–805 ms to "Listening on". In desktop mode (RYCO_MODE=desktop) it is 516 ms to the first log line and 545–575 ms to "Listening on". Desktop is faster because it skips the login-shell PATH probe and defers provider registry hydration.

Where the time goes before "Listening":

  • Loading, linking and compiling about 800 ES modules (16.9 MiB of source, including the 8.1 MiB bin.mjs and 341 separate effect files) takes 0 to about 330 ms. Compile is 180–220 ms and file resolution I/O about 60–80 ms.
  • Module evaluation takes about 100–130 ms: bin.mjs 50 ms, the src chunk 18 ms, sharp 7 ms, plus the @pierre/diffs → shiki tree.
  • In web/CLI mode only, fixPath runs a synchronous zsh -ilc that blocks the event loop for 160–200 ms.
  • Effect layer construction follows: SQLite migrations, then OrchestrationEngine init, which reads the full command read model. In web/headless mode the provider registry reconcile (about 95 ms) also sits here. It imports driver chunks, evaluates claude-agent-sdk and spawns copilot --headless.
  • Reliability bug: the public HTTP port is bound by HttpServerLive before migrations, but Node's 'request' handler is only attached when HttpRouter.serve is built, which is what logs "Listening on". Measured window: 135–305 ms traced, about 70–175 ms untraced. Any request that connects in that window never gets a response.

After "Listening" there is little CPU work: the startup command gate takes about 25–40 ms. Then every enabled provider is probed from cold: 15 child processes and a peak process-tree RSS of 1.87 GB at 423% CPU around 1.9 s, finishing at about 2.7 s. The Claude probe opens a full Claude Code session that also starts the user's MCP servers. Other boot-time work: opencode serve (739 MiB), copilot headless, codex app-server, grok agent, a keychain read, npm version checks and PostHog. The node process sits at 340–360 MiB RSS with zero sessions. About 220 MiB of that comes from module loading alone (RSS is 263 MiB at 400 ms), and V8's young generation grows to 128 MiB.

On the user's real 9.27 GB state DB, one query in getCommandReadModel scans all 563k activity rows to find 470. It takes 0.24 s warm and about 2 s cold, on synchronous node:sqlite, and it runs three times per boot.

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

Removes an indefinite hang for any client that connects during the first ~70–305 ms after bind. Saves up to 1 s on the desktop HTTP readiness fallback and about 1.8 s in the measurement harness. Requests made during startup complete as soon as the router is ready.

What happens today

What the code does: makeServerLayer provides HttpServerLive below RuntimeServicesLive (server.ts:693-701). The reason is that AdvertisedEndpointRegistryLive reads the bound port. NodeHttpServer.make calls server.listen() when the layer is built (line 84), but only adds server.on('request', handler) inside serve (line 117). serve runs when HttpRouter.serve(makeRoutesLayer) is built, after all runtime layers, and that is also where 'Listening on' is logged (HttpRouter.js:682). Node emits 'request' events with no listener into the void, so a request that connects in this window never gets a response. The 'upgrade' path behaves the same.

Measured: a load hook shows the public listener bound with requestListeners=0. The window from bind to handler was 305 ms (web) and 135 ms (desktop) with tracing on, and roughly 70–175 ms untraced (firstLog→listening medians). The window covers migrations, so it is longer on a cold first-run DB (about 300 ms). In every harness run, a fetch that connected inside the window got no answer until its 2 s timeout, so descriptor200 equals listening + ~1.8 s. A fetch without a timeout (CLI live-server calls, hosted/browser reconnects) hangs forever. Desktop readiness polling uses a 1 s per-request timeout, so a hit costs up to 1 s whenever the stdout listening detector does not win.

Proposal

Pick one of these fixes:

(a) Preferred and small. Make HttpServerLive pass a createServer factory that installs a provisional 'request'/'upgrade' gate right after creating the server. The gate parks (req, res) and (req, socket, head) in a bounded queue (for example 256 entries with a 30 s deadline that answers 503 + Retry-After: 1). On server.on('newListener', ...) for 'request'/'upgrade', or from the httpListeningLayer, re-emit the parked items to the real handler and remove the gate. Queued requests then complete about 1 ms after the router attaches instead of hanging.

(b) Structural. Delay listen until the router is built. Construct the Node server unbound, give AdvertisedEndpointRegistry the configured port (config.port, which is always set: findAvailablePort runs in resolveServerConfig), and call listen in the serve step.

Add a regression test that connects before 'Listening on' and expects either a 200 or a 503, never a hang.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Confirmed in code. NodeHttpServer.js:84 calls server.listen() when the layer is built. The 'request' and 'upgrade' handlers are only attached inside serve at :117-118. In server.ts:693-701 HttpServerLive is the outermost provideMerge, so it is built before RuntimeServicesLive, which runs migrations, the OrchestrationEngine read model and the provider hydration. HttpRouter.serve (server.ts:684) and the 'Listening on' log (HttpRouter.js:681, HttpServer.js:105) come last. AdvertisedEndpointRegistry.ts:171 already falls back to config.port via resolveListeningPort, so fix (b) is feasible.

I reproduced it with my own raw-socket script (.perf-research/verifier-server-boot/early-connect.mjs): the socket connected at 1,027 ms, 'Listening on' appeared at 1,351 ms, and there was still no response byte after 6 s. The window was 324 ms on a loaded machine.

One caveat on the claimed impact. In desktop, waitForBackendWindowReady (main.ts:1368-1384) races the stdout detector (serverListeningDetector.ts:1, which matches 'Listening on http://') against HTTP polling. The detector fires as the handler attaches, so in practice the desktop does not lose 1 s. The real victims are browser/WS reconnects during a backend or ryco serve restart, and CLI/live-server clients without timeouts. Without an 'upgrade' listener Node falls back to emitting 'request', so WS upgrades hang the same way.

The window also includes the 0.3–2 s getCommandReadModel on large DBs (see command-read-model-scan) and the hub identity build (see hub-identity-gates-router), so on the user's real DB it is much longer than 70–305 ms.

Prior work

EVIDENCE.md listed the symptom as a lead. The root cause (listen in layer build, handler only attached in serve, layer ordering) is new.

Part of Priority 7: Server cold start: compilation, imports and the login shell

Expected gain

Saves 160–200 ms on every web/CLI/headless boot (measured), and 0.6–2 s with typical heavy rc files. Removes the failure mode where the server never starts behind a hanging shell init.

What happens today

What the code does: in every non-desktop mode, fixPath calls readPathFromLoginShell for each candidate shell ($SHELL, the user shell, then the /bin/zsh fallback). That runs execFileSync(shell, ['-ilc', ...], {timeout: 5000}) on the main thread before any layer is built, with the default killSignal SIGTERM, cwd set to the server cwd, and piped stdio. If no PATH comes back on darwin it also runs launchctl (2 s timeout).

Measured:

  • 197–199 ms of synchronous spawnSync per boot with the user's light .zshrc. The CPU profile shows a 163 ms spawnSync.
  • A .zshrc that does sleep 0.8 (typical of nvm/conda/oh-my-zsh) moved listening from 804 to 1,438 ms.
  • Interactive zsh ignores SIGTERM. With a 1 s timeout and the default signal, a .zshrc that sleeps 8 s blocked for 8,030 ms; with SIGKILL it stopped at 1,004 ms. A .zshrc stuck on a prompt, a dead network mount or gpg/ssh-agent therefore stops the server from ever listening.
  • Running in the project cwd also triggers direnv/asdf hooks.

The desktop already solves this properly: a shell-environment cache file, plus a worker thread using SIGKILL, a 1.5 s timeout, ignored stdin and cwd set to homedir. The server re-implements a weaker version.

Proposal

Move the desktop's shellEnvironmentCache and shellEnvironmentWorker logic into packages/shared (for example @ryco/shared/shellEnvironment) and use it from the server, removing the duplicated logic.

  • At boot, apply the cached PATH synchronously from <stateDir>/shell-environment-cache.json (under 1 ms).
  • Refresh asynchronously in a worker_thread or child after listen, with killSignal SIGKILL, timeout ≤1.5 s, stdio ['ignore','pipe','pipe'] and cwd = homedir. Update process.env and the cache when it finishes.
  • Skip the probe when running under the service manager (RYCO_SERVICE_LABEL is set and the unit carries PATH), or when an explicit opt-out env var is set.
  • Only probes that actually spawn provider binaries need to wait for the refreshed PATH, and only on a cache miss.
Verifier (Confirmed)

Confirmed in code:

  • server.ts:599 calls fixPath synchronously inside makeServerLayer, before any layer is built. It returns early only for desktop (os-jank.ts:38).
  • os-jank.ts:63-73 loops over the candidate shells.
  • shell.ts:186-210 calls execFileSync(shell, ['-ilc', ...], {encoding, timeout: 5000}) with no killSignal, cwd or stdio overrides. The desktop worker (shellEnvironmentWorker.ts:16-28) uses SIGKILL, a 1.5 s timeout, cwd = homedir and ignored stdin.

I verified the SIGTERM claim myself (.perf-research/verifier-server-boot/zsh-term.mjs, ZDOTDIR with sleep 4, timeout 1000): SIGTERM returned after 4,029 ms and SIGKILL after 1,002 ms. Interactive zsh does ignore SIGTERM, so the 5 s timeout cannot bound a hanging rc file. The 163 ms spawnSync is already in EVIDENCE.md.

Correction to the proposal: generated service units do not carry PATH (nodeService.ts has no PATH entry), so the 'skip under service manager' branch needs that added first. The service manager is actually the case that needs the probe most. Desktop users are not affected.

Prior work

None for the server. The desktop already ships this pattern (apps/desktop/src/shellEnvironmentWorker.ts), so the fix is mostly extracting and reusing it. EVIDENCE.md flagged the 163 ms spawnSync as a lead.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

On large real-world DBs: 0.5 s (warm) to 2+ s (cold first call) less synchronous event-loop blocking per boot. Each remaining call drops to about 1–2 ms. Effect on small DBs is negligible.

What happens today

What the code does: listActionableThreadActivityRows filters kind IN (9 kinds) and orders by (thread_id, sequence, created_at, activity_id). SQLite walks idx_projection_thread_activities_thread_sequence_created_id over every row and does a table lookup per row to test kind, because no index covers kind (EXPLAIN: SCAN ... USING INDEX). Node's sqlite driver is synchronous, so the main thread blocks for the whole query. getCommandReadModel runs it at boot:

  • once in OrchestrationEngine layer construction, before listen;
  • once in startup phase 'workspace.validate', unconditionally, even though validateRestrictedWorkspaceSnapshot returns immediately when the workspace is not restricted;
  • once in reconcileOrphanedProviderSessions;
  • plus once per page in RestartContinuation.dispatchPending.

Measured read-only on the user's real state.sqlite (9.27 GB, 563,000 activity rows, 470 matching): 1.99–2.13 s on first run, 0.24 s warm. The user-message-anchor query in the same read model takes only 11–39 ms. On a synthetic 563k-row copy of the table, the query took 446–554 ms without an index and 1–2 ms with a partial index; EXPLAIN confirms the partial index is used.

Proposal

1) Add a migration: CREATE INDEX idx_projection_thread_activities_actionable ON projection_thread_activities(thread_id, sequence, created_at, activity_id) WHERE kind IN (<the same 9 literals>). Keep the IN list in one shared constant used by both the query and the migration so SQLite keeps matching the partial index. It covers only ~0.1% of rows, so write cost is negligible.

2) In serverRuntimeStartup, skip the 'workspace.validate' read when !workspaceAccessPolicy.isRestricted.

3) Have the engine expose its in-memory commandReadModel (it was loaded at OrchestrationEngine.ts:590) to reconcileOrphanedProviderSessions instead of re-querying. This makes it one read per boot instead of three.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Re-measured read-only on ~/.ryco/userdata/state.sqlite (9.30 GB) with .perf-research/verifier-server-boot/actionable-plan.mjs. EXPLAIN gives 'SCAN projection_thread_activities USING INDEX idx_projection_thread_activities_thread_sequence_created_id'. 470 of 565,348 rows match. The query took 1,282 ms on the first run (page cache partly warm) and 335 ms warm.

Migrations add no index covering kind. The only partial index is 070's local_task_start_failures, for a different kind.

Call sites:

  • OrchestrationEngine.ts:590, during layer construction, so before listen. On big DBs this also lengthens the http-accept-before-handler window.
  • serverRuntimeStartup.ts:905-913 'workspace.validate', unconditional. validateRestrictedWorkspaceSnapshot returns at :518 when the workspace is not restricted.
  • serverRuntimeStartup.ts:638, reconcileOrphanedProviderSessions.
  • RestartContinuation.ts:679, but only after listPending returns rows (:677-678), so it costs nothing when no continuations are pending.

The store is synchronous: bin.mjs imports DatabaseSync. That makes 2 unconditional calls in the startup fiber plus 1 in layer build. Proposal (3) needs a new accessor, because OrchestrationEngineService does not expose its commandReadModel. The partial-index approach was verified by the investigator; a plain (kind) index would also work.

Prior work

performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md covers thread-detail hydration in ProjectionSnapshotQuery, not this query or boot-time read amplification. This finding is new.

Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

Removes about 15 child processes, about 1.5 GB of transient RSS and about 4 cores × 1.5 s of CPU from every boot. This frees the CPU the UI's first load is competing for. It also removes 2–3 HTTPS calls, a keychain access and a possible token refresh per boot.

What happens today

What the code does: each managed provider forks its own initial refreshSnapshot when it is built (makeManagedServerProvider.ts:271-275). The registry also force-refreshes every new instance (ProviderRegistry.ts:637-651). The on-disk provider status cache is only used as a placeholder (ProviderRegistry.ts:216-285) and never counts as fresh across restarts. All probes therefore start within about 30 ms of each other, and the registry concurrency limit of 4 has no effect.

Measured on a web boot with zero sessions:

  • 15 child processes. The Claude capability probe opens a full Claude Code SDK session with settingSources user/project/local (ClaudeProvider.ts:341), which also starts the user's MCP servers: Ryco bin.mjs mcp 265 MiB, notion-mcp-server 149 MiB, npm exec token-counter-mcp 138 MiB, mcp@latest 133 MiB.
  • Other probe processes: opencode serve 739 MiB, copilot --headless 230 MiB, codex app-server 130 MiB, grok agent stdio 118 MiB.
  • Peak process-tree RSS was 1,869 MiB at 1.9 s, with 423% CPU at 1.6 s. The probes take 0.36–2.7 s and overlap the UI's first snapshot and thread load.
  • Desktop runs the same set 100 ms after layer build (Hydration.ts:174), exactly while the renderer is connecting.
  • opencode --version runs twice in sequence (about 330–470 ms each): once in the probe, once in the serve preflight.
  • The npm latest-version checks for claude-code and codex run on every boot because the cache is in memory only (1 h TTL, providerMaintenance.ts:14,61).

Reliability issue: the Claude usage probe reads Claude Code's OAuth credentials from the keychain (security spawn), may refresh the token, and writes the result back to the keychain or the credentials file (ClaudeUsage.ts:143-185). This happens at boot, concurrently with the claude CLI probe that uses the same refresh token, so the two can race on a rotating refresh token.

Proposal

1) Persist probe results with freshness. Store checkedAt in the provider status cache, key it by binary path + --version (or binary mtime/inode) + settings hash, and seed makeManagedServerProvider's lastRefreshAttemptAtMs from it. Treat cached rich data (models, slash commands, account) as fresh for hours. At boot run only the cheap version check, or nothing.

2) Make rich probes demand-driven. Run them when a client subscribes or revalidates and the cache is stale, when the model picker opens, or when a session starts. Run any background refresh with concurrency 1–2, only after the first client snapshot has been served, staggered, and never at boot in desktop.

3) Claude probe: pass mcpServers: {} with a strict MCP config (or the SDK's equivalent) so probing never spawns the user's MCP servers.

4) Reuse the version string the OpenCode probe just verified when calling startOpenCodeServerProcess for the same binary in the same probe.

5) Persist the npm latest-version cache to disk with its 1 h TTL.

6) Move the Claude usage/rate-limit probe to on-demand only, and never refresh or persist another app's OAuth token from a background probe. Use the access token as-is, or skip when it has expired.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Confirmed in code:

  • makeManagedServerProvider.ts:69 seeds lastRefreshAttemptAtMs as null, and :272-275 forks refreshSnapshot when each provider is built, so nothing counts as fresh across restarts.
  • ProviderRegistry.ts:637-651 force-refreshes newly added instances with concurrency 4. They just join the single-flight probes that the drivers already started, so the limit 4 has no effect.
  • ClaudeProvider.ts:322-375: the capability probe calls claudeQuery with settingSources user/project/local and no mcpServers override.
  • checkClaudeProviderStatus (ClaudeProvider.ts:503-512) runs both the capability probe and the usage probe on every check (capability TTL 5 min, usage 60 s, ClaudeDriver.ts:51-52, in memory only).
  • ClaudeUsage.ts:143-185 refreshes and writes back to the keychain or credentials file when the token has expired or the API returns 429.
  • opencodeRuntime.ts:145-190 runs --version before serve and is 'Deliberately not cached'. OpenCodeProvider.ts:403-420 runs it again. Two opencode --version processes show up in tree-web.txt.
  • providerMaintenance.ts:14,61: the latest-version cache is an in-memory Map only.
  • Hydration.ts:174 has the 100 ms sleep in desktop.

tree-web.txt agrees: peak tree RSS 1,869 MiB at 1,922 ms, ~420–486% CPU, and Claude's MCP children appear (notion-mcp, token-counter-mcp, mcp@latest, bin.mjs mcp). Two zsh -lc source login shells were also spawned, probably Claude Code's shell snapshot.

Caveats:

  • The latency effect on the UI's first load was not measured; only the resources were.
  • Passing mcpServers: {}/strict MCP config would drop MCP-provided slash commands from the probe result.
  • Cursor and Grok (ACP) probes are included too.

This is not covered by the Aug hardening doc, which only adds single-flight and cached state for subscribers.

Prior work

The Aug 2026 hardening (docs/research/2026-08-12-performance-hardening-results.md, 'Provider refresh and reconnect load') added single-flight, cached state for subscribers and last-good retention. That removed reconnect amplification, but the boot path still probes everything cold. Residual #6 in that doc is about packaging, not runtime. This finding is new.

Medium impactEffort S✓ ConfirmedEnable the V8 compile cache for the backend (desktop and CLI)60–84 ms less on every warm boot (measured).
Category: Build configRisk: lowInvestigator confidence: highserver-boot:node-compile-cache

Part of Priority 7: Server cold start: compilation, imports and the login shell

Expected gain

60–84 ms less on every warm boot (measured).

What happens today

What happens today: about 800 modules (16.9 MiB) are compiled from scratch on every boot. compileSourceTextModule is 177–223 ms of CPU in the profiles; bin.mjs alone takes 96–108 ms (vm.SourceTextModule). Desktop spawns [backendEntry, '--bootstrap-fd', '3'] with no compile cache, and the CLI bin is bin.mjs itself. Calling module.enableCompileCache() inside bin.mjs would be too late, because ESM static imports are compiled before the module body runs.

Measured: with NODE_COMPILE_CACHE, desktop-mode listening went from 545 to 461 ms (−84 ms, median of 7). The profile's compile time fell from 183 to 103 ms. Web mode gains about 60 ms (EVIDENCE.md). The installed T3 Code desktop already does this via --require compileCache.cjs.

Proposal

1) Emit a tiny entry, for example dist/bin.mjs = import { enableCompileCache } from 'node:module'; enableCompileCache?.(); await import('./server.mjs');, with the real graph moved to a second entry in tsdown.config.ts. With no argument Node uses a tmpdir cache, and an explicit dir under the state dir also works.

2) Desktop: set env.NODE_COMPILE_CACHE = path.join(app.getPath('userData'), 'Cache', 'node-compile-cache') in backendChildEnv. The asar itself is read-only, but the cache key is content-hash + V8 version, so app updates invalidate it automatically.

3) Call module.flushCompileCache() after 'startup phase complete' so the cache is persisted even if the process is later SIGKILLed.

Verifier (Confirmed)

No enableCompileCache or NODE_COMPILE_CACHE anywhere in apps/, packages/ or scripts/.

  • bin.ts:1-19 uses only static imports, so enabling the cache inside it is too late; the shim proposal is correct.
  • tsdown.config.ts has a single entry, src/bin.ts.
  • main.ts:2669 spawns [backendEntry, '--bootstrap-fd', '3'] and backendChildEnv (main.ts:602-628) sets no cache.

Independent corroboration from the desktop-boot agent (.perf-research/desktop-boot/backend-load-cc.txt): with Electron's Node 24.20 and a compileCache hook, the median went from 665 to 554 ms over 10 runs (−111 ms). The cache-dir key is v24.20.0-arm64, so it does work under ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE. EVIDENCE.md has ~60 ms for web mode. The −60 to −84 ms claim is plausible or conservative. module.flushCompileCache exists in Node 24.

Prior work

EVIDENCE.md measured about 60 ms for web mode. New here: the desktop numbers, the shim requirement for ESM, the desktop env wiring and flushCompileCache.

Part of Priority 7: Server cold start: compilation, imports and the login shell

Expected gain

About 50–60 MiB less steady idle RSS per backend (measured), and more when combined with the bundle changes.

What happens today

Measured: RSS is 263 MiB at about 400 ms (module loading only; an empty Node process is about 42 MiB), about 300 MiB at 1 s, and 342–360 MiB at around 3 s with zero sessions. getHeapSpaceStatistics shows new_space size 128 MiB (semi-space grown to 64 MiB), with heapTotal 207–218 MiB against heapUsed 106–115 MiB.

Proposal
  • Pass --max-semi-space-size=16 in the desktop backend spawn args (Electron's ELECTRON_RUN_AS_NODE accepts V8 flags before the entry).
  • Add it to NODE_OPTIONS in the generated launchd/systemd service units.
  • For the npx/global CLI, add it via the compile-cache shim, which can re-exec only when the flag is missing (cost is about 40 ms, so measure first), or simply document it.
  • Validate with a streaming-load benchmark, because a smaller nursery means more frequent scavenges.

Combine with sharp-static-import, eager-feature-code-in-bin and server-build-config, which lower the module-load part (bin.mjs alone is +67 MiB RSS).

Verifier (Confirmed)

That is about 50–55 MiB less idle RSS, matching the claim. --max-semi-space-size is allowed in NODE_OPTIONS. Throughput under streaming load was not tested; that remains the risk.

Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

About 95–140 ms less time to listen for ryco serve and hosted nodes (measured difference between web and desktop runs).

What happens today

What the code does: for mode !== 'desktop', ProviderInstanceRegistryHydrationLive reads settings and builds ProviderInstanceRegistryMutableLayer with the full config map during layer construction, before the router attaches. That means dynamically importing six driver chunks, evaluating claude-agent-sdk (about 48 ms, +35 MiB), copilot-sdk (14 ms) and the codex/opencode chunks, starting CopilotClient (spawning copilot --headless) and building the adapters.

Measured from the logs: 'hydration config resolved' at 822.8 ms → 'reconcile complete' at 916.8 ms → 'Listening on' at 1,014 ms. In desktop mode, where the map is empty, the same span is 432→484 ms. ryco serve and hosted nodes pay about 95 ms of reconcile plus spawn and CPU contention before they serve anything.

Proposal

Use the deferred path (DesktopSettingsReconcileLive) for every mode: start with an empty registry and reconcile in a scoped background fiber after markHttpListening, not after a fixed 100 ms sleep. The registry already serves cached snapshots, and startup reconciliation already copes with this in desktop mode. Combined with the boot-provider-probes change, provider SDKs are then never on the listen critical path.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code fact is confirmed. For mode !== 'desktop', Hydration.ts:236-251 builds the mutable registry with the full config map during layer build. server-warm1.log shows 'hydration config resolved' at .569, 'reconcile complete' at .647 and 'Listening on' at .722, so about 78 ms on the critical path.

The proposal has a regression the investigator missed. 'The registry already serves cached snapshots' is not true for the deferred path. ProviderRegistry.ts:222-285 hydrates the on-disk provider status cache only for bootInstances (instanceRegistry.listInstances at :223). In desktop mode the registry starts empty, so cachedProviders is []. Instances added later reach providersRef only after their probe completes: :619-651 subscribe and refresh, with no placeholder upsert.

Switching web mode to the desktop path as written would therefore lose the instant cached provider list. The fix needs to seed providersRef from the cache files keyed by the derived config map (instanceId + driver), without constructing drivers. Effort is M, not S.

Expected gain

Estimated 40–60 ms less module resolution I/O, about 8.6 MiB less heap for source text, smaller effect source (no JSDoc), and 10 MiB less in the npm package and desktop asar.

What happens today

What the build does: deps.alwaysBundle only covers @ryco/* and effect-acp, so effect stays external and is loaded as 341 separate files (6.1 MiB, shipped with full JSDoc). Together with semver (46 files), ws (14), @effect/platform-node(-shared) (30) and others, about 800 files are resolved one by one at boot.

Measured: the profile shows about 60–80 ms in internalModuleStat (16 ms), open (15 ms), realpathSync (10 ms), package_json_reader (about 16 ms), pathToFileURL, resolve and syncLink.

bin.mjs contains 1,155 non-Latin1 characters, mostly em-dashes in JSDoc (893 of those lines are comments). V8 therefore stores the 8.32M-char source as a two-byte string: 15.9 MiB in the heap snapshot instead of about 7.3 MiB. About 22% of bin.mjs is comments.

format: ['esm','cjs'] also emits 10 MiB across 32 .cjs files. Nothing loads them: package.json bin points to bin.mjs, and the desktop spawns bin.mjs. They still ship in the npm tarball (files: ['dist']), which slows cold npx ryco installs.

Proposal
  • Add effect, @effect/platform-node(-shared), semver, ws, mime and the other pure-JS deps to deps.alwaysBundle so they are tree-shaken into a few chunks. Keep native and SDK packages external: sharp, node-pty, @github/keytar and the provider SDKs.
  • Set rolldown outputOptions.comments: { jsdoc: false, legal: true, annotation: true } and add a renderChunk step (or minifier option) that escapes non-ASCII to \uXXXX, so source strings stay one-byte.
  • Drop 'cjs' from format, unless a consumer is confirmed.
Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Facts confirmed:

  • tsdown.config.ts:9 has format ['esm','cjs'].
  • dist contains 32 .cjs files totalling 10 MiB, and they ship in the installed app.asar (32 .cjs under apps/server/dist).
  • The repo itself calls them unused: scripts/lib/validate-runtime-dependencies.test.ts:111 says 'ignores the unused server CJS variant'.
  • package.json bin points to dist/bin.mjs.
  • bin.mjs has 8,322,008 chars, 2,142 non-ASCII and 1,155 non-Latin1, so V8 stores it as a two-byte string (~15.9 MiB).
  • alwaysBundle (tsdown.config.ts:17) covers only @ryco/* and effect-acp.

The headline gain of 40–60 ms from bundling effect and the pure-JS deps is an unmeasured estimate. Bundling also makes bin.mjs larger, which partly offsets the gain once the compile cache is enabled. Dropping CJS and stripping JSDoc/escaping non-ASCII are low-risk quick wins. Bundling effect is the medium-risk part.

Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

Desktop cold launch shows the last-known provider list, models and auth state at the first server-config snapshot instead of empty or pending for roughly 0.5–2.7 s. This matters for opening a new thread or the model picker right after launch. Cost is one small JSON read per instance (~1 ms each).

What happens today

In desktop mode, ProviderInstanceRegistryHydrationLive starts the instance registry with an empty config map (Hydration.ts:238-244) and reconciles in a fiber after Effect.sleep("100 millis") (:174). ProviderRegistryLive is built right after the hydration layer, and its boot path reads the per-instance status cache only for bootInstances = instanceRegistry.listInstances (ProviderRegistry.ts:223). That list is empty in desktop mode, so cachedProviders (:276-285) is [] and providersRef starts empty.

When the deferred reconcile adds the instances, syncLiveSources (:606-651) subscribes to their change streams and refreshes them. No placeholder or cached snapshot is upserted. A provider reaches providersRef only when its probe completes and publishes: the Claude SDK session, opencode --version plus serve, codex app-server and so on, which per tree-web.txt is about 0.4–2.7 s.

The cache files are still written on every probe (persistProvider) but are effectively write-only on desktop. Web mode does use them (Ref.make(cachedProviders)).

This is from reading the code. I did not runtime-verify it with an authenticated client, and I did not check whether the web client keeps its own copy of the server config.

Proposal

Seed providersRef from the status cache independently of driver construction.

  • At ProviderRegistry build time, derive instance IDs and driver kinds from ServerSettings via deriveProviderInstanceConfigMap (or from the cache directory itself, which is keyed by instanceId).
  • Read <providerStatusCacheDir>/<instanceId>.json, validate identity with isCachedProviderCorrelated against a pending snapshot built from the derived config, and publish those entries immediately.
  • When the deferred reconcile adds instances, keep the cached entry until the first probe replaces it.

This is the same change the web-mode deferral needs (web-mode-registry-on-critical-path), so do both together: drivers are built off the critical path in every mode, and every mode starts from the cached provider list.

This finding was added by the adversarial verifier while checking the investigator's report. It has not been verified a second time.

Prior work

None. The Aug hardening doc covers cached state for subscribers once providersRef is populated, not the desktop boot gap. It overlaps with the web-mode-registry-on-critical-path proposal in this report.

Part of Priority 7: Server cold start: compilation, imports and the login shell

Expected gain

Estimated 40–60 ms less compile + evaluation (27 ms Codex + 8 ms ACP measured) and roughly 30–40 MiB less RSS and heap at boot, with the same work paid only when a feature is first used.

What happens today

What happens: driver chunks are lazy, but other statically imported modules pull their protocol packages into bin.mjs anyway.

  • SessionImport.ts:28 (SessionImportLive, static in server.ts), CodexMcpService.ts:30 and CodexResetCredits.ts pull effect-codex-app-server/client, which includes the 1,100 KiB generated schema.
  • ws/providerRpc.ts:12-16 → provider/acp/AcpRegistrySupport pulls effect-acp, 445 KiB including provider/acp.
  • Region attribution of bin.mjs also finds: computer use 580 KiB; hub/E2EE (noble, relayE2ee*, hubConnector, hubIdentity, client-runtime) 1,211 KiB; source-control providers 471 KiB; agent-control/external MCP 316 KiB; device 177 KiB; CLI admin commands 167 KiB.
  • cliRemote → client-runtime → zustand also drags in React (both the production and development CJS builds, 53 KiB).

Measured:

  • The Codex schema costs 27 ms of compile + eval and +10.8 MiB heap; the ACP schema costs 8 ms and +1.1 MiB.
  • Reading and compiling bin.mjs alone costs about 100 ms and +67 MiB RSS (24 MiB source + 43 MiB compile), which scales with file size.
  • The heap snapshot shows 24k Schema closures, 12k Union and 18.5k PropertySignature objects created at module evaluation.
Proposal

Put the heavy, optional features behind dynamic-import boundaries. The codebase already does this for PTY and HttpServer via Layer.unwrap(Effect.promise(() => import(...))).

  • Codex: SessionImport's Codex path and CodexMcpService should await import('effect-codex-app-server/client') inside the operation that needs it.
  • ACP: providerRpc should lazy-load AcpRegistrySupport/AcpRegistryCatalog in the ACP RPC handlers.
  • Computer-use, device, htmlRender, Atlassian and source-control provider implementations should sit behind lazy layer facades.
  • Hub/E2EE code should load only when hubConnector.enabled.
  • CLI admin and remote subcommands should be dynamic imports in their Command handlers, so ryco serve never evaluates them and React/zustand drop out of the server path.

Add a server bundle guard test that asserts bin.mjs size and forbids these regions in the entry chunk.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The static imports are confirmed:

  • SessionImport.ts:28, CodexMcpService.ts:30 and CodexResetCredits.ts:10-11 import effect-codex-app-server client and schema.
  • providerRpc.ts:12-16 imports AcpRegistryCatalog and AcpRegistrySupport.
  • server.ts:58-62 imports the source-control CLIs and APIs statically.
  • bin-regions.txt shows 1,100 KiB codex, 389 KiB effect-acp, 125 KiB noble curves and 52 KiB react.

The savings are overstated, though. With the current boot behaviour (boot-provider-probes), the Codex driver chunk and the ACP drivers (Cursor, Grok) are loaded and probed within ~0.1–1 s of every boot, and they need these same schemas. Lazy-loading the Codex/ACP schemas therefore mostly moves the 27 + 8 ms off the time-to-listen path. It does not remove the ~12 MiB heap unless the probes also become demand-driven.

The RSS savings that hold unconditionally come from computer use, hub/E2EE when the hub is disabled, source-control providers, CLI admin commands and React/zustand. Those were not measured individually.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

About 24 ms per boot on the scratch DB (measured), and an estimated 150–250 ms (capped at 1 s) for the user's 32 projects, removed from command-gate readiness.

What happens today

What the code does: ProviderCommandReactor.start, which runs inside startup phase reactors.start before the command gate opens, calls projectionSnapshotQuery.getShellSnapshot() only to find threads whose goal synchronization is still 'pending'. getShellSnapshot resolves repository identity for every active project root, running git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git remote -v per root with concurrency 4 and a 1 s budget. Results are cached in memory for only 1 minute (positive and negative TTL).

Measured on the scratch DB: reactors.start took 27.4 ms, of which RepositoryIdentityResolver.resolve was 23.6 ms for one project. The user's real DB has 32 projects, which means up to 64 git spawns at boot, under heavy CPU contention from the provider probes, and the web client's first shell snapshot repeats the work after the 1-minute TTL expires.

Proposal
  • Replace the startup scan with a narrow SQL query (threads whose goal_json says synchronization is pending), or add { withRepositoryIdentity: false } to getShellSnapshot for internal callers.
  • Persist repository identity per workspace root (keyed by .git HEAD/config mtime) or lengthen the TTL, so the client's first snapshot does not spawn git either.
Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Code confirmed:

  • ProviderCommandReactor.ts:3151 calls getShellSnapshot only to find threads whose goal synchronization is pending.
  • getShellSnapshot at ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:2658-2661 resolves identities with a 1 s budget and concurrency 4 (:530, :560-591).
  • RepositoryIdentityResolver.ts:93-94 sets 1-minute TTLs, and :103-138 runs two git spawns per root.

The trace in my scratch home has reactors.start at 36.5–37.0 ms, of which RepositoryIdentityResolver.resolve was 32.7–33.4 ms (one project). The user's DB has 29 distinct active workspace roots, not 32, so up to 58 git spawns.

Correction: the same trace shows the next resolve calls are cache hits (0.01–0.03 ms). The boot-time resolution therefore warms the cache for the client's first shell snapshot, which normally arrives within the 1-minute TTL. Removing it from reactors.start shortens command-gate readiness, but it moves the git cost onto the first client snapshot unless identities are also persisted. That makes proposal part 2 (persisting identities) the essential half. The full shell snapshot (all threads) being built just to scan pending goals is also wasteful on large DBs.

Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

Estimated 10–100+ ms off time-to-serve on hub-enabled nodes and desktops, depending on keychain latency, and a shorter hang window.

What happens today

What the code does: HttpRouter.serve(makeRoutesLayer).pipe(Layer.provide(HubConnectorLive)) means the HTTP request handler (and 'Listening on') waits for makeHubConnectorService. When hubConnector.enabled, that service awaits the process lock and then makeHubIdentityRuntime. makeHubIdentityRuntime awaits about 10 stores one after another: state, retirement, protected secret store selection (dynamic import of @github/keytar plus keychain inspection), prekey, continuity anchor, continuity, E2EE policy, fallback counter, client authorization, authorization client and local-introduction ledger. Most of these are independent JSON files. The connector itself starts non-blocking (void connector.start()).

Not measured: the perf home has no hub identity. The user's real state dir does have hub-identity.json, so hub-enabled desktops pay this cost.

Proposal
  • Load the independent stores with Promise.all once stateStore and retirementStore are open.
  • Better, take hub identity off the router's critical path: provide a lazy HubConnectorService whose identity is a Deferred built in a forked fiber after markHttpListening. Hub HTTP routes answer 503/Retry-After until it resolves.
  • Add startup spans around makeHubIdentityRuntime and the keychain step so the cost becomes visible in server.trace.ndjson.
Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The structure is confirmed:

  • server.ts:684-686 provides HubConnectorLive to HttpRouter.serve, so it is built before the request handler attaches.
  • HubConnectorLive.ts:465-500, when hubConnector.enabled, awaits processLock.acquire() (possibly twice) and then makeIdentityRuntime.
  • HubIdentityRuntime.ts:824-891 awaits about 11 store constructors one after another. selectProtectedSecretStore (:548ff) does stateStore readOrCreate/update and dynamically imports @github/keytar (ProtectedSecretStore.ts:323-326).

Nothing was measured: the perf home has no hub identity. Each store is a small JSON read, so 10–15 ms of sequential fs is plausible. The keychain or keytar dlopen cost is unknown. This only affects hub-enabled nodes and desktops (the default config is disabled). It does lengthen the hang window from http-accept-before-handler.

Startup request black hole 10 findings · 2 high · 3 medium · 5 low

Root-caused: the port is bound ~150–280 ms (longer on big DBs) before any request handler exists, and requests in that window are dropped forever. A prototype gate fixed it: 0 of 118 early requests hung.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

Root cause, confirmed by measurement and a Node-level trace: the Effect Node HTTP layer binds the port early and attaches the request handlers only much later. In apps/server/src/server.ts:683-701, HttpServerLive is provideMerged underneath RuntimeServicesLive, so NodeHttpServer.make runs first and calls server.listen() at NodeHttpServer.ts:135. That happens about 11-15 ms before "Running all migrations". The 'request' and 'upgrade' listeners are added only when HttpRouter.serve runs HttpServer.serve (NodeHttpServer.ts:181-182), and that happens after the whole runtime graph is built: migrations about 20 ms, provider-registry hydration about 100 ms, the remaining runtime layers about 75 ms. "Listening on" is logged in the same millisecond the handlers are attached. A connection accepted in this gap is parsed by Node, which emits 'request' to zero listeners. The trace shows this for plain GETs and for GET /ws with Upgrade: websocket, because Node sends an upgrade to 'request' when no 'upgrade' listener exists. The request is lost. The socket is never answered and never closed: I held 7 such sockets for 330 s, past Node's headersTimeout (60 s) and requestTimeout (300 s). Across 8 runs, 190/190 in-window probes hung (HTTP and WebSocket alike). The dead window lasts about 145-215 ms on an idle machine and up to about 280 ms under CPU load. With hub enabled it also includes HubConnectorLive's keychain and identity I/O, because that layer is provided to the serve layer. The Bun dev path answers 404 in the same window instead of hanging.

Consequences found. 1) Any poller with a per-probe timeout pays that timeout once. The SSH remote-launch wait_ready script and the desktop's waitForHttpReady (100 ms interval, 1 s timeout) detected readiness 0.89-0.98 s after Listening in 5/5 runs; the 5 ms/2 s harness took +1.74-1.82 s. Desktop hides this today because it also parses the INFO log line "Listening on", but that line can be suppressed by RYCO_LOG_LEVEL. 2) Clients have no timeouts on the control-plane fetches (descriptor, session, ws-token) or on the WebSocket URL provider. A reconnect attempt that lands in the window stalls the loop with no end, and saved-environment connects pile onto the hung promise. Desktop currently hides this by force-reloading the renderer after a backend crash-restart. 3) Shutdown has two bugs. Any hung startup socket, and also any normally connected WebSocket, makes graceful shutdown wait the full 20 s preemptiveShutdown timeout: 20.4 s measured, against 1.0-1.5 s with no clients. The cause is that NodeHttpServer's serve finalizer awaits server.close() before it interrupts the request/WebSocket fibers. The desktop sends SIGKILL after 2 s, so every desktop quit, relaunch or update with an open window ends in SIGKILL and skips the runtime finalizers.

Fix, validated against the unmodified production bundle with a --import prototype (.perf-research/startup-hang/fix-preload.mjs): put a startup gate on the http.Server before listen(). It holds early requests and upgrades (bounded) and replays them into the real handlers when they are attached, detected via 'newListener'; overflow gets 503 with Retry-After. Result: 0 hung out of 118 early probes, with early WebSocket upgrades reaching the real router; the readiness pollers dropped from +0.9-1.8 s to +3-19 ms. This can be done locally, because NodeHttpServer.layer takes an evaluate server factory and calls it before listen(). Follow-ups: client-side deadlines, a 20 s shutdown fix (reorder or shorten the timeout), and a few overlap opportunities (serve the static shell at bind time so the desktop renderer can start loading while the runtime builds).

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

Removes indefinite hangs (190/190 in-window requests hung today) and turns them into a wait of at most the startup window (≤~280 ms measured). Removes the ~0.9 s (1 s-timeout pollers) and ~1.8 s (2 s-timeout pollers) readiness penalties and the 20 s shutdown stall caused by hung sockets.

What happens today

HttpServerLive (server.ts:177-199) is provideMerge'd under RuntimeServicesLive (server.ts:693-696), so NodeHttpServer.make runs first and calls server.listen() (NodeHttpServer.ts:135) about 11-15 ms before migrations start. Handlers are attached only in serve() (NodeHttpServer.ts:181-182). HttpRouter.serve calls serve() after it has built the routes layer, and that build waits for the whole runtime graph. Effect then logs 'Listening on' (HttpServer.ts:317-333). The Node trace shows 8 'request' events emitted with zero listeners, including GET /ws carrying Upgrade: websocket, because Node treats an upgrade as a normal request when no 'upgrade' listener exists. Measured: 190/190 in-window probes (HTTP and WS) hung across 8 boots. 7 sockets were held 330 s and never answered or closed, because Node's headersTimeout and requestTimeout only cover receiving the request. The window is 145-215 ms on an idle machine (trace: 201 ms from bind to handler) and up to ~280 ms under load. Hung sockets also stall graceful shutdown for 20 s (see shutdown-blocked-20s-by-open-websocket). In the Bun dev path the platform's placeholder handler answers 404 'not found' during the same gap (BunHttpServer.ts:142-150). Clients treat 404 as non-transient: only 502/503/504 are retried (primaryAuth.ts:88).

Proposal

Add apps/server/src/httpStartupGate.ts and use it at server.ts:193: NodeHttpServer.layer(() => withStartupGate(NodeHttp.createServer()), {...}). NodeHttpServer.make calls evaluate() before listen(), so no fork of the platform package is needed. The gate attaches 'request' and 'upgrade' listeners before bind. Each listener returns early if listenerCount(ev) > 1, meaning the real handler is present. Otherwise it holds (req, res) or (req, socket, head) in bounded sets: at most 256 entries, at most 10 s each. Once full or expired: 503 with Retry-After: 1, Cache-Control: no-store, Connection: close; for an upgrade, write a raw 503 and end the socket. Entries are removed when the client closes. server.on('newListener') sees the real handler arrive and, on the next tick, replays every held entry into it and removes the gate. If the server closes while still gated, answer 503 to everything held. Validated with the identical logic injected via --import into the unmodified bundle: 0/118 hung, every early probe answered by the real router once handlers were attached (at most 264-281 ms wait), and readiness pollers went from +0.9-1.8 s to +3-19 ms. Also report upstream (Effect's NodeHttpServer drops requests between layer build and serve; Bun answers 404), and add a regression test: build the serve layer behind a deliberately slow route layer, send a request before serve, assert it is answered.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Checked the layer chain at server.ts:693-699. serverApplicationLayer.pipe(provideMerge(RuntimeServicesLive), provideMerge(WorkspaceAccessPolicyLive), provideMerge(HttpServerLive), ...) builds HttpServerLive before RuntimeServicesLive and before the serve layer, which is mergeAll'd at 683-691. In NodeHttpServer.ts, evaluate() runs at :106 and server.listen at :135, so the port is bound inside make(). The handlers are attached only in serve() at :181-182. HttpRouter.serve (HttpRouter.ts:1340-1396) builds the routes layer first and then calls HttpServer.serve and withLogAddress (HttpServer.ts:317-334). dist/bin.mjs:169668 imports @effect/platform-node externally, so this source is what runs. The repo patches (effect@4.0.2 = RpcClient, platform-node-shared = ChildProcessSpawner) do not touch it. The raw outputs support every claim. run8-traced shows listen() at 699 ms, migrations at 714 ms, 8 'request' events emitted with zero listeners (including GET /ws with upgrade=websocket), and handlers plus 'Listening on' at 899 ms. run7 shows 7 sockets held for 330 s, never answered or closed. fix-hold-1/2 and fix-503 show 0 hung. The poller simulations go from +892..981 ms to +4..19 ms. The Bun 404 placeholder is real (BunHttpServer.ts:143-148). Simply binding later is not a cheap alternative: AdvertisedEndpointRegistry.ts:165 and startupAccess.ts:263 (inside RuntimeServicesLive) need the bound HttpServer. That makes the evaluate()-based gate the right local fix. Practical exposure: desktop cold boot is masked by the log detector; SSH cold launch, readiness pollers, browser and mobile reconnects during a server restart, and shutdown stalls are exposed. The rating stays high because the failure is an indefinite hang and the fix is S effort.

none. This is the lead in EVIDENCE.md; the root cause and fix are new.

Part of Priority 3: Bound shutdown and crash handling

Expected gain

About −19 s per CLI or service shutdown while a tab or remote client is connected. Desktop quit, relaunch and update: roughly −0.5-1 s, and finalizers actually run instead of SIGKILL every time.

What happens today

preemptiveShutdown is timeoutOrElse(server.close, gracefulShutdownTimeout ?? 20 s) (NodeHttpServer.ts:121-126). In serve(), the per-request scope that runs HTTP and WebSocket fibers is forked at :164, before the preemptive finalizer is registered at :173. Finalizers run in reverse order, so server.close() waits for WebSocket sockets that are closed only after it finishes; the timeout is the only way out. Measured SIGTERM to exit: 1.05-1.47 s with no clients, 20.38/20.39/20.41/20.38 s with one authenticated /ws connection. The WS was closed by the server at +20.006-20.008 s, http.Server.close() completed at +20.007 s, and the Agent Control MCP listener (a RuntimeServicesLive finalizer) closed only at +20.36-20.40 s, so finalizers sequenced after the HTTP layer wait too. 10-11 hung startup sockets gave 20.44-20.49 s. server.ts passes no gracefulShutdownTimeout. The desktop renderer always holds a WS, and stopBackendAndWaitForExit sends SIGKILL 2 s after SIGTERM (main.ts:2820-2824). So, from the code path, every desktop quit, relaunch or update install with an open window waits about 2 s and ends in SIGKILL. That skips RuntimeServicesLive finalizers, likely including restart-continuation shutdown hints (serverRuntimeStartup.ts:845-859) and the SQLite close; this part is inferred from the finalizer order, not directly observed. In CLI mode, Ctrl-C with an open browser tab takes about 20.4 s.

Proposal

Immediate mitigation: pass gracefulShutdownTimeout: "750 millis" (at most 1 s) in the NodeHttpServer.layer options at server.ts:193-196, so the HTTP stage ends well inside desktop's 2 s budget. Proper fix: carry a patch to @effect/platform-node, using the existing patches/ mechanism (effect@4.0.2 and @effect/platform-node-shared are already patched). In the serve finalizer, close the per-request scope first or concurrently: interrupt WS fibers so clients get a 1001 close, call server.closeIdleConnections(), then await server.close(). Send the change upstream. After that, measure p99 graceful shutdown and set the desktop SIGKILL grace above it, or make it acknowledgement-based. Add a test: open a WS, send SIGTERM, assert exit within 3 s.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Checked the finalizer order in effect/src/internal/effect.ts. scopeForkUnsafe (:4003-4011) registers the child-scope close on serveScope when Scope.forkUnsafe runs (NodeHttpServer.ts:164). addFinalizerExit(preemptiveShutdown) is registered later (:173). scopeCloseFinalizers (:3976-3995) runs finalizers in reverse, so server.close() waits on WebSocket sockets whose fibers are interrupted only afterwards, and only the 20 s timeoutOrElse (:121-126) ends the wait. No gracefulShutdownTimeout, closeAllConnections or disablePreemptiveShutdown is set anywhere for the main server (git grep). Measured outputs agree: ws-shutdown.txt shows 20384/20390/20413 ms with a WS against 1249/1470 ms without one. ws-shutdown-trace shows main close completing at +20007 ms and the Agent Control MCP listener (a RuntimeServicesLive finalizer) closing at +20363-20398 ms, so runtime finalizers really are queued behind the HTTP stage. shutdown-with-hung shows 20444/20493 ms. Desktop side: the before-quit cleanup (main.ts:4119-4146) calls stopBackendAndWaitForExit while windows, and therefore the renderer WS, are still open, and SIGKILL fires at 2 s (main.ts:2818-2825). Relaunch (1256) and update install (2460) use the same path. recordShutdownHints is reached only through the startup finalizer (serverRuntimeStartup.ts:845-858; no other caller per git grep). So restart-continuation hints are lost on every desktop quit, relaunch or update with an open window; this is inferred from the order plus the MCP-listener evidence. This is a reliability bug, not only latency. No prior work covers it (the hardening doc:134 covers draining queued output only).

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

−0.85 to −0.95 s per remote SSH environment cold launch (measured by emulation, 5/5 boots)

What happens today

After nohup ... serve, the remote launch script runs wait_ready: http.get('/') with a 1,000 ms timeout (SSH_READY_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS), then sleep 100 ms, in a loop. A refused probe returns in about 1 ms, so probes repeat every ~100 ms. The dead window is 145-280 ms, so one probe always lands in it and waits its full timeout. Emulated against real cold boots: ready at Listening +893, 923, 979, 941 and 896 ms (5/5 hits); for example, a probe sent at 715 ms timed out at 1718 ms. The local tunnel waitForHttpReady uses the same 100 ms / 1 s pattern, though by then the server is usually already up.

Proposal

Fixed by startup-accept-before-handler-blackhole: with the gate, readiness lands at +18-19 ms. As defense in depth, lower the remote loopback probe timeout to about 250 ms (a healthy loopback answer takes about 1 ms) and treat 503 as not ready (it already only accepts 2xx).

Verifier (Confirmed)

Checked the timing constants (tunnel.ts:53-57, SSH_READY_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS=1000). The wait_ready script (255-300) does http.get('/') with a 1 s timeout and a 100 ms sleep. It is injected at 375-379 and run right after nohup serve at 463-470, and RYCO_READY_PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS is substituted at :543. The remote runner execs node, ryco or npx (tunnel.ts:326-339), so the Node dead window applies on the remote, not Bun's 404. The emulation in sim-pollers.txt (A_ssh_remote_wait_ready: +893/923/979/941/896 ms) and sim-pollers-fix.txt (+18-19 ms) match. This is a direct consequence of startup-accept-before-handler-blackhole rather than an independent root cause. The local waitForHttpReady at :1088 runs after the remote is ready, as the investigator said.

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

Turns an indefinite stall (estimated 2-14% chance per server restart seen by an open client) into a delay of 5-10 s at most. Also stops leaked hung sockets from eating Chromium's 6-per-origin limit.

What happens today

Every primary reconnect attempt first resolves its URL through authenticatedSocketUrl, which POSTs /api/auth/ws-token (service.ts:906-911) using a plain fetch with no signal (httpClient.ts:6-9). That call is not even wrapped in retryTransientBootstrap (primaryAuth.ts:139-150). protocol.ts:291-318 wraps url() in Effect.tryPromise with no timeout and does not pass the AbortSignal. If the POST hangs, the socket acquire never completes; the Effect 10 s open timeout (Socket.ts:1093-1104) only starts after the URL resolves, so the retry schedule (1, 2, 4 ... 64 s) never advances. The UI stays 'reconnecting' until a foreground/online event fires reconnectAfterResume (supervision.ts:822-845) or the user reloads. fetchDescriptor and fetchSessionState treat AbortError as transient (primaryAuth.ts:106-118), but nothing ever aborts them. For saved/remote environments, fetchRemoteJson (remoteApi.ts:47-66) has the same gap, and ensureSavedEnvironmentConnection (supervision.ts:629-636) de-duplicates per environment, so every retry or Connect click joins the hung promise; the 60 s slot timeout rejects only the slot. Hit probability (estimate): about window/gap for the first attempt after the restarted server binds, roughly 7-14% if the server returns within 1-3 s and 2-7% later. Desktop crash-restart is a near miss on this machine (attempt 1 at about 1.0 s, bind measured at 1.07-1.45 s; 0/13 stalls in the sweep) and is also hidden by desktop-crash-restart-full-reload. Chromium/Electron fetch has no response-header timeout (estimate), so a hit is indefinite, and each hung request holds one of Chromium's 6 HTTP/1.1 sockets per origin. iOS React Native fetch times out at about 60 s (NSURLSession default, estimate).

Proposal

Add a shared fetchWithDeadline(httpClient, url, init, timeoutMs = 5_000) in client-runtime/connection that combines AbortSignal.timeout with any caller signal via AbortSignal.any. Use it for fetchSessionState, issuePrimaryWebSocketToken (also wrap this one in retryTransientBootstrap), exchangeBootstrapCredential, fetchDescriptor and fetchRemoteJson. These are tiny control-plane calls that answer in about 1 ms locally, and AbortError is already classified as transient. In protocol.ts, call Effect.tryPromise({ try: (signal) => url(signal) }) followed by Effect.timeout("10 seconds") mapped to WsUrlProviderError so it is retried, and pass the signal down so an abandoned ws-token request releases its socket. In supervision, give each saved-env attempt an AbortController that is aborted on slot timeout and drop it from pendingSavedEnvironmentConnections, so the next retry starts fresh.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code facts hold. webHttpClient (apps/web/src/platform/httpClient.ts:6-9) and the mobile adapter (11-20) add no signal. issuePrimaryWebSocketToken (primaryAuth.ts:139-150) is not wrapped in retryTransientBootstrap (106-118). authenticatedSocketUrl (service.ts:906-911) is the per-attempt URL provider (:914). protocol.ts:291-318 wraps url() in tryPromise with retry only on errors, not on hangs. Effect's open timeout (Socket.ts:1093-1104) applies only after acquire, which includes URL resolution. supervision.ts:629-672 de-duplicates onto the pending promise, and connectWithinSlot (683-701) times out only the slot. The ping timeout (protocol.ts:457-466) needs an open socket. Only resume or online events (822-845) rescue a stuck acquire. However, the trigger was never observed: sim-reconnect shows 0/13 stalls, and the 2-14% per-restart figure is an unvalidated estimate. Once the startup gate lands, the startup-window trigger goes away. The rating stays medium because the same missing deadline also covers half-open TCP to saved remote environments after sleep or network change, where the 60 s slot comment already admits hung connects. The hosted-Hub deadline precedent at authorization/api.ts:2970-2995 is confirmed.

Prior work

Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

Estimate: −100 to −250 ms desktop cold-start time to first app render. This is the overlap of renderer boot with the measured 145-280 ms runtime window; it is larger on slow disks or hub-enabled nodes.

What happens today

Desktop calls window.loadURL(backendHttpUrl) only after 'Listening on', which comes after the whole RuntimeServicesLive build. Trace: bind at T, migrations done T+22 ms, registry reconcile T+120 ms, reaper T+196 ms, handlers T+201 ms. Only then does the renderer fetch index.html and the 75-file, 2,023 KiB raw boot graph and evaluate it before its first API call. The static route needs only ServerConfig, FileSystem and Path (http.ts:741-826), all available at bind time because PlatformServicesLive is built below HttpServerLive.

Proposal

Builds on the startup gate. (a) Extract the static-file logic into a plain function and, while gated, serve GET requests for static assets directly; API, auth, /.well-known and WS requests are still held until the real router attaches. (b) Emit 'http-bound' on the desktop fd right after listen(). (c) On 'http-bound', desktop calls loadURL, so renderer boot overlaps the runtime build and the renderer's first descriptor/session calls are held and answered the moment the router attaches.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed that staticAndDevRouteLayer (http.ts:741-826) needs only ServerConfig, FileSystem, Path and HttpPlatform (via HttpServerResponse.file in staticFileResponse, http.ts:211-244). All of these come from layers built before bind, since NodeHttpServer.layer provides the HttpPlatform services. Desktop calls loadURL only after readiness (main.ts:1461-1494 → 1441-1459). The saving is unmeasured. It is bounded by min(runtime window ≈145-280 ms, renderer time from loadURL to its first API call). After the first launch, hashed assets are served immutable (http.ts:106-115) and come from HTTP cache, so overlapped work is mostly parse and eval of the boot graph, and the desktop boot page is already visible meanwhile. Implementing it needs a second, pre-router static serving path. That path must share one extracted function with the router route (devUrl redirect, traversal checks, cache headers) to avoid duplicated security-sensitive logic. It also needs a new 'http-bound' fd protocol and depends on the gate. Medium risk and M effort hold. The impact estimate is plausible but unverified.

none. Complements the boot-graph size findings in EVIDENCE.md without repeating them.

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

Avoids +0.9 s on desktop cold start in configurations where the log line is suppressed or changed; removes a fragile coupling to log text

What happens today

The fast readiness signal is a string emitted by Effect's HttpServer.logAddress at Info level. backendChildEnv forwards process.env, including RYCO_LOG_LEVEL (cli.ts:308), so a user with RYCO_LOG_LEVEL=Warning or Error, a logger format change, or disableListenLog would silently remove it. Readiness then falls back to waitForHttpReady (/.well-known/ryco/environment, 100 ms / 1 s), which measured +892, 920, 981, 938 and 893 ms after Listening (5/5) because it always hits the dead window. The desktop already passes structured pipes to the child (bootstrap fd 3, telemetry fd 4; main.ts:2669-2675).

Proposal

After handlers are attached, have the serve layer write an explicit structured readiness frame such as {type:'http-serving', port} to the desktop telemetry or bootstrap fd. Optionally also write {type:'http-bound'} right after listen(), for early-static-serving-desktop-overlap. Desktop waits on that frame and keeps the log detector and HTTP poller as fallbacks. With the startup gate in place, the HTTP fallback costs at most the remaining window instead of a full probe timeout.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The coupling is real. LISTENING_LOG_FRAGMENT='Listening on http://' (serverListeningDetector.ts:1,43). waitForBackendStartupReady runs the HTTP poller in parallel (backendStartupReadiness.ts:9-65). waitForHttpReady defaults to 100 ms / 1 s (backendReadiness.ts:11-13), and RYCO_LOG_LEVEL is honoured (cli.ts:308). The trigger scenario is rare, though. backendChildEnv (main.ts:602-628) forwards process.env, but the desktop shell-environment import is allowlisted (shellEnvironmentCache.ts:8-18, 141-157: PATH, SSH_AUTH_SOCK, HOMEBREW_*, XDG_*, FNM_*). RYCO_LOG_LEVEL therefore reaches the packaged backend only through launchctl setenv or launching the app binary from a terminal. Development uses Bun, where the window returns 404 and is retried within 100 ms. After the gate fix, the fallback costs at most the remaining window, not 0.9 s. Worth doing as a robustness change (a structured readiness frame on the existing fd 3/4 pipes, main.ts:2669-2675), but low impact.

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

Correctness: guarantees the ready event, pairing output and browser open happen only after requests can be served (matters for hub-enabled and headless service starts)

What happens today

httpListeningLayer only needs HttpServer, which is already bound, and ServerRuntimeStartup. It sits in a Layer.mergeAll with the serve layer, and mergeAll builds all members concurrently (Layer.ts:1625-1640). Nothing makes it wait for serve. Today this is hidden because the routes build is synchronous unless HubConnectorLive awaits (hub enabled), and the command gate usually opens 22-32 ms after 'Listening on'. In run1, though, the gate opened 5 ms before 'Listening on'. Once markHttpListening fires, the startup fiber logs 'http listener ready', publishes ready, and prints headless pairing output or opens the browser, possibly while requests are still being dropped.

Proposal

Make the mark depend on serve: Layer.effectDiscard(startup.markHttpListening).pipe(Layer.provideMerge(HttpRouter.serve(...))), or have the serve layer return a service whose construction marks it. Rename it markHttpServing. Keep runtimeStateLayer and tailscaleServeLayer in the mergeAll.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Structurally correct. mergeAllEffect (Layer.ts:1625-1636) builds every member with concurrency equal to layers.length. httpListeningLayer (server.ts:601-607) depends only on HttpServer and ServerRuntimeStartup, both already built, so nothing orders the mark after HttpServer.serve. markHttpListening resolves the Deferred (serverRuntimeStartup.ts:1113-1116) that gates 'http listener ready', the ready publish, headless output and browser open (1029-1046, 1084-1104). In all 11 recorded boots, though, 'startup http listener ready' was logged after 'Listening on': run1 853 → 854, and the others 22-48 ms later, because the startup fiber also waits for the command gate. The early-publish case needs an async gap inside the serve build (hub enabled) that outlasts the gate. That case is plausible but unobserved, and once the gate fix lands early requests are held rather than dropped. Low-impact correctness hardening with an S fix.

Part of Priority 3: Bound shutdown and crash handling

Expected gain

About −0.3-1 s on each restart, relaunch or quit, and fewer SIGKILLed shutdowns on desktop (estimate)

What happens today

SIGTERM to exit, measured 1.5 s after startup: 1158, 1198, 1163, 1181, 1166, 1051, 1249 and 1470 ms. SIGINT 0.3 s after startup: 2757 and 1749 ms. Shutdown trace: main HTTP closed at +1 ms; the Copilot SDK stop waits for its CLI child to exit (+333 to +589 ms, with a 10 s timer); opencode child exited at +153 to +760 ms; the last listener closed at +1.01 to +1.45 s. The analytics finalizer (AnalyticsService.ts:212) flushes buffered events with a POST to the PostHog host (line 110) and no timeout, so on a slow or captive network the shutdown waits on network I/O. Desktop sends SIGKILL at 2 s. Attribution of the remaining ~0.5 s is partial.

Proposal

Wrap the shutdown flush in Effect.timeout('300 millis') and drop events on timeout. Check that provider stops (Copilot, opencode) run in parallel and are bounded. Add a 'shutdown phase' span or log for each finalizer group so the tail can be attributed. Then set the desktop SIGKILL grace from measured p99, or make it acknowledgement-based, together with the 20 s WebSocket fix. Perf harnesses should set RYCO_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=0.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The analytics finalizer is confirmed: AnalyticsService.ts:212 calls flush (137-171), which loops sendBatch, a POST to posthogHost/batch/ (110-114) with no timeout, using the FetchHttpClient provided at server.ts:698. shutdown-timers.txt shows a setTimeout(1000) from scheduleFlush (bin.mjs:112420 area) at +7 ms and an undici request at +137 ms. Telemetry network I/O really was on the measured shutdown path, and the harness did not disable telemetry. Copilot SDK waitForChildExit with a 10 s timer is confirmed (client.js:52-63). Measured SIGTERM-to-exit of 1.05-1.47 s matches the trace files. Attribution of the remaining ~0.5 s is still partial. The measured shutdown is close to desktop's 2 s SIGKILL even with no clients, so bounding the flush (for example 300 ms) and adding per-finalizer timing are worthwhile. The rating stays low.

Part of Priority 3: Bound shutdown and crash handling

Expected gain

Saves a full renderer re-boot (several hundred ms plus all data refetch, estimate) and preserves route state after each backend crash-restart

What happens today

startBackend() always ends with ensureInitialBackendWindowOpen() (main.ts:2776). After readiness it calls loadPackagedBackendAppWindow, which returns early only if the current URL is not on the backend (main.ts:1448-1455). A window showing any backend route therefore gets window.loadURL(backendHttpUrl): a full reload that loses the current route and repeats the boot-graph download and parse (2,023 KiB raw) plus all snapshot fetches. That reload is what currently rescues a renderer whose ws-token POST hung in the dead window during the restart (crash restart backoff is 500 ms, main.ts:443-444).

Proposal

Once the startup gate and client deadlines are in place, call loadURL only when the window is on the desktop boot page or about:blank. Otherwise let the persistent WS reconnect and resync from the snapshot. If a reload is needed for a backend version change, decide that from the server version reported on reconnect.

Verifier (Confirmed)

startBackend ends with ensureInitialBackendWindowOpen() (main.ts:2776). Readiness then calls loadPackagedBackendAppWindow (1441-1459), which returns early only when the current URL is outside the backend and is not about:blank or the boot URL. Any backend route therefore gets loadURL(backendHttpUrl): a full reload to the root that loses the route. Restart backoff starts at 500 ms (main.ts:443-446). Correction to the impact: hashed assets are served with immutable cache headers (http.ts:106-115), so the reload mostly repeats parse/eval and all snapshot fetches rather than downloading 2,023 KiB. Backend crash-restarts are rare. The reload may also be deliberate state hygiene after a crash, so removing it needs a version-change check, as the investigator proposed. Low impact, medium risk.

Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

Unmeasured. Removes keychain and identity I/O (estimated 20-200 ms, unbounded if an access prompt appears) from time-to-first-response and from desktop readiness on hub-enabled nodes.

What happens today

HttpRouter.serve(makeRoutesLayer).pipe(Layer.provide(HubConnectorLive)) means HubConnectorLive must finish before HttpServer.serve attaches handlers. When the hub is enabled, construction awaits processLock.acquire(), possibly twice, and then makeHubIdentityRuntime, which runs a chain of sequential awaits: state store, retirement store, selectProtectedSecretStore with OS keychain probing, prekey, continuity, policy, fallback, authorization and introduction stores. With the hub disabled the measured reaper-to-handler gap was about 5 ms. The hub-enabled cost was not measured here because it would touch the user's keychain. Keychain access can also block on an OS permission prompt, during which every request accepted on the port hangs (or, with the gate, waits).

Proposal

Expose HubConnectorService immediately with a Deferred-backed identity and fork identity custody with Effect.forkScoped after serve. Hub-specific routes and RPCs await the deferred with a timeout, or return 503 while it is loading, so the request handler and the desktop readiness signal no longer depend on keychain I/O. Add a timing span or log for identity runtime construction so the cost becomes visible.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed that HubConnectorLive is provided only to the serve layer (server.ts:684-686), so it is built before handlers attach. With the hub enabled, construction awaits processLock.acquire() (twice if 'unavailable', HubConnectorLive.ts:465-474). It then awaits makeIdentityRuntime (476-499), which runs about 11 sequential awaits (HubIdentityRuntime.ts:824-887) plus keychain probing in selectProtectedSecretStore (592-640). However, the hub is disabled by default (config.ts:71-72); the disabled path uses a synchronous readOnly() (:512), and the gap measured about 5 ms. The hub-enabled cost is unmeasured. The proposal underestimates the risk. The comments at HubConnectorLive.ts:452-464 say the lock and identity startup ordering is deliberate: owner-relied-on writes happen before the runtime exists. Deferring custody past serve means re-proving those invariants and making every hub route, RPC, local-introduction and native-claim path await a deferred. That is more like L effort and medium-to-high risk. Location correction: 773-781 is the opt-in cloud-history sync (RYCO_HUB_THREAD_CACHE_ENABLED, default false), not identity construction; the layer export is at 838-842. Adding a timing span for identity construction is a cheap first step.

SQLite and snapshots at boot 17 findings · 4 high · 8 medium · 5 low

Boot cost grows with the database: the command read model is loaded 3× before the command gate, one query scans every activity row (0.24–2 s on your 9.27 GB DB), and the first client connect triggers 2P+1 full shell snapshots.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

Boot (DB side): Sqlite.ts opens a single synchronous node:sqlite connection. It sets only busy_timeout, WAL and foreign_keys, so cache_size stays at 2 MB, mmap at 0 and synchronous at FULL. It then runs the 82 migrations and compatibility repairs. That part is cheap: 6 ms on a warm 784 MB DB. The cost comes next. Building the OrchestrationEngine layer runs the projector catch-up (one event per transaction) and then a full getCommandReadModel. That model is 9 queries: every project, thread, both user-message anchors per thread, actionable activities, all proposed plans with markdown, sessions, latest turns. The actionable-activity query and the boot checkpoint-revert recovery both full-scan projection_thread_activities, because no index leads with kind. The HTTP socket is already bound but routes are not served until this finishes, which widens the accept-but-never-respond window noted in EVIDENCE.md. The startup phases then run getCommandReadModel two more times: in workspace.validate, whose result is unused when the workspace is not restricted, and in provider-session reconcile. They also build a full shell snapshot in ProviderCommandReactor.start just to find pending goal syncs. That snapshot waits for git repository-identity probes (2 spawns per project, chats included, 1 s budget). Only then does the command gate open.

Measured on a synthetic copy of the perf-home DB (5k threads, 120k messages, 400k activities, 400k events, 784 MB) with the production bundle: migrations to Listening went from about 164 ms (tiny DB) to 2.43 s cold and 0.46 to 0.85 s warm. The startup span (Listening to gate) went from 34 ms to 0.87 s cold and 1.22 to 1.38 s warm. Most of it is three command-read-model loads (about 200 to 376 ms each warm, 1.9 s for the first one cold) plus about 250 to 380 ms of git probes. On the first client subscription the server forks reconcileAllWorktrees. That pass builds 2×P+1 full shell snapshots (P = projects plus chats whose folders exist) while it also builds the client's own snapshot: about 100 ms SQL plus decode, about 30 ms encode, 5.65 MiB for 4.5k threads.

Steady state: the hub connector rebuilds the full shell up to once per second whenever events flow, and its upload throws for more than about 1.6k threads. Every reconnect decodes up to 1,000 events per stream just to check whether it can resume. Statistics recompute everything (about 0.4 to 0.57 s) inside a transaction that blocks the only connection, and any write invalidates the cache. Thread windows are already fast (0.8 to 3.9 ms; earlier work).
