Measurements (15)
  • Synthetic DB built from a COPY of /tmp/ryco-perf-home/userdata/state.sqlite with .perf-research/persistence-boot/gen.sql (sqlite3 3.54): 101 projects (10 deleted), 5,001 threads (500 deleted, 1,250 archived), 60k turns, 120k messages, 400k activities, 1k plans of 4 KB, 300 worktrees, 400k events; 784 MB. Machine load average 8-18 from parallel research jobs, so treat absolute ms as directional. 'Cold' means a fresh APFS clone (cp -c), so the new vnode has no cached pages. Large DB copies were deleted afterwards; gen.sql regenerates one in about 4 s.
  • Real server code via measure-snapshots.ts (node 24.21, node:sqlite, production layers): getCommandReadModel 1,837-1,930 ms first call (cold clone), 202-236 ms warm, 19.20 MiB JSON, heap +45-69 MiB. getShellSnapshot 96-104 ms warm: 4,501 threads, 5.65 MiB JSON, 1,292 B per thread shell. getThreadWindow 0.8-3.9 ms (66 KiB); getThreadDetailById 0.7 ms; getCounts 0.2 ms.
  • getStatistics on the synthetic DB: 559-575 ms cold, 0.1 ms cached, 396-413 ms after one unrelated UPDATE of projection_state (total_changes cache key). Output: 5,086 daily buckets, 1.58 MB JSON.
  • Production boot (apps/server/dist/bin.mjs via .perf-research/persistence-boot/boot-harness-db.mjs, 3 runs each, port 24791). Tiny DB: migrations to Listening about 164 ms, server.startup span 34 ms. Synthetic DB cold run: migrations to Listening 2,432 ms, Listening to command gate 871 ms. Warm runs: migrations to Listening 458 / 851 ms; server.startup span 1,219 / 1,384 ms, made of workspace.validate 322 / 376, reactors.start 552 / 633 (incl. resolveRepositoryIdentitiesForProjects 337 / 377 for 91 roots) and provider-sessions.reconcile 344 / 374.
  • Cold-boot trace (server.trace.ndjson sqlite spans): inside engine hydration, thread rows 326 ms, user-message anchors 674 ms, actionable activities 1,057 ms. An unrelated AgentControl MCP installation query waited 1,956 ms behind that transaction on the single connection.
  • Per query, cold vs warm, via cold-queries.mjs (node:sqlite, server PRAGMAs): actionable activities 948-1,559 / 69-168 ms; checkpoint-revert scan (0 rows) 986-1,732 / 53-103; user-message anchors 528-675 / 26-41; thread rows with latestCompletedTurnAt 201-295 / 16-26; latest turns 162-275 / 10-22; statistics tool uses 1,139-1,976 / 100-577; statistics turns 180-462 / 26-58.
  • Index experiment: CREATE INDEX on projection_thread_activities(kind, thread_id, sequence, created_at, activity_id), 28.5 MB at 400k rows. Checkpoint-revert scan 0.4 ms cold / 0.0 warm; actionable 26 ms warm; tool uses 46 cold / 41 warm. sqlite3 CLI: actionable 74 to 18 ms, statistics token UNION 129 to 74 ms, tool uses 105 to 52 ms. A partial index WHERE kind IN (...) was NOT used by the planner for either kind = 'checkpoint.revert' or the identical IN list (EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN).
  • mmap_size = 256 MiB under the same load (cold-default-2 vs cold-mmap-2): cold thread rows 295 to 196 ms, anchors 675 to 400, latest turns 275 to 98, checkpoint turns 462 to 110, checkpoint-revert scan 1,732 to 962; warm 10-50% lower. cache_size = -32768 alone showed no clear gain under the noise.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

Removes 2 of the 3 pre-gate hydrations: about 450-750 ms off boot-to-command-ready at 5k threads / 400k activities (warm), more on cold disks. No change on tiny DBs.

What happens today

The engine hydrates commandReadModel at construction (OrchestrationEngine.ts:590). startup then calls getCommandReadModel() again for workspace.validate. In the default non-restricted mode, validateRestrictedWorkspaceSnapshot returns immediately after the load (serverRuntimeStartup.ts:518), so that load is wasted. A third load happens in reconcileOrphanedProviderSessions (line 638), and RestartContinuation.dispatchPending loads it once per page (line 679). Each load runs 9 full-table reads (projects, all threads incl. deleted, anchors, actionable activities, all plans with markdown, sessions, latest turns, state) plus mapping. Measured at 5k threads / 400k activities: about 200-236 ms warm, 1.84-1.93 s for the first cold call. Boot trace spans: workspace.validate 232-376 ms and provider-sessions.reconcile 213-374 ms, both before the command gate opens.

Proposal

Add OrchestrationEngineShape.getReadModel (Effect.sync returning the worker-maintained commandReadModel; it is already the decider's source of truth). Use it in reconcileOrphanedProviderSessions, RestartContinuation.dispatchPending and restricted-workspace validation. In serverRuntimeStartup.ts:905, check workspaceAccessPolicy.isRestricted BEFORE loading anything. Keep the SQL getCommandReadModel only for engine bootstrap, CLI offline mode and the HTTP debug endpoint.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Checked OrchestrationEngine.ts:589-590 (bootstrap, then getCommandReadModel). serverRuntimeStartup.ts:904-913 loads the model unconditionally for workspace.validate, and validateRestrictedWorkspaceSnapshot returns at :518 when the workspace is not restricted, so that load is wasted. reconcileOrphanedProviderSessions loads again at :638. RestartContinuation.ts:677-679 loads only when listPending returns rows, so it is not paid on every boot; the 'once per page' wording is right but conditional. The engine has no read accessor today. getReadModel was deliberately removed in upstream commit aca0fa4e5 (#2204), so reintroducing it needs care: the in-memory model holds anchors plus messages and activities seen since boot, not the SQL shape. Callers here (settleStaleProjectedTurns, capture, restartFenceUserMessageId) use only fields the decider already relies on. Impact: measured in isolation, loads #2 and #3 cost 202-236 ms each (measure-run1.txt), so removing both saves about 0.42-0.47 s at 5k threads. The boot spans of 213-376 ms include connection queueing behind the forked orphan sweep, so 750 ms is an upper bound. The saving scales with DB size: the whole startup span is 34 ms on a tiny DB. Moving the isRestricted check ahead of the load is a one-line quick win.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

Estimated from measured per-snapshot cost: P=30 means about 61 snapshots, roughly 6 s; P=200 roughly 40 s of serialized main-thread and DB work starting at first paint. After the fix: 1 snapshot or a few ms of indexed reads.

What happens today

subscribeShell forkDetaches reconcileAllWorktrees (throttled to once per 5 min, so the first subscription after boot always runs it). The pass loads one shell snapshot, then for each available project, 4 at a time: getProjectShellById (plus identity probe), listWorktreePaths (git), ensureProjectMainWorktree (another full getShellSnapshot, plus git status when no main worktree exists), then a full getShellSnapshot again. partitionReconcilableProjectRoots only checks existsSync, so chat projects are included. Each snapshot measured 96-104 ms SQL+decode at 4.5k threads, all serialized on the one connection and blocking the main thread while the client waits for its own first shell snapshot and thread window.

Proposal

Load the rows once and pass them in: give reconcileProjectWorktrees and ensureProjectMainWorktree the project's worktrees and threads from a single snapshot, or better, from narrow indexed queries (worktrees by project_id via idx_projection_worktrees_project_archived, threads via idx_projection_threads_project_id). Skip isChatProject. Delay the pass until after the first shell and thread window are served (for example 15-30 s after the first subscription, or on idle) and run it at low priority.

That means it reruns on any reconnect or hub subscription after 5 min, not only the first after boot. Total is 2P+1 snapshots. partitionReconcilableProjectRoots (worktreeReconciliation.ts:42-52) only checks existsSync. For a non-git chat folder, listWorktreePaths returns [] on a non-zero exit (GitVcsDriverCore.ts:2884-2892), so chats still pay both snapshots plus a git status spawn. Identity probes are cached from the boot snapshot (1-min TTL), so each snapshot costs about 96-104 ms SQL plus decode at 4.5k threads (measure-run1.txt). The 6 s and 40 s figures are extrapolations for that size; at around 500 threads it would be about 10 ms per snapshot. The client's own snapshot interleaves on the FIFO semaphore rather than waiting for all of them, but CPU and connection contention at first paint is real.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

250-380 ms less boot-to-command-ready at about 90 projects; up to 1,000 ms less on each shell snapshot built after an idle minute (reconnect or hub first paint); 0 instead of 2×(projects+chats) git spawns per snapshot.

What happens today

After the SQL, getShellSnapshot awaits resolveRepositoryIdentitiesForProjects for every non-deleted project (concurrency 4, timeoutOption 1,000 ms). Each root runs git rev-parse and git remote -v (24.9 ms median per project, measured). Both positive and negative cache entries live 1 minute. Chat projects (one Ryco-managed folder per chat) are not skipped. At boot, ProviderCommandReactor.start builds a full shell snapshot only to find threads with a pending goal sync; the trace shows 245-377 ms of identity probing inside reactors.start (91 non-existent roots, 1 spawn each). The 1 s budget runs out at roughly 160 projects plus chats, after which the snapshot returns null identities and the UI loses repo info. Correctness issue. Any snapshot built more than 1 minute after the previous one (reconnect, hub client, AgentControl tool) pays the probes again.

Proposal

Persist identity in projection_projects (repository_identity_json plus a fingerprint of <gitdir>/config and HEAD size/mtime), and serve snapshots from the DB without waiting on git. Refresh in the background (stale-while-revalidate, roughly 30-minute TTL or fs.watch on .git/config) and dispatch a project meta event when the identity changes. Skip isChatProject and non-existent roots before spawning. Replace 'git remote -v' with parsing .git/config, or a single 'git config --get-regexp remote' spawn. In ProviderCommandReactor.start, use a targeted query (goal_json IS NOT NULL AND json_extract(goal_json,'$.synchronization.state')='pending').

Verifier (Confirmed)

RepositoryIdentityResolver.ts:92-95 (1-min positive and negative TTL, 1 s per-probe timeout) and :103-171 (rev-parse, then 'remote -v', i.e. 2 spawns per root). ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:560-599 filters only deletedAt; chat projects are not skipped. Concurrency is 4 (:530) and the 1 s overall budget applies at :2658-2661. ProviderCommandReactor.ts:3151 builds a full getShellSnapshot inside start() only to find goal.synchronization.state==='pending'. That snapshot sits inside reactors.start, which precedes provider-sessions.reconcile and the gate; the trace shows identity resolution at 245-377 ms in that window. No persisted identity exists (no repository_identity in persistence). Quick wins (S): skip isChatProject and !existsSync roots, and use a targeted pending-goal query at boot. Part of Priority 4: Take provider probing and heavy runtime layers off the boot path

Expected gain

Static shell and descriptor available about 0.3-2.3 s earlier at 5k threads, and far earlier during a projector catch-up. Narrows the hang window from EVIDENCE.md.

What happens today

HttpServerLive is provideMerge'd (socket bound early). HttpRouter.serve and the 'Listening on' log need RuntimeServicesLive, which includes the engine, which runs projectionPipeline.bootstrap and getCommandReadModel during layer construction. Migrations to Listening: about 164 ms on a tiny DB, 2.43 s cold and 0.46-0.85 s warm at 5k threads, 29.1 s with 50k lagging events. That is exactly the window in which EVIDENCE.md reproduced connections that never get a response. The web shell (served by this server) cannot load during it either.

Proposal

Build the engine without blocking: fork hydration and catch-up into the existing startup phase. dispatch already queues behind the command gate, and read RPCs can await an engine-ready Deferred. Let HttpRouter.serve start immediately so static assets, the environment descriptor and the WebSocket upgrade are answered while hydration runs. Together with the 3x-hydration, kind-index and anchor fixes, the remaining hydration also shrinks.

A cheaper reliability mitigation is to not accept connections, or to answer 503, until routes are mounted.

Expected gain

About 30% less CPU per build from dropping the redundant decode. Payload 25-80% smaller depending on the archived share. N concurrent subscribers or priority fan-outs become 1 build.

What happens today

Every row is already Schema-decoded by SqlSchema.findAll, yet the assembled snapshot is decoded again with decodeShellSnapshot (28-37 ms measured at 4,501 threads); the RPC then encodes it (29-35 ms) and stringifies it (8-10 ms). The CPU profile of repeated builds shows about 45 ms SQLite and about 55 ms Effect/Schema per build. listProjectRows and listThreadRows read ALL rows, including deleted ones, which are decoded and then filtered out in JS. All archived threads (25% in the synthetic set) are shipped at about 1.3 KB each. Every thread-priority change runs the full snapshot effect once per connected subscriber (Stream.mapEffect(() => snapshot)).

Proposal

(a) Remove the final decodeShellSnapshot from the production path; keep it in tests and dev assertions. (b) Add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL to the shell project and thread queries, and compute updatedAt with SELECT max(updated_at). (c) Single-flight and memoize the built snapshot per (snapshotSequence, priority batch, liveness version) so concurrent subscribers and internal callers share one build. (d) Send priority changes as a small stream item instead of N full snapshots. (e) Ship archived threads lazily (counts plus a paged RPC) and omit null or default fields from thread shells.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The redundant whole-snapshot decode is real: rows are decoded by SqlSchema.findAll, then decodeShellSnapshot runs again at ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:2742 (defined at :98). The 28-37 ms figure is not persisted anywhere: measure-decode.ts exists but has no output file. It is plausible but unverified. listProjectRows and listThreadRows (:601-666) have no deleted_at filter, but they are shared with getCommandReadModel, which needs deleted rows, so (b) requires shell-specific queries. The per-subscriber priority rebuild is real (orchestrationStreams.ts:558-559) but only fires on thread-priority ranking batches, which are rare. Lazy archived threads (e) is a UX and protocol change, not a perf tweak. Single-flight (c) is the most valuable sub-item because boot, reconcile and client snapshots overlap.

Part of Priority 9: Statistics: memoize, aggregate incrementally, never block the server

Expected gain

First open about 0.5 s down to under 50 ms with rollups. No 0.4-0.6 s connection stalls per open or refresh during activity.

What happens today

Measured 559-575 ms cold, 0.1 ms cached, and 396-413 ms after a single unrelated write, because total_changes() bumps on every event commit and cursor upsert, so the cache never hits while an agent is active. computeStatistics runs inside sql.withTransaction, so event appends and projections wait for the full SQL plus JS duration. Each run parses 60k checkpoint_files_json values (8.6 MB) and parses each per-turn payload up to 3 times (lines 502-525). Profile: about 130 ms JS per run; SQL about 250 ms warm.

Proposal

(1) Read rows in the transaction but aggregate after it commits. (2) Key the cache on max(orchestration_events.sequence) plus max(projection_worktrees.updated_at), with data_version, instead of total_changes(). (3) Persist incremental daily rollups (date, project, provider, model, last_sequence) and recompute only dirty days. (4) Store files_changed, additions and deletions per turn when checkpoints are projected. (5) Parse each payload once. (6) Benefit from the kind index (activities-kind-index).

Verifier (Confirmed)

The cache key is total_changes() plus data_version, so any write on the server connection invalidates it. Payloads are parsed up to 3 times in the lastPerTurn loops (:502-525). checkpoint_files_json is parsed per turn (:570). The token query full-scans activity events with json_extract (:243-271). Measurements in measure-run1.txt agree: 559-575 ms cold, 0.1 ms cached, 396-413 ms after one write. Proposals (1), (2) and (5) are S; rollups are M.

Expected gain

Upgrade boots with a new projector go from minutes to seconds: event-type filtering skips most of a log dominated by activity and message events, and batching amortises commit cost about N times.

What happens today

bootstrapProjectors streams every event after the minimum cursor, Schema-decodes it, opens a transaction, and upserts cursors even when ORCHESTRATION_EVENT_PROJECTORS routes the event to no lagging projector. Measured: projection.worktrees set 50,000 events behind gave 29.1 s from migrations to Listening (about 580 us/event). This happens whenever an upgrade adds a projector; the worktrees projector was added on 2026-05-09 without cursor seeding (git log). A 400k-event log would take about 4 minutes with no listener and no progress output.

Proposal

For lagging projectors, read only event_type IN (the inverse of ORCHESTRATION_EVENT_PROJECTORS) and advance the cursor once at the end. Batch about 500 events per transaction. For new projectors, seed the cursor in the migration after an SQL backfill, or run catch-up after the listener is up, behind the command gate, with progress logs.

The impact is limited to upgrades that add or reset a projector, but it is catastrophic there.

Category: MemoryRisk: mediumInvestigator confidence: mediumpersistence-boot:command-read-model-bloat
Expected gain

Roughly 50-70% less engine read-model heap (about 30-45 MiB at 5k threads) and bounded growth during long sessions; faster hydration.

What happens today

getCommandReadModel at 5k threads serialises to 19.2 MiB (heap +45-69 MiB). It includes every plan's markdown (4 MB synthetic), 2 full-text user-message anchors per thread (3 MB) and the actionable activity payloads. The decider and invariants use message id and role only, and look plans up by id. At runtime each thread.message-sent appends or concatenates text into the in-memory thread (streaming text + delta) up to MAX_THREAD_MESSAGES = 2,000. Each activity append re-sorts up to 500 entries. updateThread maps the whole threads array, O(T) per event.

Proposal

Slim the command model: message anchors become {id, role, createdAt, turnId} with no text; plans become {id, turnId, implementedAt, implementationThreadId, createdAt, updatedAt}; message events keep only anchor bookkeeping; keep threads in a Map for O(1) updates. Select the slim columns in the hydration queries too, which reduces bytes read at boot.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

projector.ts:821-879 keeps full message text (streaming concatenation) in the engine model, capped at MAX_THREAD_MESSAGES=2000 per thread (:75). Activity appends re-sort (:1156-1185), and updateThread is an O(T) map (:79-85). The decider and invariants read messages only for id/role (decider.ts:1470,1494; commandInvariants.ts:374,448) and plans by id (decider.ts:1514); planMarkdown is not referenced in decider, projector or invariants. The heap estimate is inflated: text (plans about 4 MB plus anchors about 3 MB) is about 36% of the 19.2 MiB serialized model, and actionable activity payloads are needed by the decider. Expect about 30-40% less, not 50-70%. The orchestration/http.ts:45 debug endpoint and cli.ts:1170 also return getCommandReadModel, so slimming changes their output. The unbounded-ish runtime growth from streamed text is the more relevant part.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

Removes 100-600 ms main-thread stalls per heavy read at 5k threads and the head-of-line blocking of unrelated queries during boot.

What happens today

A single DatabaseSync is guarded by Semaphore(1), and transactions hold it for their whole Effect scope. In the cold boot trace an AgentControl MCP installation lookup waited 1,956 ms behind the engine-hydration transaction; statistics holds it 0.4-0.6 s; shell builds hold it for about 45 ms of SQL each. Because node:sqlite is synchronous, sqlite3's busy handler sleeps on the main thread for up to 5 s when another process (the offline CLI) holds the write lock, stalling WebSocket heartbeats and all RPCs.

Proposal

Add a read-only WAL connection in a worker_thread for heavy read paths (shell and command snapshots, statistics, search, history pages, replay probes), returning plain rows or structured clones. Keep the single writer on the main thread. On the main connection use a short busy_timeout with async retry and backoff instead of a synchronous 5 s sleep.

Verifier (Confirmed)

NodeSqliteClient.ts:219-230: one DatabaseSync behind Semaphore(1); transactionAcquirer holds the permit for the transaction scope. Sqlite.ts:35 sets busy_timeout=5000, and node:sqlite runs synchronously on the main thread, so the busy handler sleeps on the event loop when another process (the CLI) holds the write lock. The trace's 1,956 ms installation lookup is queue wait behind cold hydration, which is consistent. The earlier research doc (performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md:271-272) says to keep node:sqlite and tune queries first; a read worker keeps the engine. L effort, medium payoff, best after the cheaper query fixes.

Expected gain

20-30 ms less main-thread work per resubscribed stream on every reconnect; scales linearly in reconnect storms.

What happens today

Every shell and thread subscription that carries resumeFromSequence calls readEventsPage(seq-1, 1) and then readEventsPage(seq, 1000). Each decodes full payload_json rows with the OrchestrationEvent schema and then discards them. Measured 20-32 ms per probe on activity events; message events are bigger. If the gap exceeds 1,000 events the work is wasted and a full snapshot follows. Otherwise the replay stream reads and decodes the same events again. This happens on every reconnect of hub and mobile clients, for the shell plus each open thread.

Proposal

Add a payload-free probe to the event store, e.g. eventStore.countAfter(seq, limit): SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orchestration_events WHERE sequence = ?) and SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT 1 FROM orchestration_events WHERE sequence > ? LIMIT 1001). Both are rowid range reads that never touch payload_json. Use it in canResumeAfter.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

canResumeAfter (orchestrationStreams.ts:494-504) does call readEventsPage(seq-1,1) and readEventsPage(seq,1000), and readPage (OrchestrationEventStore.ts:401-440) decodes every returned row. The cost is proportional to the actual gap, though, not always 1,000 events. The 20-32 ms measurement (measure-replay.ts uses from = latest-5000, so hasMore is true) is the worst case, and there a snapshot follows anyway. For typical short reconnects (tens of events) the probe costs about 1 ms, and the double decode is small. EXPLAIN confirms that a count over a rowid range is a cheap PK range read. Worthwhile S cleanup, low impact.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

30-65% faster cold index-heavy reads (about 0.5 s off a cold boot at 5k threads) and 10-50% on warm hydration reads.

What happens today

Effective PRAGMAs measured through the server client: synchronous=2, cache_size=-2000, mmap_size=0, temp_store=0, wal_autocheckpoint=1000, and no sqlite_stat1 (ANALYZE and optimize are never run). With mmap_size = 256 MiB under the same load, cold reads fell sharply: thread rows 295 to 196 ms, anchors 675 to 400, latest turns 275 to 98, checkpoint turns 462 to 110, kind scan 1,732 to 962; warm reads 10-50% lower. synchronous FULL vs NORMAL gave 254-267 vs 170-263 us/commit (noisy; macOS fsync is not a full flush), so changing durability is not worth it.

Proposal

In the setup layer add: PRAGMA mmap_size=268435456; PRAGMA cache_size=-32768; PRAGMA temp_store=MEMORY; PRAGMA journal_size_limit=67108864; and PRAGMA optimize=0x10002 after migrations, plus a periodic (hourly or on shutdown) PRAGMA optimize. Keep synchronous as is, consistent with docs/streaming-sqlite.md.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Sqlite.ts:30-43 sets only busy_timeout, WAL and foreign_keys; no other PRAGMA or optimize exists in server src. My copy of the DB shows cache_size=-2000, mmap_size=0, synchronous=2, temp_store=0. The benefit evidence is noisy and cherry-picked. cold-mmap.txt actionable is 1236/1337 ms vs 948 ms in cold-default.txt. Warm actionable is 135-148 ms with mmap vs 70 ms in default run 1. checkpointReverts is 944/962 vs 986 ms. The quoted gains compare against the slower cold-default-2 run. The cache_size run (cold-cache.txt) is slower in nearly every cold row. A low-risk S change, but it needs a repeated A/B benchmark first. PRAGMA optimize/ANALYZE can change plans (an EXPLAIN guard test exists for the anchor plan), so add plan guards.

docs/streaming-sqlite.md deliberately left synchronous unchanged (kept here); page cache, mmap and optimize were never covered.

Expected gain

Makes the cloud index work above about 1.6k threads (today it never uploads). Removes about 140 ms of main-thread work per second of activity at 4.5k threads.

What happens today

Every domain event calls notifyChanged; publishes are spaced at least 1 s apart. Each tick reads the snapshot sequence, and if it changed, builds a full getShellSnapshot, re-validates it with Schema.decodeUnknownSync(ThreadReadCacheShell) (the full OrchestrationShellSnapshot schema), JSON.stringifies it and throws 'Cloud thread index exceeds the upload limit' when it exceeds MAX_BATCH_BYTES (2,093,056 B). Measured shell size is 1,292-1,316 B per thread, so the upload fails above about 1,590 non-deleted threads (archived included). Each retry (backoff 10-60 s) rebuilds the snapshot. At 4.5k threads one cycle is about 100 ms build + about 30 ms decode + about 9 ms stringify, roughly 14% of the main thread during agent streaming.

Proposal

(1) Fix the hard failure: upload the shell as paged items across batches, or as a compact index (id, projectId, title, updatedAt, archivedAt, session status) instead of the full snapshot. (2) Stop rebuilding from SQL on every sequence change: maintain the cloud shell from shell events (shellEventsFromDomainEvents already exists), or rebuild only when a shell-affecting event type arrives. (3) Replace the full schema re-decode with cheap length checks.

Expected gain

For heavy Claude/Codex users: no 0.3-0.6 s synchronous parse on the first usage open and no full-cache rewrite per open. Avoids the cliff above roughly 500k records (estimated).

What happens today

Every transcript record is serialised as a tuple that includes a 64-character SHA-256 dedupe key, about 110-130 B each, so the 64 MiB cap is reached at roughly 500k records. Past it, readBoundedUsageFile throws usage-file-oversized and the cache is treated as empty: a full transcript rescan plus a rewrite of more than 64 MiB on every open. An active, growing transcript marks the cache dirty on every open, triggering a full JSON.stringify and atomic rewrite. This is an estimate; the perf home has no transcript corpus.

Proposal

Move the scan cache into SQLite (usage_scan_files keyed by file key with size, mtime and fingerprint, plus per-file per-day aggregates and a dedupe-key table) and update only changed files. Alternatively, shard the JSON per root or file.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

UsageService.ts:183-212: the whole scan-cache.json (64 MiB cap via readBoundedUsageFile) is read and parsed on first load and fully rewritten when dirty. A read failure, including usage-file-oversized, is swallowed as 'no cache', which forces a full rescan. The serialized tuple carries a 64-hex dedupe key (usageScanCache.ts:36-49, 87-90). All size and time figures are estimates with no corpus. SCAN_CACHE_RETENTION_MS = 120 days (UsageService.ts:71) prunes aged files when startDate is given, which bounds growth. Only affects the usage page for heavy transcript users.

Web bootstrap waterfall 15 findings · 2 high · 7 medium · 6 low

Shell code → WebSocket → thread code load strictly one after another, each lazy phase pays a 300 ms React Suspense throttle, assets are served uncompressed, and the boot graph grew 32% since August (mostly hosted/E2EE code the standard build never runs at boot).

How it works today (investigator's summary)

How the web client boots today (desktop renderer, browser and hosted-static all use the standard build), measured in headless Chromium 153 against the production server on a scratch home with 1 project and 1 thread:

1. The HTML paints the inline boot shell in about 12 ms. The inline loader (index-*.js) waits for main-*.css to finish loading (587 KiB raw), then dynamically imports main-*.js.

2. The browser then discovers the 75-file static graph of main (2.0 MiB raw) in 4 levels: 1, then 31, then 26, then 17 files. Evaluation ends at web-entry.import-end, about 143-150 ms locally.

3. Only then does the root beforeLoad run its two auth/descriptor fetches in parallel (about 7 ms).

4. Only after that does RootAppShell's React.lazy start loading 59 more files (1.68 MiB). That graph is loaded and rendered by about 200 ms.

5. React 19.2's Suspense reveal throttle (FALLBACK_THROTTLE_MS=300) then holds the commit until about 300 ms after the fallback was shown. The shell commits around 420-460 ms.

6. Only in a passive effect after that commit does startEnvironmentConnectionService POST /api/auth/ws-token (twice: /ws and /ws/device), open the WebSocket and receive the shell snapshot. Usable is about 529 ms (median of 5 cold runs).

7. The welcome payload then redirects to the last thread. Only now is ChatThreadRouteView requested (about 82 more files, roughly 2.9 MiB raw including the 1.1 MiB "ChatRightPanel" merged chunk). It is throttled again by about 230-280 ms, and the composer is ready at about 940 ms (LCP about 920 ms).

On a fast local machine more than half of time-to-composer is idle: two 300 ms Suspense throttles plus strictly serial phases (shell code, then WS, then thread code). Neutralizing just the throttle timer cut usable from 529 to about 308 ms and composer from 938 to about 577 ms. The same throttle adds about 250 ms to every first open of Statistics (345 to 85 ms) and Settings (345 to 95 ms). Settings pays it even though its chunk was already idle-preloaded.

On a remote/hosted-like profile (40 ms RTT, 20 Mbit/s, CPU x4) the bottlenecks change to bytes and CPU:

  • The Ryco server sends every asset uncompressed over HTTP/1.1: 186 files and 6.0 MiB raw to reach the composer, against 1.8 MiB gzip.
  • 93 of 184 JS requests are under 2 KiB.
  • Results: import-end about 1.6 s, usable about 3.1 s, composer about 4.6 s.

The boot graph grew 32% since August (1,536 to 2,023 KiB raw). About 398 KiB (20%) of it is hosted/relay/E2EE code (client-runtime authorization/relay, shared/relayE2ee*, @noble/*, cborg, HostedConnectionControls) that the standard build never runs at boot. It is reached through:

  • static route imports (no route code-splitting): _chat.tsx → useHandleNewThread → the authorization barrel; _chat.index → NoActiveThreadState and _settings.diagnostics → HostedConnectionControls;
  • barrels: main → wsConnectionState → platform barrel → passkeyCeremony → the relay barrel;
  • __root → PreviewFileNavigationGuard → hostedConnectionCoordinator.

VITE_RYCO_CLIENT_MODE is a compile-time define, but it only guards runtime branches, never the imports. No workspace package declares "sideEffects", so barrels pull in everything.

Part of Priority 13: Serve compressed assets and flatten chunk waterfalls (remote clients)

Expected gain

-4.2 MiB per cold load (6,075→1,853 KiB). Measured -0.35 to -0.55 s on usable/composer on the 20 Mbit+CPU×4 profile. Transfer-only math: -1.7 s at 20 Mbit/s, -6.7 s at 5 Mbit/s.

What happens today

staticFileResponse streams HttpServerResponse.file with Cache-Control/ETag only; there is no Content-Encoding negotiation and no precompressed variants. MEASURED: curl with 'Accept-Encoding: gzip, br' on /assets/runtime-*.js returns content-length 645226 with no Content-Encoding, and Chrome transferSize ≈ decodedBodySize for every asset. A cold load to the composer is 186 files, 6,075 KiB raw, vs 1,853 KiB gzip / 1,566 KiB brotli (-70%/-74%). On the 40 ms/20 Mbit/CPU×4 profile, CSS alone (601 KB) took 102→376 ms and import-end was 1.61-1.67 s. Simulating compressed transfer (×3.6 throughput): import-end 1.25-1.31 s, usable 2.63-2.86 s (vs 3.07-3.14), composer 4.05-4.32 s (vs 4.59-4.63). This affects remote browsers, LAN/Tailscale access, phone browsers and hosted-static clients served by a node. Desktop loopback is barely affected.

Proposal

(1) Add a small build plugin in apps/web/vite.config.ts that writes .br (quality 11) and .gz siblings for js/mjs/css/svg/json/wasm/html assets ≥1 KiB into dist (and the server's dist/client copy).

(2) In staticFileResponse: parse Accept-Encoding, prefer br then gzip. When ${filePath}.br/.gz exists, stream it with Content-Encoding, Vary: Accept-Encoding, the original content type, and a variant-specific ETag (e.g. suffix -br). Keep the 304 path. Never compress on the fly (no CPU on the boot path).

(3) Optionally skip variants for loopback desktop requests.

(4) Consider HTTP/2 via the existing Tailscale/TLS paths.

Verifier (Confirmed)

staticFileResponse (http.ts:211-245) sets only Cache-Control/ETag and streams HttpServerResponse.file. An rg for content-encoding/accept-encoding/gzip/brotli in apps/server/src finds only PreviewBrowser (outbound) and zip code, so no negotiation and no precompressed variants exist. vite.config.ts:185-190 has no compression plugin. Scope corrections: (1) Electron loads the UI from loopback (apps/desktop/src/main.ts:1459 loadURL(backendHttpUrl)), so desktop gains ~0. (2) Hashed assets get public, max-age=31536000, immutable (http.ts:45, 106-115), so the gain applies to first visits and to the first load after each update (all hashes change), not to every boot. (3) The '-0.35 to -0.55 s' is a throughput-scaled simulation (browser-boot.mjs hostedgz: downloadThroughput ×3.6), not real compressed serving, and decode CPU is not modelled. (4) Shipping .br+.gz siblings for the whole 23 MiB dist grows the desktop artifact and server package by several MiB. Consider br-only variants, or skip them in desktop packaging. Still the single biggest lever for LAN/Tailscale/remote-browser cold loads (~4.2 MiB less on the wire to reach the composer).

Prior work

docs/perf/package-size-measurement.md and the Aug report measured gzip/brotli sizes, but nothing serves compressed bytes. Not previously proposed.

Part of Priority 1: Remove the 300 ms React Suspense reveal delay from every navigation

Expected gain

Local/desktop: ~-220 ms to usable shell (529→~308 ms) and ~-360 ms to composer (938→~577 ms). ~-250 ms on every first open of Statistics/Settings/Projects/Pull requests/new-thread (measured 345→~90 ms).

What happens today

Every route body and the RootAppShell use hand-rolled React.lazy inside <Suspense>. When a fallback commits, React 19.2 stores globalMostRecentFallbackTime and delays the retry commit until 300 ms after it (FALLBACK_THROTTLE_MS=300; throttled path at react-dom-client.production.js:10804, found via sourcemap from the setTimeout stack). MEASURED at boot: the RootAppShell graph was ready at ~150-200 ms, React scheduled the commit with a 237 ms timeout, the shell committed at ~418 ms (first DM Sans request at 421) and ws-token followed at 441. Thread route: chunks done ~540 ms, throttle timers 284/220 ms, commit ~794 ms. Statistics: all 9 chunks (456 KiB) arrived 64-68 ms after the click, but the heading appeared at 342-347 ms. Settings: zero network (chunk already idle-preloaded by SettingsRouteBridge, whose stated aim in settingsRoute.ts:12 is 'so it never flashes empty'), yet 342-354 ms of blank SidebarInset, because the route's own React.lazy creates a new promise and suspends once. That is effectively a bug: the preload cannot do its job. Experiment that only zeroes this timer: usable 529→~308 ms, composer 938→~577 ms, LCP 920→~536 ms, Statistics 345→85-97 ms, Settings 345→90-103 ms. On the CPU×4/20 Mbit profile there was no gain, because the throttle is hidden behind downloads.

Proposal

Stop using Suspense fallbacks as the code-loading mechanism on navigation paths.

(1) Routes: replace lazy()+Suspense in the route files with TanStack route-level splitting, e.g. component: lazyRouteComponent(() => import('../components/routeViews/ChatThreadRouteView'), 'ChatThreadRouteView'), or .lazy.tsx files, or tanstackRouter({ autoCodeSplitting: true }). router-core's loadRouteChunk awaits component.preload() before the match renders, so the component renders synchronously: no fallback, no retry lane, no throttle. Keep pendingComponent/pendingMs for genuinely slow loads.

(2) Root shell: start import('../components/RootAppShell') at the top of resolveRootBeforeLoadContextAsync and await it in the same Promise.all as auth. Keep the module in a module-level variable and render it directly, with no React.lazy. TanStack renders the root pendingComponent as normal content (Match.js renderPending for status 'pending'), so the reveal becomes a default-lane update.

(3) Add one shared preloadableLazy(load) helper in apps/web/src/lib that renders the resolved component synchronously once .preload() has settled. Use it for SettingsPage (wire SettingsRouteBridge's idle preload to it), HostedHubRoot, PhoneHome, CommandPaletteDialog, AutomationsDialog and PromoteChatDialog.

(4) Add a browser test asserting that the time from chunk-resolved to commit is < 50 ms for root, thread and statistics.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Checked react-dom 19.2.8, the version apps/web resolves. In react-dom-client.production.js:10790-10815, when (lanes & RetryLanes) === lanes, the retry commit is delayed until globalMostRecentFallbackTime + 300 (scheduleTimeout(commitRootWhenReady)). All the cited route files use hand-rolled lazy()+<Suspense>; __root.tsx:29-31 and 241-247 do the same for RootAppShell. TanStack react-router 1.170 MatchInner (Match.js:105-108) renders pendingComponent directly for status 'pending' rather than through a Suspense throw, and router-core load-client.js:21-37 awaits component preload. So proposals (1) and (2) really do avoid the retry lane. The investigator's raw data supports the numbers: browser-boot-local.json usable 490-712 ms vs nothrottle 287-384 ms; composer 871-1112 vs 543-615 ms; page-nav-local.json Statistics 342-347 vs 85-97 ms; Settings 342-354 vs 90-103 ms with 0 chunks fetched. So SettingsRouteBridge's idle preload (SettingsRouteBridge.tsx:33-43) really is defeated. Caveats: (a) Projects, Pull requests and new-thread were not measured; they are extrapolated. (b) Proposal (2) must only await the RootAppShell import when authGateState is authenticated/hosted-static. Awaiting it in the same Promise.all on /pair or requires-auth would make the pairing surface wait for the 1.7 MiB shell graph. (c) webBundleSplitting.test.ts:15 asserts lazy( in the chat route files and needs updating. (d) There is no gain on bandwidth-bound links (the hosted-nothrottle runs did not improve). Desktop loads over loopback, so it gets the full ~220 ms. Nothing equivalent exists in the codebase (no lazyRouteComponent, autoCodeSplitting or defaultPreload).

Prior work

none. The Aug 2026 hardening pass introduced these lazy boundaries ('lazy route boundaries for statistics/diagnostics/pairing/native-auth'), but no doc mentions the reveal throttle. SettingsRouteBridge's idle preload exists but is defeated by it.

Part of Priority 14: Trim the JS on the boot and thread paths

Expected gain

~-600 KiB raw / ~-190 KiB gzip (est.) from the shell critical path (~-36% of RootAppShell beyond-boot bytes). ~-15 to -30 ms eval locally; ~-0.2 to -0.3 s on 20 Mbit uncompressed (est.).

What happens today

RootAppShell adds 59 files / 1,681 KiB raw beyond boot.

  • The 334 KiB CommentThread chunk (react-markdown, remark-gfm/micromark, rehype-raw/parse5, hast/property-information) enters the shell because pullRequests/primitives.tsx imports only CommentAvatar from CommentThread.tsx, which statically imports MarkdownView. primitives is used by WorkspacePullRequestsPopover in SidebarWorktreeList.
  • Modules only reachable through LinkedWorktreeItemDialog (also in SidebarWorktreeList): 139 KiB (WorkItemDetail 36, WorkflowRunsSection 27, PullRequestDetail 24, IssueDetail 9, PullRequestFilesTab 8).
  • Only through NewWorktreeDialog (SidebarProjectDialogOwner): 91 KiB.
  • Only through getEditorLabel (useThreadMenuActions → SettingsPanels.editor): JetBrainsIcons 35 KiB.

Measured with cutsize.mjs over the real-build sourcemaps. None of these render at boot.

Proposal
  • Move CommentAvatar to projectExplorer/CommentAvatar.tsx (no markdown import).
  • Move getEditorLabel and editor metadata into settings/editorLabels.logic.ts without icon imports.
  • Mount LinkedWorktreeItemDialog and NewWorktreeDialog through the existing lazy-mount pattern (hasOpened state, as in RootAppShell.tsx:105-141), using preloadableLazy plus preload on pointerenter of the menu item that opens them.
  • Add the shell rule to the dist guard: no parse5/micromark/react-markdown in the RootAppShell closure.
Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The total (~600 KiB) holds, but the causal story is incomplete. Moving CommentAvatar alone is not enough. CommentThread.tsx (which imports MarkdownView → react-markdown/rehype-raw/parse5/micromark, the 342,091 B CommentThread-*.js chunk) is also reached through LinkedWorktreeItemDialog → WorkItemDetail.tsx:69, PullRequestDetail.tsx:45 and IssueDetail.tsx:16 (CommentComposer/CommentItem). In the dist, CommentThread-*.js is statically imported by the shell chunks InboxStatusGlyph-*.js and useSidebarThreadActions-*.js; the latter imports CommentThread.tsx exports, which I mapped via sourcemap. Ran cutsize.mjs from RootAppShell: cutting pullRequests/primitives alone frees only 6 KiB. Cutting CommentThread alone frees 33 KiB of app code plus the markdown stack only if the dialog edges are also cut. Cutting LinkedWorktreeItemDialog + CommentThread + NewWorktreeDialog + SettingsPanels.editor frees 65 modules / 315 KiB of app code plus the ~300 KiB markdown stack. So all four changes are required together. The dialogs are mounted closed (SidebarWorktreeList.tsx:224-231; SidebarProjectDialogOwner.tsx:115-125). ChatView.tsx:212-217 also statically imports both dialogs, so this defers them to thread open rather than removing them. That is fine for the shell.

Part of Priority 13: Serve compressed assets and flatten chunk waterfalls (remote clients)

Expected gain

Remote: removes 3 serial discovery levels per phase (~120-160 ms at 40 ms RTT per phase, ×3 phases), the CSS→JS gap (~0.27 s uncompressed / ~40 ms compressed at 20 Mbit) and ~90 request slots of HTTP/1.1 queueing. Local: <10 ms.

What happens today
  • The built loader (assets/index-*.js) runs Vite's preload helper with only the CSS dep: it waits for main-*.css to load before calling import(main). Measured: local CSS 8-9 ms → main.js requested at 15 ms; hosted profile CSS done 376 ms → main.js starts 389 ms.
  • With modulePreload:false the browser discovers each graph level by level: main 4 levels (1/31/26/17 files), RootAppShell 4 levels (1/63/60/10), ChatThreadRouteView 4 levels (1/23/121/16).
  • 93 of the 184 JS requests before the composer are <2 KiB (78 <1 KiB, 50 KiB total): per-icon lucide chunks and micro shared chunks, each a separate request on Chromium's 6-connection HTTP/1.1 pool.
  • Experiment: preloading all 176 files at document start improved composer on the hosted profile (4.11-4.34 s), but contention delayed beforeLoad 1.69→2.40 s. Preloading must be per phase and prioritized.
Proposal

(1) build.modulePreload: { polyfill: false, resolveDependencies: (file, deps, { hostId }) => CRITICAL.test(file) ? deps : [] }, where CRITICAL covers main, RootAppShell, ChatThreadRouteView, DraftChatThreadRouteView, HostedHubRoot and route page chunks. Each phase's static closure is then fetched in parallel the moment its import starts, and main's JS is preloaded in parallel with its CSS (the helper awaits only CSS links). The boot-shell-first behaviour of index.html is kept.

(2) build.rolldownOptions.output.codeSplitting groups with entriesAware: true and entriesAwareMergeThreshold: 8192-16384 (rolldown 1.2.7 supports both), e.g. a lucide-icons group and an app catch-all, so sub-2 KiB shared chunks merge into neighbours. Target: <60 JS requests to composer and no new chunk >400 KiB on the boot path.

(3) Re-measure with .perf-research/graph.mjs and depth.mjs.

Verifier (Confirmed)

vite.config.ts:188 sets modulePreload:false. The built loader dist/assets/index-Ca8qsKFg.js calls the preload helper with only main-*.css in __vite__mapDeps, and the helper returns a load promise only for CSS links. So import(main) waits for the 587 KiB stylesheet (index.html:127-130 in source). My recount of the static closure of index+main+RootAppShell+ChatThreadRouteView: 176 files / 5,302 KiB, of which 90 are <2 KiB (76 <1 KiB, 48 KiB total). This matches the claim. rolldown 1.2.7 is installed and exposes entriesAwareMergeThreshold. This is a documented residual (performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md:97, 268, 374); the new specifics are valid. The per-phase savings (~120-160 ms × 3) are an upper bound: on the 20 Mbit HTTP/1.1 profile, bandwidth dominates, and the investigator's own full-preload experiment showed contention. Local gain is negligible.

Residual in docs/research/performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md:97,268,374 ('retest modulePreload after chunk splitting'). New specifics: measured depth, the CSS-before-import serialization, tiny-chunk counts, and the contention result showing a curated resolveDependencies list is required.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

Per client boot/reconnect: -1 HTTP POST, -1 WebSocket and -4 to -5 child processes (~0.45 s server time).

What happens today

createEnvironmentConnection calls bindDeviceConnection for every primary connection. It subscribes device events and calls client.list({ includeShutdown: true }) straight away. Client side, this costs a second POST /api/auth/ws-token plus a /ws/device WebSocket (MEASURED: 2 token POSTs at 441 ms; /ws/device open at 456 ms, first message 830 ms). Server side, DeviceManager.list() runs backend.availability(), which spawns xcode-select -p and xcodebuild -version and lists devices via simctl. It then runs listDevices again (a second simctl list devices --json), plus the device-type catalogue, with no caching. Measured on this Mac: simctl list 0.20-0.22 s per call, xcodebuild -version 0.05 s. That is ~0.45 s of child-process wall time per web client boot or reconnect, on a server that is busy with its own startup, even if the simulator UI is never opened.

Proposal
  • Client: bind the device runtime lazily. Create the DeviceWsTransport subscription and run the inventory on the first device-store subscriber (SimulatorPanel/device picker mount) through an ensureDeviceRuntime(environmentId) in client-runtime/state/device, then dispose on idle.
  • Server: memoize availability() for ~30 s and let list() reuse the device listing that availability() already fetched (one simctl spawn instead of two). Invalidate on boot/shutdown events.
Verifier (Confirmed)

connection.ts:281-283 binds the device runtime for every connection that has a device client. The primary web connection always gets one: service.ts:923-935 creates DeviceWsTransport with its own authenticatedSocketUrl('/ws/device'), i.e. a second ws-token POST. bindDeviceConnection (runtime.ts:22-75) subscribes and calls refreshInventory → client.list({includeShutdown:true}) immediately; it runs again on resubscribe (runtime.ts:59-62) and on reconnect (connection.ts:318-324). Correction: the server spawns more processes than claimed. DeviceManager.list() (DeviceManager.ts:338-345) calls availability(), which runs xcode-select -p (IosSimulatorBackend.ts:358→1070), xcodebuild -version (1082-1089, whose toolchainEnv spawns xcode-select -p again) and listDevicesUnchecked (simctl() → toolchainEnv → xcode-select -p, then simctl list devices --json). discover() → listDevices (467) then repeats xcode-select -p + simctl list. Total ≈ 4 xcode-select + 1 xcodebuild + 2 simctl list, plus a one-time simctl list devicetypes (memoized at 1036). Spawns are async (they do not block the event loop) and happen only on darwin servers. Client cost is +1 POST and +1 WebSocket per boot. This does not gate usable, but it is wasted work on every connect, and simctl may start CoreSimulatorService for users who never use simulators (not measured). Impact on boot latency is low; as server efficiency it is medium.

Part of Priority 2: Stop dropping requests during server startup, and give clients deadlines

Expected gain

Turns indefinite hangs (boot or reconnect) into self-healing retries within ≤5-10 s. No cost on the happy path.

What happens today

fetchSessionState, exchangeBootstrapCredential, fetchDescriptor and issuePrimaryWebSocketToken call httpClient.fetch with no AbortSignal. retryTransientBootstrap only retries after a thrown TypeError/AbortError or a 502-504, so an unanswered request blocks root beforeLoad indefinitely (boot logo forever). In protocol.ts the WS URL provider (which performs the ws-token POST) is wrapped in Effect.tryPromise + retry but has no timeout. The heartbeat timeout only applies to an open socket, so a hung token POST during a backend restart stalls reconnect forever. EVIDENCE.md reproduced 5/5 that HTTP requests connecting ~0-180 ms before 'Listening on' never get a response, which is exactly the window a reconnect loop or renderer reload can hit after a desktop backend restart.

Proposal
  • Pass signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5_000) per attempt in the primaryAuth and primaryContext fetches. AbortError is already treated as transient, so attempts are retried inside the existing 15 s budget.
  • Add Effect.timeout('10 seconds') (or Effect.timeoutFail) to resolvedUrl in protocol.ts so the existing reconnect schedule continues.
  • Let RootRouteErrorView show its Retry/Reload actions after the budget is exhausted.
Verifier (Confirmed)

webHttpClient (platform/httpClient.ts:6-9) passes init through and adds no signal. fetchSessionState (primaryAuth.ts:125-138), exchangeBootstrapCredential and fetchDescriptor (primaryContext.ts:77-91) pass no AbortSignal. retryTransientBootstrap (primaryAuth.ts:106-120) only retries on thrown TypeError/AbortError/502-504 within 15 s, so a never-answered request blocks forever. issuePrimaryWebSocketToken (primaryAuth.ts:139-150) is not even wrapped in the retry helper. In protocol.ts:291-317, resolvedUrl is Effect.tryPromise + retry with no timeout. The only timeout nearby is wsRpcClient.ts:491 (guarded writes). The desktop window loads only after the backend listens, so the realistic exposure is the reconnect loop or a renderer reload during a backend restart, which is exactly the pre-listen hang window documented in EVIDENCE.md. A real reliability gap with a cheap fix.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

webBundleSplitting.test.ts is indeed source-text only (string contains/not-contains checks). But 'nothing checks the real dist' is overstated. scripts/perf (perf:compare, .github/workflows/external-performance.yml) already measures whole-dist raw/gzip/brotli bytes (scripts/perf/bundleMeasurement.ts), bootstrapEncodedBytes and usableMs, with regression thresholds (scripts/perf/model.ts:226-251: bundle +5%, bootstrapEncodedBytes +10%, usableMs +15%). scripts/measure-web-bundle.ts also exists. Its gaps: it runs only on manual workflow_dispatch, uses whole-dist totals with no per-closure budgets, and has no forbidden-module rules. So the proposal should extend that harness (closure budgets for main/RootAppShell/ChatThreadRouteView, forbidden-source lists, PR-triggered on apps/web and packages changes) rather than add a parallel script. Still worthwhile and preventive.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

Remote/hosted-like profile: ~-0.5 to -0.8 s to composer (the thread chunk fetch currently starts ~0.7 s after usable) and ~-0.1 to -0.2 s to usable. Local: ~-60 to -150 ms (estimates from the measured phase timings).

What happens today

The phases are serialized:

  • The RootAppShell import is only triggered when RootRouteView renders after beforeLoad (MEASURED local: beforeLoad ready ~160 ms, RootAppShell requested ~162 ms).
  • The primary connection only starts in a passive effect after the shell commits (EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap → startEnvironmentConnectionService → connectPrimary). Each socket then first POSTs /api/auth/ws-token (authenticatedSocketUrl), and two are issued at ~496 ms local.
  • The bootstrap-thread route chunk is requested only after welcome → ensureEnvironmentConnectionBootstrapped → navigate (~560 ms local). Its ~2.9 MiB graph then loads in 4 discovery levels.
  • createRouter sets no defaultPreload, so hovering sidebar links prefetches nothing.

Hosted profile: RootAppShell chunk end 1.86-1.92 s, ws-token 2.81-2.92 s, usable 3.07-3.14 s, ChatRightPanel end 3.78-3.87 s (0.7 s after usable), composer 4.6 s. Shell code, WS+snapshot and thread code are independent but never overlap.

Proposal

(a) In resolveRootBeforeLoadContextAsync, start import('../components/RootAppShell') before the auth fetches and await it in the same Promise.all. Discard the result on the pairing path (the chunk is cached for later).

(b) Standard (non-hosted) mode only, once authGateState is 'authenticated': kick the primary connection from beforeLoad via connectPrimaryEnvironment() (the supervisor is idempotent and RootAppShell's start() keeps ownership through refCount). At minimum, pre-issue one ws-token promise (TTL ≤30 s, consumed once by authenticatedSocketUrl), so the token RTT + WS upgrade + shell snapshot overlap the shell download/eval. Hosted mode stays as is (single lifecycle owner).

(c) Desktop tier: after shell commit, requestIdleCallback(() => router.loadRouteChunk(router.routesById['/_chat/$environmentId/$threadId'])). Also start that chunk load as soon as welcome carries bootstrapThreadId, before awaiting ensureEnvironmentConnectionBootstrapped. Use low fetch priority so it never competes with boot-critical requests: the preload experiment showed contention can delay beforeLoad by ~0.7 s on HTTP/1.1.

(d) Set defaultPreload: 'intent' (with defaultPreloadDelay ~50 ms) in router.ts.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code confirms strict serialization. EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap (RootAppShell.tsx:182-193) starts connections in a passive effect. service.ts:906-935 POSTs /api/auth/ws-token per socket (/ws and /ws/device) via issuePrimaryWebSocketToken (primaryAuth.ts:139-150). The thread navigation waits for ensureEnvironmentConnectionBootstrapped (RootAppShell.tsx:225, 259). router.ts:7-14 has no defaultPreload. The impact estimate is inflated: the investigator's own experiment preloading boot+shell+thread at document start on the hosted profile gave composer 4.11-4.34 s vs 4.59-4.63 s (-0.25 to -0.5 s), and on HTTP/1.1 at 20 Mbit reordering cannot beat bytes/bandwidth. The local version of that experiment never reached usable (browser-boot-local-nothrottle-preload_boot+shell+thread.json: usable=false), which is itself a warning. Proposal (d) defaultPreload:'intent' preloads no component code today, because route components are plain functions with internal lazy(). It only helps after react-suspense-reveal-throttle (1). Risk of (b) is lower than feared: welcome is a latest-value atom (rpc/serverState.ts:70-74), so an early connection does not lose the bootstrap redirect. A cleaner alternative to pre-issuing tokens: authenticate same-origin WS upgrades with the session cookie plus a strict Origin check, which removes the ws-token RTT (2 POSTs per boot/reconnect) entirely.

What happens today

  • routeTree → _chat.tsx → useHandleNewThread, which imports only nodeMutationLeaseIsCurrent from the authorization barrel → nativeE2eeEnrollment → relayE2eeKeys → @noble/curves; api.ts → relayE2eeTranscripts → cborg

VITE_RYCO_CLIENT_MODE is a define, but it only feeds runtime isHostedHubMode() branches. The imports are static and modules such as hostedHub/state.ts build stores at module scope, so nothing is eliminated. History: the E2EE stack was created 2026-07-31 (relayE2eeHandshake now 2,838 lines) and 48 commits touched authorization/relay/E2EE after 2026-08-12, all inside already-eager modules. New eager edges were added on 09-11 (deviceName→hostedHub/state), 09-15 (PreviewFileNavigationGuard in __root), 09-30 (useHandleNewThread→authorization, sidebarUndo→coordinator) and 10-01 (HostedConnectionControls→readCache). Separately, vite.config.ts:129 defines VITE_RYCO_CLIENT_MODE from the module-level clientMode, not the resolvedClientMode parameter, so createWebViteConfig('hosted-hub') builds hosted plugins with standard code.

Proposal

Introduce a compile-time client-mode seam:

(1) A small resolveId plugin in vite.config.ts that maps a fixed list of seam modules (hostedHub/state, hostedHub/hostedConnectionCoordinator, hostedHub/readCache, hostedHub/transport, components/hostedHub/HostedConnectionControls, pwa/lifecycle) to *.standard.ts(x) siblings when resolvedClientMode==='standard'. The siblings are inert implementations with the same exports: static 'not hosted' snapshot hooks, null leases, a null component, hostedPwaLifecycle=null. Add a type test asserting export parity.

(2) For relay code the standard desktop build really needs (desktop workspace Hub connections: platform/desktopWorkspaceSocket.ts, HostedWsTransport in connectDesktopWorkspaceEnvironment; passkey ceremonies), use dynamic import('@ryco/client-runtime/relay') at those call sites. Drop webPasskeyCeremony from the platform barrel.

(3) Replace barrel imports on hot paths: add an ./authorization/nodeMutationLease subpath export; import webAppLifecycle from '../platform/appLifecycle' in rpc/wsConnectionState.ts.

(4) Fix vite.config.ts:129 to use resolvedClientMode.

(5) Lock it in with the dist guard (see bundle-guard finding).

Part of Priority 14: Trim the JS on the boot and thread paths

Expected gain

Chunks that import one contract or helper stop carrying whole packages (tens to hundreds of KiB per affected chunk). Prerequisite for getting contracts/effect-rpc out of the boot graph (-~200 KiB raw there once wsTransport moves, est.).

What happens today

No workspace package sets "sideEffects" (grep over packages/*/package.json and apps/web/package.json). effect and @noble/curves do declare it. @ryco/contracts/src/index.ts has 63 export * lines over Schema modules whose top-level Schema.Struct(...) calls the bundler must treat as side-effectful. A single brand import therefore keeps every contracts module in its chunk, and all of their schemas are constructed at startup. ~200 KiB raw of contracts sit in the boot graph (orchestration 34, agentControl 26, rpc 26, hostedIdentity 11, settings 11…). effect/Schema construction is ~25% of non-idle boot CPU at 4x (178 ms). client-runtime barrels (connection/index.ts re-exports 22 modules including nodeE2eeOperator and supervision; rpc/index.ts includes wsTransport) behave the same. AGENTS.md defines contracts as 'schema-only — no runtime logic', and grep found no global side effects in contracts/src.

Proposal
  • Add "sideEffects": false to packages/contracts/package.json.
  • Do the same for packages/shared after a per-file check.
  • For client-runtime, use an explicit allowlist array ("sideEffects": ["./src/**/register*.ts", ...]) for modules that really register globals.
  • Alternatively, scope it in the web build: build.rolldownOptions.treeshake.moduleSideEffects: [{ test: /packages[\\/](contracts|shared)[\\/]src[\\/]/, sideEffects: false }].
  • Verify with a graph.mjs diff and the browser suite.
Verifier (Partially confirmed)

True that no packages/*/package.json or apps/*/package.json declares sideEffects (rg). contracts/src/index.ts has 63 export * lines. effect 4.0.2 Schema.Struct (dist/Schema.js:1945) carries no @__NO_SIDE_EFFECTS__, so top-level schema calls are retained. But the claimed boot-graph effect will not materialize: packages/contracts/src/rpc.ts statically imports ~37 contract modules to build the RPC group, which wsTransport uses. So those modules are used, not dead, while wsTransport is in the graph. sideEffects/moduleSideEffects only drops modules whose exports are entirely unused; it does not prune unused top-level statements inside used modules. Savings are limited to lazy chunks that import a few helpers, and are unquantified. Risk is medium: a missed module-scope registration in shared or client-runtime would silently disappear.

Part of Priority 19: Connecting to a Hub

Expected gain

Hosted Hub: removes ~2 RTT plus import-chain serialization before the 1.8 MiB download and the ~300 ms throttle (est. -0.3 to -0.6 s at 40-80 ms RTT).

What happens today

1. The hosted branch of resolveRootBeforeLoadContextAsync awaits import('../hostedHub/logging'), then import('../hostedHub/state'), then import('../hostedHub/readCache'), one after another.

2. bootstrapWithHostedReadCache races the local restore against hostedHubController.bootstrap(), i.e. restoreSession() followed by refreshDirectory() (two sequential Hub RTTs).

3. Only after the root context resolves does RootRouteView render React.lazy(HostedHubRoot): 66 files / 1,796 KiB raw beyond boot, which also statically includes RootAppShell.

4. Its Suspense fallback then triggers the same 300 ms reveal throttle measured for the standard shell.

Code download is serialized behind the network handshakes even though fetching code has no lifecycle side effects.

Proposal
  • Run the three imports with Promise.all.
  • At the top of the hosted branch, start import('../components/hostedHub/HostedHubRoot'). This is a code-only prefetch: no session, ticket, relay or store side effects, so the single lifecycle owner required by AGENTS.md is untouched. Await it together with bootstrapWithHostedReadCache.
  • Render it through preloadableLazy (no throttle).
  • Include HostedHubRoot in the curated modulepreload list and confirm the hosted CDN serves brotli.
Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code matches. __root.tsx:121-131 awaits three imports in sequence. readCache.ts:481-527 races local restore against bootstrap(). authorization/state.ts:535-543 bootstrap → #restoreAccess (621-635) runs restoreSession, then refreshDirectory, i.e. two sequential Hub RTTs. HostedHubRoot.tsx:35 statically imports RootAppShell; in the standard dist it is 66 files / 1,796 KiB beyond boot. The impact is overstated, though. hostedHub/state (in runtime-*.js) and readCache-*.js are already static members of the boot closure, so two of the three dynamic imports resolve without network; only logging (a tiny chunk) can cost ≤1 RTT. For returning users with a read cache, the race resolves on the local restore, not on the two Hub RTTs. The throttle part is already counted under react-suspense-reveal-throttle and is hidden on slow links, per the investigator's hosted data. Realistic: -1 to -2 RTT (~40-160 ms) on first/no-cache visits. Not measurable here (no hosted-hub build); the CDN compression status is unverified.

Part of Priority 13: Serve compressed assets and flatten chunk waterfalls (remote clients)

Expected gain

-60 to -80 KiB raw (~-12 to -15 KiB gzip, est.) from render-critical CSS. Removes one post-paint font swap/reflow. Remote: ~-30 to -60 ms on the CSS→JS gap (est.).

What happens today

main-*.css is 587 KiB raw / 79 KiB gzip: @layer utilities 406 KiB, plain rules 108 KiB, phone-tier rules ~14 KiB. index.css @imports the projects/pullRequests/automations/overview stylesheets (~117 KiB source), used only by lazy pages. The loader awaits this CSS before importing main.js (local 1-6 ms; hosted profile 0.27 s uncompressed). DM Sans latin (36 KiB woff2, font-display: swap) is first requested when the shell commits text (421 ms local, 2,731 ms hosted profile), so sidebar text re-lays out right after first meaningful paint.

Proposal
  • Import each feature stylesheet from the lazy chunk that owns it (ProjectsPage, PullRequestsPage, AutomationsDialog, overview/ChatView), as already done for xterm.css in ThreadTerminalDrawer. Vite then emits per-chunk CSS that the preload helper loads with the chunk.
  • Add <link rel="preload" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin href="<dm-sans-latin-wght-normal.woff2 via node_modules path>"> to index.html. Vite rewrites it to the same hashed asset, so the font is ready before the shell commits.
  • Once modulePreload is on, the CSS no longer delays the JS download.
Verifier (Confirmed)

index.css:1-5 imports the pullRequests/projects/automations/overview stylesheets. Those are tiny barrels that @import ~118 KiB of source CSS (wc over the transitive files: 118,129 B), matching the ~117 KiB claim. DM Sans is the default font (index.css:14-21, font-display: swap; appearancePreferences.ts:32), and index.html has no font preload. Caveat: overview CSS is needed by the default thread view (overview visible by default, ChatView.tsx:653/4722), so moving it only shifts it to the thread phase. The local gain is negligible (loopback font fetch takes milliseconds). Low impact, as stated.

Part of Priority 14: Trim the JS on the boot and thread paths

Expected gain

Boot graph -1.3 to -1.5 MiB raw (est.). Auth starts ~90 ms earlier locally and ~0.9-1.0 s earlier on the hosted profile. This overlaps the shell download rather than removing bytes; expect -30 to -60 ms locally, -0.2 to -0.4 s remote (est.).

What happens today

tanstackRouter() runs with defaults (no autoCodeSplitting), so routeTree.gen.ts statically imports all 12 route files with their components. main-*.js (310 KiB) contains every route plus DesktopAccountConnect, NoActiveThreadState and PairingRouteSurface. Through them the boot graph pulls in:

  • runtime-*.js (630 KiB: composer draft store 71, threads store 65, session 40, message-queue 22, @base-ui 56…)
  • wsTransport-*.js (432 KiB: effect RPC/Schema 196 + ~60 contracts modules), only needed once the shell connects the WebSocket.

main.tsx:38 initializeWsConnectionState() also pulls the rpc barrel from the entry. All of this is downloaded and evaluated before beforeLoad's auth fetches can start: import-end 143-150 ms local, 1.61-1.67 s on the hosted profile (one 205 ms long task at CPU×4). CPU at 4x: effect 178 ms (SchemaAST 46), (program)/compile 292 ms. __root's await import('../hostedPairing') / await import('../environments/primary') (lines 132, 154) do not split anything: both modules are already static deps of main.

Proposal
  • Enable tanstackRouter({ autoCodeSplitting: true }) with codeSplittingOptions that keep /pair eager (the webBundleSplitting test requires it), or convert to .lazy.tsx route files. Only beforeLoad/validateSearch stay eager.
  • Move the seedWsConnectionOnlineStatus call into EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap.
  • Lazy-load PreviewFileNavigationGuard.

The boot graph then shrinks to react/react-dom/router/root/AppBootLoadingSurface/primary auth (~0.45-0.6 MiB raw est.), and the shell graph (including runtime + wsTransport) downloads in parallel with the auth round trips (combine with serial-shell-ws-thread-phases (a) and the modulepreload change).

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Verified: tanstackRouter() uses defaults (vite.config.ts:92). routeTree.gen.ts:10-21 statically imports all 12 routes. main-*.js.map contains all 12 route files. The __root dynamic imports (lines 132, 154) target hostedPairing-*.js (806 B) and primary-*.js (80 KiB), both already in main's static closure, so they split nothing. The estimate is inflated, though. The primary-*.js closure that beforeLoad needs is 519 KiB, including wsTransport-*.js (432 KiB). main.tsx:19/38 (rpc barrel), :9-10 (hostedHub/nodeRoutes, pwa/lifecycle) and react-dom/router remain eager. So the post-split boot graph would be ~0.9-1.0 MiB, not 0.45-0.6 MiB, unless primary's dependency on that chunk is also cut. More importantly, the shell needs runtime+wsTransport anyway, so the bytes before usable do not change. The gain is overlapping the auth round trip with the shell download: measured beforeLoad is ~5-9 ms local and ~63-77 ms on the hosted profile (1625→1688, 1678→1743). A cheaper way to get most of that: start /api/auth/session + descriptor from the inline index.html script (or the top of main.tsx) and let beforeLoad reuse the promise. Route-level splitting is still the right enabler for react-suspense-reveal-throttle (1) and react-suspense-reveal-throttle (4)/hosted-relay deferral.

Prior work

The Aug pass moved route bodies behind lazy() and guards them with string checks (webBundleSplitting.test.ts), but the route modules and their non-body imports stay eager. New.

Main-thread CPU at boot 16 findings · 2 high · 8 medium · 6 low

At 2,000 threads the Sidebar re-derives everything on every store commit (30–70 ms of JS each), and streaming produces up to ~60 such commits per second.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

Web boot today: index.html paints the inline boot shell, then the Vite loader (dist/assets/index-*.js) waits for the 601 KB main CSS load event before it calls import(main). Evaluating the ~75-file boot graph creates the persisted zustand stores synchronously: composer drafts (including base64 image hydration), uiStateStore, and useTheme's module-level applyTheme, which calls getComputedStyle. main.tsx's sync* helpers only use matchMedia and attribute writes, so they are cheap. After root beforeLoad, RootAppShell connects the primary WebSocket and subscribes to the shell. With the synthetic fixture of 30 projects and 2,000 threads (60% archived), the shell snapshot is one 2.19 MB JSON frame. It is JSON.parsed, fully decoded with Effect Schema (all threads, archived included), mapped into fresh store objects, and followed by several O(N) UI syncs (uiStateStore.syncThreads, a draft-promotion scan, terminal cleanup). Then the whole Sidebar renders: the projects tree and the inbox tree, even though one of them is hidden with CSS.

Where the time goes (V8, Apple M5 Max, shared machine under load average 9–25, so absolute numbers are noisy): snapshot decode 8–22 ms warm and 14–42 ms cold, plus 2–4 ms JSON.parse and 1.4–9 ms store build. Sidebar re-derivation is 18–27 ms warm and about 35–42 ms cold. The 30 project-item derivations are 16–30 ms. The hidden inbox model is 14 ms warm and 32–35 ms cold. The UI sync after each shell event is 3.7–14 ms. So the first sidebar render after the snapshot costs roughly 120–150 ms of pure JS on this very fast CPU. That excludes React reconciliation of about 360 mounted rows and style/layout, which is 60–150 ms for about 4.4k nodes with this stylesheet (synthetic, measured in Chrome). A typical laptop is estimated 2–4x slower. At 200 threads the same JS costs about 5–10 ms.

The bigger problem is steady state, and it also hits boot. The Sidebar subscribes to the whole environmentStateById. Because it is not compiled by React Compiler, it also builds a new grouping-settings object on every render. Together these re-run all of the derivations above, plus the hidden inbox model, on every store commit. Store commits happen once per WebSocket message: every thread-detail event, every prewarmed thread-window snapshot, and every shell thread-upserted. While a turn streams, the server flushes deltas every 32 ms and bumps the thread row's updatedAt, so each flush produces a thread-detail event and a shell upsert. That is about 60 commits/s, each costing tens of ms at 2,000 threads. This would saturate the main thread, which is a responsiveness and reliability problem. This is an inference from the measured per-function costs and the code paths; the end-to-end trace still needs to be captured with the measurement plan in finding boot-cpu-measurement-plan.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

Removes ~30–70 ms of main-thread JS per store commit at 2,000 threads on an M5 Max (~5 ms at 200 threads). That is every commit that does not change sidebar data: about 30 thread-detail commits/s while one thread streams, plus the 4+ thread-window snapshots at boot.

What happens today

Sidebar.tsx:253 subscribes to state.environmentStateById. commitEnvironmentState (store.ts:1924-1946) gives that object a new identity on every orchestration event, thread-window snapshot, history page and shell event, so the whole Sidebar re-renders on every WebSocket message that touches the store. On each render, Sidebar.tsx:271-274 calls useSettings((settings) => ({…})). useSettings memoizes on selector identity (useSettings.ts:146), and Sidebar is NOT compiled by React Compiler (verified in the built RootAppShell chunk), so this returns a new object every render. That invalidates physicalToLogicalKey (:585), which cascades into threadsByProjectKey (:646), worktreesByProjectKey, sortedProjects (:742, spreads every visible thread), projectTreeRows (:773) and visibleSidebarThreadKeys (:910, which runs sort + adapt + composeSidebarTree for every project). useLogicalProjectSnapshots.ts:46-48 documents exactly this hazard but Sidebar still has it. inboxEnvironments (:351) also depends on environmentStateById, so its new array makes InboxSidebar.tsx:117 rebuild the whole inbox model. The inline renderProjectRow (:1416) defeats the memo on SidebarProjectsContent. Measured pure derivations at 2,000 threads: Sidebar chain 18–27 ms warm / 35–42 ms cold, inbox model 14 ms warm / 32–35 ms cold. At 200 threads: 2 ms + 1.4 ms. On top of that come React re-renders of 30 project items and about 184 hidden inbox rows.

Proposal

(1) Replace Sidebar.tsx:253 with useStore(useShallow(selectCacheHydratedEnvironmentIds)) (already exists, store.ts:3114) and read hydratedFromCache as set membership in inboxEnvironments. (2) Take projectGroupingSettings from useLogicalProjectSnapshots (already stable) or select the two fields separately and combine them with useMemo. (3) useCallback renderProjectRow and other inline props passed to memoized children. (4) Fix the React Compiler bailout for Sidebar.tsx (see finding react-compiler-bailouts-hot-components). (5) Add a browser perf test that mounts Sidebar with a 2,000-thread store, applies thread-detail events for an unrelated thread, and asserts zero Sidebar commits via React.Profiler.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Checked the code and the source. Sidebar.tsx:253 subscribes to state.environmentStateById. Sidebar.tsx:271-274 passes an inline selector that returns an object. useSettings memoizes on [merged, selector] (useSettings.ts:146), so this yields a new object on every render. commitEnvironmentState (store.ts:1924-1946) spreads a new environmentStateById for every env-state change. The built chunk .perf-research/web-dist-sm/assets/RootAppShell-KkbzvhlV.js shows the Sidebar function (Gh) with oe(e=>e.environmentStateById) and the inline B(e=>({sidebarProjectGroupingMode:…})) and no (0,X.c)(N) memo cache, so it is not compiled. The cascade is real: physicalToLogicalKey (:585) → threadsByProjectKey (:646), worktreesByProjectKey, sortedProjects (:742), projectTreeRows (:773), visibleSidebarThreadKeys (:910-968). inboxEnvironments lists environmentStateById in its deps (:477-490). ConnectedInboxSidebar is not memo-wrapped, so InboxSidebar's model useMemo (InboxSidebar.tsx:117-152) rebuilds, and InboxThreadRow is not memo-wrapped either, so about 184 rows re-render. CORRECTION: the 30 SidebarProjectItems are memo (SidebarProjectItem.tsx:72) and get stable props on unrelated commits: the project snapshot comes from useLogicalProjectSnapshots, threadJumpLabelByKey is EMPTY_THREAD_JUMP_LABELS unless hints are showing (:1081), and the compiled SortableProjectItem handle props are stable. So their 16-30 ms derivations do NOT re-run per unrelated commit. Only SidebarProjectsContent plus 30 SortableProjectItem/useSortable re-render, because renderProjectRow is inline (:1416). SidebarProjectDialogProvider receives the unstable object, but its context value stays stable (the useSidebarProjectGroupingDialog deps use only the overrides field), so it does not cascade. I re-ran bench-sidebar.ts on the loaded machine: Sidebar chain 19.6 ms warm / 38 ms cold with 0% worktrees, and 36.8 ms warm with the default 30%-worktree fixture. The default sidebarMode is 'inbox' (uiStateStore.ts:140), so the per-commit inbox rebuild hits the visible pane for most users. The 30-70 ms/commit estimate at 2,000 threads (Sidebar chain + inbox model + row renders) is plausible. Fixes (1)-(3) are S.
