Category: CPURisk: mediumInvestigator confidence: mediumweb-boot-cpu:streaming-per-event-on-work

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

At 2,000 threads: −4–14 ms per streaming delta from the UI sync alone (×30/s ≈ 100–400 ms/s of main thread). Frame batching cuts React commits from ~60/s to ≤ display rate. Shell-upsert coalescing cuts sidebar re-sorts from ~30/s to 2–4/s per streaming thread and removes ~25 SQL shell reads/s per subscriber on the server.

What happens today

Server side: assistant deltas flush every 32 ms (ProviderRuntimeIngestion.ts:170). Each thread.message-sent bumps the projected thread row's updatedAt (ProjectionPipeline.ts:1116-1120). The shell stream maps every thread-aggregate domain event to thread-upserted with a fresh SQL read (orchestrationStreams.ts:254-268), and the progress coalescer only keys activities and plans. Client side: the thread-detail stream commits once per event (supervision.ts:448 -> service.ts:764 -> 707-728, one zustand set per WebSocket message), and so does the shell stream. The shell coalescer only batches above 10 events/ms (store.ts:3636-3637, i.e. more than 80 events in 8 ms), so in practice it never batches. For every thread-upserted, afterShellEventApplied (environmentStateSink.ts:75-89) calls syncThreadUiFromStore. That rebuilds keys for ALL threads, runs uiStateStore.syncThreads (6 Object.entries/fromEntries rebuilds of thread-keyed records), and calls markPromotedDraftThreadsByRef over all threads x all drafts (draftStore.ts:2323-2345). It does this even when nothing about the thread set changed, and line 77 already handles the single thread. Measured: 3.7–4.9 ms warm / 10 ms cold at 2,000 threads with 5–10 drafts, 14 ms with 50 drafts, 0.3 ms at 200 threads. These events also legitimately change the sidebar summary, which re-runs the finding-1 derivations about 30x/s.

Proposal

Client (S): in afterShellEventApplied for thread-upserted, call syncThreads only when the thread is new, removed, or its archive/trash state changed; otherwise seed lastVisited for the single key in O(1). Drop the global markPromotedDraftThreadsByRef from the upsert path, since environmentStateSink.ts:77 already promotes this thread. Client (M): batch incoming shell and thread-detail events per environment into one store commit per animation frame (make createShellEventCoalescer always frame-batched, add the same for detail events) and run derived UI sync once per batch. Server (M): give the shell stream its own progress key that coalesces thread-upserted per threadId over a 250–500 ms window, since the shell only needs the latest row. Never coalesce message text on the thread-detail stream.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Server: decider.ts:2580-2604 turns each assistant.delta command into thread.message-sent (streaming:true), and the flush interval is 32 ms (ProviderRuntimeIngestion.ts:170, 1464). ProjectionPipeline.ts:1105-1121 upserts the thread row with updatedAt = occurredAt. toShellStreamEvent's default branch (orchestrationStreams.ts:254-268) re-reads getThreadShellById for every thread-aggregate event, per shell subscriber. orchestrationProgressFrameKey (orchestrationEventCoalescing.ts:28-52) coalesces only activities and plans. Client: applyEnvironmentThreadDetailEvent → applyRecoveredEventBatch([event]) makes one zustand set per event (service.ts:707-766). afterShellEventApplied runs syncThreadUiFromStore on every thread-upserted (environmentStateSink.ts:75-89), which rebuilds keys for all threads via selectThreadsAcrossEnvironments (it derives full Thread objects only to read the key and updatedAt), runs uiStateStore.syncThreads (6 entries/fromEntries rebuilds; it returns the same state when nothing changed, so the cost is CPU, not renders), and calls markPromotedDraftThreadsByRef, which does Object.entries(draftThreadsByThreadKey) per thread (draftStore.ts:2323-2343). Coalescer (store.ts:3636-3637): it batches only above 10 events/ms within an 8 ms window, or for same-millisecond bursts (span 0 → Infinity), so 32 ms-spaced deltas are never batched. Each upsert changes updatedAt, so sidebarThreads legitimately changes and Sidebar re-runs the full chain plus the inbox model about 30 Hz per streaming thread. At 2,000 threads that is the larger cost, so the server-side upsert coalescing is the key part of the proposal. The end-to-end rate is an inference (no trace), so medium confidence is appropriate.

Prior work

The Aug 2026 report introduced the progress-frame coalescer (activities/plans) and the 32 ms delta flush, and says live events are prefiltered before detail reducers. Shell thread-upserted per message and the per-event O(N) client sync are not covered there. RELIABILITY: at large thread counts sustained streaming can saturate the main thread, which breaks 'predictable under load'.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

Boot and per commit at 2,000 threads: −14–35 ms of model build + ~184 row renders (projects mode), or −16–30 ms + ~180 rows (inbox mode). Also fewer DOM nodes, so style recalc gets cheaper.

What happens today

Sidebar renders both <SidebarProjectsContent> (30 SidebarProjectItems, about 180 rows) and <ConnectedInboxSidebar> and only hides one with className="hidden" + inert (Sidebar.tsx:1377-1466). The hidden inbox still runs buildInboxSidebarModel (14 ms warm / 32–35 ms cold at 2,000 threads) and renders every row of the unsettled sections: 184 InboxThreadRows in the fixture, each with useGitStatus, useSourceControlChangeRequestDetail, useSettings, uiStateStore selectors and its own IntersectionObserver. Because of finding 1 this happens on every store commit. The reverse also holds: in inbox mode the full project tree (16–30 ms of derivations) stays live.

Proposal

Render only the active mode's subtree. Alternatively wrap the inactive one in React 19.2 <Activity mode="hidden"> (react 19.2.8 is installed), which keeps state but defers its rendering and unmounts its effects. Also compute mode-specific inputs (inboxEnvironments, sidebarChatRows, visibleSidebarThreadKeys) only for the active mode.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Sidebar.tsx:1377-1466 always renders both SidebarProjectsContent and ConnectedInboxSidebar. It only toggles hidden (display:none) and inert. Corrections: (a) the default sidebarMode is 'inbox' (uiStateStore.ts:140), so by default the hidden pane is the projects tree. That costs a one-time mount of 30 SidebarProjectItems (17-44 ms of derivations measured) plus about 180 rows, but those items are memo'd and mostly bail out on unrelated commits. The per-commit hidden cost (inbox model + about 184 rows) applies to projects-mode users. (b) The claim 'fewer DOM nodes so style recalc gets cheaper' is weak: descendants of a display:none subtree are not styled or laid out. The saving is React render/commit plus effects (observers, git-status hooks), not style. Caveats for the proposal: InboxSidebar keeps local state (settledOpen, snoozedOpen, expandedHostKeys) that a plain unmount loses, which <Activity mode="hidden"> preserves. visibleSidebarThreadKeys also drives keyboard thread traversal and jump labels (Sidebar.tsx:1084-1182), not only the tree, so making it mode-specific needs care. Prewarm is already projects-only (Sidebar.logic.ts:427-434). <Activity> appears unused in the codebase today. Impact downgraded to medium because the per-commit part overlaps with finding 1's fix.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

~0.6 ms × markdown mounts (≈10–25 ms when opening a long thread) plus listener churn; avoids a potential ~100 ms recalc per mount whenever appearance inputs differ from the applied text.

What happens today

Each useTheme consumer runs useEffect(() => applyTheme(theme), [theme]) on mount (useTheme.ts:226-228). ChatMarkdown calls useTheme for every rendered message, so opening a thread runs applyTheme once per markdown mount. applyTheme does the following: (a) parses custom themes from localStorage twice (registry.ts:186-216); (b) moves the appearance <style> to the end of <head> and rewrites its textContent (appearancePreferences.ts:741, 371); (c) dispatches APPEARANCE_PREFERENCES_CHANGE_EVENT, which synchronously re-reads storage in every useAppearancePreference subscriber and schedules the htmlRenderTheme probe pass; (d) calls getComputedStyle twice (useTheme.ts:94-97), forcing a synchronous style recalc in the middle of the commit. getSnapshot also runs matchMedia and localStorage on every render. Each consumer adds its own matchMedia and storage listeners. Measured in Chrome 155 on a 4.4k-node DOM with the production CSS: 0.6 ms per call when the text is identical (Blink dedupes the sheet), but ~96 ms per call when the text differs.

Proposal

Mount one root-level ThemeController that owns applyTheme, subscribes once and re-applies only on real changes. Make useTheme read-only with a cached snapshot invalidated by events, with no effect and no per-instance listeners. In applyAppearancePreferencesToDocument, append the style element only when it is created and skip the write and event when the generated text is unchanged. Cache the parsed custom themes.

Verifier (Confirmed)

I verified the following. useTheme runs useEffect(() => applyTheme(theme), [theme]) per consumer (useTheme.ts:226-228). ChatMarkdown calls useTheme for every message (ChatMarkdown.tsx:731), and there are 12 files that use it. applyTheme → findTheme and getActiveThemeId each JSON-parse the custom themes from localStorage (registry.ts:186-216). For non-default themes, applyThemeToDocument rewrites the theme style textContent (registry.ts:272-283). applyAppearancePreferencesToDocument re-appends the style element, rewrites it and dispatches the change event (appearancePreferences.ts:367-373, 741). syncBrowserChromeTheme calls getComputedStyle twice (useTheme.ts:92-104). The investigator missed an amplifier: every consumer's subscribe() registers its own matchMedia 'change' and window 'storage' handlers, and each one calls applyTheme(..., true) (useTheme.ts:174-194). A system color-scheme flip or a cross-tab theme write therefore runs applyTheme N times (N = mounted consumers, including every ChatMarkdown), each with a forced reflow (offsetHeight) and an rAF. getSnapshot also re-parses custom themes on every render of every consumer (useTheme.ts:147-164). The 0.6 ms/call figure is from a synthetic Chrome bench. The single root ThemeController proposal fixes all of this.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

−7–38 ms per Sidebar recompute and −the same again in the project items at 2,000 threads (more for worktree-heavy users); about 10x less at 200 threads.

What happens today

For every merged worktree node, composeSidebarTree runs materializedThreads.filter(thread => belongsToWorktree(...)) (useSidebarTree.ts:150-172), once for active and once for archived nodes. belongsToWorktree recomputes sidebarDirectoryGroupKey (normalizeProjectPathForComparison + JSON.stringify) for both the thread and the worktree on every pair (:528-537). ensureProjectWorktrees synthesizes one node per thread (:475-490). sortWorktrees runs twice, and dedupeSidebarThreads JSON.stringifies every thread (:179-190). Archived threads go through the whole pipeline. The tree is built once in Sidebar's visibleSidebarThreadKeys for every project (Sidebar.tsx:938-951) and again in each SidebarProjectItem via useSidebarTree (useSidebarProjectThreadPresentation.ts:144-168). Measured at 2,000 threads across 30 projects: 6.9 ms (no worktree paths), 9.8 ms (5%), 20–38 ms (30% of threads in worktrees) per full pass, and the Sidebar pass is repeated on every Sidebar render (finding 1).

Proposal

Assign threads in a single pass. Precompute each thread's directory key and each merged node's key once, build Map<nodeId, threads[]> via directory key, then worktreeId, then branch fallback, and bucket in O(T+W). Memoize normalized paths in a bounded Map. Skip archived threads unless the archive section is expanded. Compute one tree per project and share it between Sidebar.visibleSidebarThreadKeys and SidebarProjectItem, for example through a WeakMap cache keyed by the per-project thread array identity. Keep the existing composeSidebarTree tests as the parity oracle.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Verified useSidebarTree.ts:104-177. For every merged node (archived and active), materializedThreads.filter(belongsToWorktree) runs. belongsToWorktree (:277-320) recomputes threadDirectoryGroupKey and worktreeDirectoryGroupKey (normalizeProjectPathForComparison + JSON.stringify, :507-537) per pair. ensureProjectWorktrees (:475-490) synthesizes one node per unlinked thread, sortWorktrees is called twice, and dedupeSidebarThreads (:179-190) stringifies each thread. The tree is built twice per project, in Sidebar.tsx:938-951 and in useSidebarProjectThreadPresentation.ts:144-168. I re-ran bench-sidebar-breakdown: composeSidebarTree across all 30 projects took 5.7 ms (0% worktree), 9.6 ms (5%) and 24.3 ms (30%) warm, matching the claim. Caveat: the fixture gives every worktree thread a unique path (fixture.mjs), which is the worst case for node count. Real users usually share a few worktrees across many threads, so the quadratic term is smaller. At realistic ratios the saving is about 5-10 ms per pass at 2,000 threads and under 1 ms at 200, so I downgraded to medium. It still matters because the pass repeats on every Sidebar render (finding 1) and at about 30 Hz while streaming.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

For reconnects and ranking updates: avoids re-rendering all rows (hundreds at 2,000 threads) and the derived recomputation; the server change also removes ~2.2 MB and ~15–40 ms of decode per ranking batch per client.

What happens today

syncEnvironmentShellSnapshot builds new shell, session, turnState and summary objects for every thread via mapThreadShell and never reuses previous ones, even though the equality helpers already exist (threadShellsEqual, sidebarThreadSummariesEqual, threadSessionsEqual, threadTurnStatesEqual at store.ts:578-733). Every snapshot therefore invalidates every row selector and memo. Snapshots arrive at boot, on every non-resumable reconnect, on every hosted reconnect, on Hub node switches, and on every AI-Focus ranking batch: the server merges threadPriorityChanges into the shell stream as a full {kind:"snapshot"} (orchestrationStreams.ts:558-572). Cost per 2,000-thread snapshot (measured): 2.19 MB frame, JSON.parse 2.2–3.7 ms, decode 8–22 ms warm, store build 1.4–9.3 ms, plus reconcileSnapshotDerivedState and a full sidebar and row re-render.

Proposal

In syncEnvironmentShellSnapshot, reuse the previous shell, summary, session and turnState object whenever the equality helpers say it is unchanged. If no thread changed, keep the previous record objects so selectors short-circuit. On the server, replace the priority-driven full snapshot with targeted thread-upserted events for threads whose ranking changed, or a small priorities-updated item.

Verifier (Confirmed)

syncEnvironmentShellSnapshot (store.ts:1948-2025) creates fresh containers and calls mapThreadShell (store.ts:385-465) for every thread with no reuse. The equality helpers exist at store.ts:560-733 (threadSessionsEqual 560, sidebarThreadSummariesEqual 578, threadShellsEqual 658, threadTurnStatesEqual 726) and are used only on the per-thread upsert path (store.ts:1095-1140). Server: prioritySnapshotStream maps every threadPriorityChanges tick to a full snapshot (orchestrationStreams.ts:558-564), published per ranking batch (ThreadPriorityCoordinator.ts:207-208). Scope correction: aiFocusEnabled defaults to false (packages/contracts/src/settings.ts:88), so priority-driven full snapshots affect opt-in users only. On a cold first boot there is no previous state to share. The real wins are cache-hydrated → live transitions (hosted/desktop hub caches), non-resumable or hosted reconnects, Hub node switches, and AI Focus users. Medium impact stands for the hub-connection scenario.

Prior work

The Aug 2026 report covers bounded thread-window snapshots and resume-from-sequence for direct reconnects. The shell snapshot's lack of structural sharing and the priority full-snapshot push are not covered.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

−5–25 ms of cold-boot main-thread work at 2,000 threads (about 60% of decode, plus proportional JSON.parse, store and selector work); bytes over the wire drop by a similar share.

What happens today

The shell snapshot contains every non-deleted thread, archived ones included (60% in the fixture). The RPC client decodes it on the main thread with full Effect Schema: Schema.Trim transforms on every id and title (baseSchemas.ts:3-4), a ModelSelection transformEffect per thread (orchestration.ts:116), and withDecodingDefault fields. Measured at 2,000 threads: decode 7.9–21.7 ms warm and 14.5–41.6 ms cold, about 98% of it in threads. Decoding only the 831 non-archived threads costs 40% of the full decode in the same run. Validation alone (Schema.is) is 12.9 ms, so a validation-only fast path is not a large win.

Proposal

Short term: have the server send archived threads in a slim form (id, projectId, title, archivedAt, updatedAt, lineage) or fetch them on demand when the archive view opens or lineage walking needs them. Medium term: decode and map the snapshot in a Worker and hand the store pre-built records, or add a trusted server-to-client codec for the shell stream. Apply the same split to the hosted read cache shell.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Verified the schemas: TrimmedString = Schema.Trim (baseSchemas.ts:3-4), the ModelSelection transformEffect (orchestration.ts:116-150), and withDecodingDefault on several OrchestrationThreadShell fields (orchestration.ts:1124-1166). getShellSnapshot (ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:2556+) lists threads filtering only deleted/trashed rows, so archived threads are included. I re-ran bench-decode-split.ts: full decode 13.5 ms warm / 28.1 ms cold, the non-archived subset (831 threads) 5.3 ms warm (39%), and Schema.is validation alone 7.3 ms. This matches the claim. Medium risk is right: archived threads feed composeSidebarTree archived sections, lineage/delegated-child lookups and search, so the slim form needs an on-demand path. protocol.ts:472 is only the layerJson wiring, not the decode site.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

Turns accidental O(N) recomputation into memo hits automatically; complements finding 1 and prevents regressions. Not separately quantified.

What happens today

Sourcemap analysis of the hidden-sourcemap build (.perf-research/web-boot-cpu/compiler-coverage.mjs) shows 495 of 551 web .tsx sources contain compiler output. Sidebar.tsx, SidebarProjectItem.tsx, InboxSidebar.tsx, ConnectedInboxSidebar.tsx, ChatComposer.tsx and BranchToolbarBranchSelector.tsx contain none (ChatView opts out explicitly). These are exactly the per-commit hot paths, so they rely on hand-written useMemo deps, which is where the finding-1 bug lives. A likely cause is ref writes during render (e.g. sidebarThreadByKeyRef.current = … at SidebarProjectItem.tsx:155-157 and ConnectedInboxSidebar.tsx:57-58), which violate the Rules of React; this is not verified.

Proposal

Run the React Compiler with a logger (or eslint-plugin-react-compiler) once to list bailout reasons for these files, then fix them (move ref syncing into useLayoutEffect or useEffectEvent, remove render-time mutations). Add a guard test next to apps/web/src/perf/webBundleSplitting.test.ts that asserts the listed hot components compile, for example by checking the build output for the memo-cache call.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

Removes several full sidebar/inbox row re-render passes at boot (one per provider-status or config push; hundreds of rows at 2,000 threads) and all later settings-unrelated config churn.

What happens today

useSettings subscribes to the whole serverConfigAtom (useServerConfig → useAtomValue) and to the full client-settings store, and only applies the selector during render (useSettings.ts:146). The doc comment says the selector narrows the subscription, but it does not. applyProvidersUpdated and applyServerConfigEvent create a new ServerConfig for every provider-status push (serverState.ts:85-117), which happens several times during boot while providers probe. Every consumer re-renders each time: 5 per SidebarProjectItem (150 at 30 projects), one per InboxThreadRow, and every row using useGitStatus (gitStatusState.ts:279 calls useSettings).

Proposal

Implement useSettings with selector-level subscriptions and Object.is equality: useSyncExternalStoreWithSelector over a merged-settings store, or derived per-key atoms (e.g. an Atom.map of serverConfigAtom down to settings and key). Keep the API; select primitives. Optionally have useGitStatus read the poll interval once through a non-reactive getter.

Verifier (Confirmed)

useSettings (useSettings.ts:130-147) calls useServerSettings → useServerConfig → useAtomValue(serverConfigAtom) (apps/web/src/rpc/serverState.ts:44-52), so any ServerConfig change re-renders every consumer. The selector only runs inside a render-time useMemo. applyProvidersUpdated and applyServerConfigEvent call resolveServerConfig with a new object for each provider-status push (client-runtime serverState.ts:85-117). The doc comment ('Selector narrows the subscription', useSettings.ts:108-111) is wrong and also sits detached above getClientSettings. Correction: React re-renders a component once per atom update no matter how many useSettings calls it makes, so that is 30 SidebarProjectItem re-renders, not 150. Additional amplifier: Sidebar's inboxEnvironments depends on useServerConfig() (Sidebar.tsx:350, 477), so each provider-status push also rebuilds the whole inbox model and its rows. useGitStatus reads gitStatusPollIntervalMs via useSettings (gitStatusState.ts:279).

Part of Priority 22: Make startup measurable

Expected gain

Makes the ~120–150 ms (M5 Max) boot JS and the per-commit streaming cost visible and gateable; required to validate the findings above end to end.

What happens today

primary-shell-snapshot-received is marked inside syncShellSnapshot (supervision.ts:734), after the RPC layer has already JSON.parsed and Schema-decoded the frame, so the 8–42 ms decode is invisible. primary-shell-usable is marked synchronously right after the store write (service.ts:204-213), before reconcileSnapshotDerivedState, before React renders the sidebar and before paint. The external harness waits for #root by default (runner.ts:67), records only long-task count and max plus CDP TaskDuration, and does not collect ryco:startup:* measures or CPU profiles. ClientPerfBudget.browser.tsx only replays synthetic marks and renders nothing. VITE_RYCO_PERF_PROFILE is a build-time flag, and usePerfMark registers a layout effect per render even when disabled.

Proposal

(1) Marks: add primary-shell-frame-received at raw socket message receipt, measure decode separately, and mark primary-sidebar-committed (layout effect in Sidebar on the first bootstrapComplete) and primary-shell-painted (requestAnimationFrame then a MessageChannel tick); report the derived measures. (2) Fixture: a generator for a sanitized Ryco home with 30 projects and 2,000 threads (60% archived, realistic branches and worktrees, 10 drafts), used with perf:external --fixture-home. (3) Harness: read performance.getEntriesByType('measure') for ryco:startup:*, and capture a CDP Profiler.start/stop CPU profile (100 µs sampling) from navigation to primary-shell-painted + 5 s on a RYCO_WEB_SOURCEMAP=hidden build, summarizing self time by source file. Gate on boot long-task total and on sidebar commit count. (4) A Vitest browser test that mounts Sidebar with the 2,000-thread store, wraps it in React.Profiler, applies 50 thread-detail events for an unrelated thread and 50 shell upserts, and asserts Sidebar commit counts and actualDuration budgets. (5) Keep the Node micro-benchmarks in .perf-research/web-boot-cpu as perf regression scripts for the pure functions (decode, syncServerShellSnapshot, sidebar chain, composeSidebarTree, buildInboxSidebarModel).

Expected gain

−0.3 ms and −2k allocations per store commit at 2,000 threads (~10–20 ms/s and GC pressure while streaming).

What happens today

ChatView ('use no memo') subscribes with useStore(useShallow(state => selectThreadsAcrossEnvironments(state).map(thread => scopedThreadKey(...)))). On every store commit, including every streaming event of the open thread, this derives every thread, allocates N strings and shallow-compares N entries. The result is only used to filter openTerminalThreadKeys, which is usually 0–2 keys (:960-963). Measured: 0.27–0.29 ms plus 2,000 string allocations per commit at 2,000 threads.

Proposal

Select existence only for the open terminal keys: useStore(useShallow(s => openTerminalThreadKeys.filter(k => { const ref = parseScopedThreadKey(k); return ref !== null && selectThreadExistsByRef(s, ref); }))), merged with draftThreadKeys. That makes it O(open terminals).

Its only use is at :960-963, which filters openTerminalThreadKeys. When the key list changes it also builds a 2,000-entry Set. ChatView has 'use no memo' (:521). The proposed O(open terminals) selector is correct. The impact is low as stated.

Part of Priority 13: Serve compressed assets and flatten chunk waterfalls (remote clients)

Expected gain

Remote and hosted boot: ~1 RTT + CSS transfer time (≈50–300 ms on mobile/remote, estimate); localhost ≈5 ms.

What happens today

The built loader (dist/assets/index-Ca8qsKFg.js) wraps import('./main-*.js') in Vite's preload helper with deps [main-BKvXLkrW.css]. It inserts the stylesheet link, waits for its load promise (s.then(… return i())), and only then calls the dynamic import. With modulePreload: false, nothing else starts the JS fetch early, so the main graph download waits for the 601 KB (79 KiB gzip) CSS. Locally the CSS load took 5 ms (measured); for hosted Hub and remote environments it costs one RTT plus the CSS transfer before any JS is requested.

Proposal

Start the JS and CSS in parallel. Emit <link rel="modulepreload" href="/src/main.tsx"> (Vite hashes it) or a plain preload for the main chunk in index.html. Alternatively move the CSS into index.html as a non-render-blocking <link rel=stylesheet> and drop it from the dynamic-import deps, so the import runs immediately. Keep the boot-shell-first-paint intent.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The mechanism is right. The built loader apps/web/dist/assets/index-Ca8qsKFg.js has __vite__mapDeps → ['assets/main-BKvXLkrW.css'], appends the stylesheet, waits for its load promise and only then calls import('./main-C8t65ccR.js'). Note the main JS chunk is main-C8t65ccR.js; main-BKvXLkrW is the CSS. modulePreload is false (vite.config.ts:188). Prior work: this overlaps the documented residual 'retest modulePreload' (docs/research/performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md:97, 252, 268, 344), so it is not entirely undocumented. Impact downgrade: desktop and localhost lose about 5 ms. Hosted Hub has a PWA service worker that precaches the whole reachable asset graph, including CSS and dynamic imports (apps/web/src/pwa/buildArtifacts.ts:67-107, 137, 172), so only the first visit or the first visit after a deploy pays the extra RTT plus CSS transfer. The proposed <link rel=modulepreload href="/src/main.tsx"> is not reliable, because main is reached through a dynamic import and Vite will not rewrite that href to the hashed chunk. A small build plugin that emits the CSS as a non-blocking link and drops it from the dynamic-import deps, or a resolveDependencies filter, is more practical. With modulePreload off, the bigger first-visit cost is probably the static-import discovery waterfall of the 75-file boot graph, which this finding does not quantify.

Prior work

The Aug 2026 report made the loader start the main graph after the boot shell paints, with modulePreload disabled. The CSS-wait serialization is a side effect of that loader and is not documented.

Expected gain

Avoids ~100–250 ms jank spikes on theme or appearance changes and on system color-scheme flips with large DOMs (measured synthetic).

What happens today

Measured in headless Chrome 155 with the production CSS and a 4,410-element synthetic DOM: a full-document recalc (html.dark toggle) costs 22.6 ms with no classes on the elements, 61 ms with 2 utility classes per element and 91–120 ms with 8, versus about 0 ms with the stylesheet disabled. The sheet registers 344 :root custom properties and 100 @property rules. applyTheme with suppressTransitions adds and removes no-transitions on <html> and forces a synchronous reflow in between (useTheme.ts:108-124), which costs two full-document recalcs plus a layout. Any appearance-variable change rewrites :root (≈96 ms measured per call when the text changes). These paths are user-triggered (theme change, system scheme or storage events), not per-boot.

Proposal

Keep root-level mutations rare and batched. Replace the no-transitions class toggle with a scoped transition: none on a theme-swap layer, or with View Transitions. Skip appearance or theme writes when the generated CSS is unchanged (see use-theme-applies-per-mount). Track a 'full recalc on 4k nodes' metric in the external harness so CSS growth (now 587 KiB, up from the Aug baseline) is visible.

Verifier (Confirmed)

applyTheme(…, true) adds no-transitions, toggles dark, rewrites the style elements, forces a reflow through offsetHeight and removes the class in an rAF (useTheme.ts:106-125). The dark variant is &:is(.dark, .dark *) (index.css:7), so toggling it re-matches the whole document. The 22-120 ms recalc numbers come from a synthetic headless-Chrome bench (browser-style-results.txt). These paths are user-triggered, not per boot. Per the finding-10 note, a system scheme flip calls applyTheme once per mounted useTheme consumer, but only the first call changes the dark class. Low impact is correct.

Expected gain

Boot: −~2 ms per MB of draft images; typing: −several ms per debounced write when drafts hold images (proportional to blob size).

What happens today

The zustand persist middleware hydrates all drafts synchronously when the store is created. composerDraftStore becomes reachable from almost every module because lib/utils.ts (the cn helper) imports DraftId from it. Each persisted image is decoded with atob and a per-byte loop into a File (composerDraftPersistence.ts:83-88). Measured in Chrome: 3 drafts with 1 MB images = 3.8 MiB blob, JSON.parse 0.7 ms, image hydration 6.5 ms (≈2.2 ms/MB). Every debounced draft change (300 ms) re-stringifies and writes the whole multi-MB blob (setItem alone 2.5 ms for 3.8 MiB) while the user types. verifyPersistedAttachments calls readPersistedAttachmentIdsFromStorage, which Schema-decodes the entire blob to get one thread's attachment IDs.

Proposal

Hydrate images lazily (keep the data URL or blob reference, create the File only on send or preview). Move image bytes to IndexedDB Blobs keyed by attachment ID and keep only metadata in localStorage. Persist drafts per thread key so a keystroke rewrites one small entry. Have lib/utils import DraftId from @ryco/client-runtime/state/composer directly so cn does not instantiate the web draft store.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Data-URL images are hydrated synchronously at store creation via merge → toHydratedThreadDraft → hydrateImages (draftStore.ts:2262-2290; atob plus a per-byte loop at composerDraftPersistence.ts:83-88). verifyPersistedAttachments flushes storage and then schema-decodes the whole blob to read one thread's IDs (draftStore.ts:917-934, composerDraftPersistence.ts:41-59). CORRECTION, and it is worse than claimed: the stringify is NOT debounced. zustand 5.0.15 persist calls partialize plus createJSONStorage's JSON.stringify on every set (apps/web/node_modules/zustand/esm/middleware.mjs:300, 358-369). Only the underlying localStorage.setItem goes through createDebouncedStorage (apps/web/src/lib/storage.ts:42-66). ChatComposer calls setPrompt on every input change (ChatComposer.tsx:1436), so each keystroke stringifies the whole multi-MB draft blob. I measured 2.1 ms median (p90 2.7) for a 4.0 MB state in Node (.perf-research/verifier-web-boot-cpu/stringify-bench.mjs). A quick fix is a custom PersistStorage that keeps the object and stringifies inside the debounced flush. The lib/utils.ts:4 point is moot: composerDraftStore is already in the boot graph through environmentStateSink.ts:7-11 (draftStore.ts is 23 KiB of the boot graph per EVIDENCE). Hosted mode uses memory storage (composerDraftPersistence.ts:30), so it pays neither hydration nor writes.

Live browser measurements 14 findings · 2 high · 7 medium · 5 low

Measured in Chrome: composer visible at 764 ms on a cold loopback load, ~500 ms of it idle; removing the Suspense throttle gives 412 ms. On a slow link the composer takes 38.7 s, dominated by 6.3 MB of uncompressed assets.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

I measured the production build in Chrome 155 against a local apps/server/dist/bin.mjs on loopback, with 3 scratch git projects. Partway through, I found another agent driving the same Playwright tab. From then on I ran everything in a separate BrowserContext with the session cookie copied over. Results from the shared tab and the separate context agree within about 50 ms.

**Cold / load (1x CPU, cache disabled, n=3).**

  • Timings: boot splash 7 ms, React root 89 ms, sidebar 403 ms, WS open 423 ms, shell usable 428 ms, composer 764 ms, LCP 808 ms.
  • Volume: 195 requests (184 JS), 6.32 MB, all uncompressed.
  • Warm reload (n=3): sidebar 360 ms, composer 717 ms. Caching saves almost nothing, because the time is not spent in the network.
  • Root cause: React 19.2 holds back every Suspense "content after fallback" commit until 300 ms after the most recent fallback was shown (in react-dom performWorkOnRoot, globalMostRecentFallbackTime + 300 - now()). It hits twice on boot: the lazy RootAppShell is ready at about 71 ms but only shows at about 352 ms, and the lazy thread route is ready about 230 ms before it shows. The main thread is idle in those windows; the CPU profile shows ~0 ms busy between 250 and 450 ms.
  • Proof: a timer hook caught react-dom's scheduleTimeout calls with delays of 299, 298 and 282 ms. In an A/B test where I patched the served main chunk so the 300 becomes 0, composer time dropped from 803 to 412 ms and LCP from 852 to 440 ms.
  • Every first page open pays the same toll: settings 326→40 ms, projects 324→41 ms, statistics shell 313→36 ms, pull requests 391→125 ms. Settings stays at 336 ms even though its chunk was already prefetched.

**Slow device and network (4x CPU, 150 ms RTT, 1.6 Mbps).**

  • A cold load reaches the composer at 38.7 s. It is dominated by 6.1 MB of uncompressed assets (1.85 MB gzip / 1.68 MB brotli).
  • Vite's preload helper waits for the 601 KB CSS before it even requests main.js (CSS done 3,581 ms, main.js requested 3,623 ms).
  • The 4 KB shell snapshot waits about 3 s on the single socket behind two copies of the ~113 KB server config (the subscription snapshot plus a redundant server.getConfig).
  • At 4x CPU alone, the main thread is busy for 2.1 s. The biggest frames are the snapshot/config decode in wsTransport (202 ms), main-chunk module evaluation (160 ms) and the RootAppShell render (155 ms).

**Page opens.**

  • Statistics first fetches the full config (127 KB, about 1 s on the slow link), then getUsageSummary, which takes 2.5–8.2 s on the server for every open (no memoization; sources scanned one after another).
  • Projects and the first new draft also re-fetch the full config before rendering or navigating.

**Bugs and wasted work along the way.**

  • Loading /statistics directly shows "No usage environments are connected" permanently: getUsageSummary is never sent (reproduced in the separate context).
  • Every page load opens a second /ws/device socket and runs device.list, which spawns xcrun simctl on the server (~400–470 ms).
  • Every project icon is resolved twice per load (once over HTTP, once over RPC), and each resolution spawns a new Node child process (127–182 ms each).
  • vcs.listRefs is sent twice with an identical payload on thread open.

The hosted-hub connect flow is not served by this standard build, so it is not covered here.

Part of Priority 1: Remove the 300 ms React Suspense reveal delay from every navigation

Expected gain

Measured A/B: about -390 ms time-to-composer on every cold and warm load (803→412 ms), about -410 ms LCP, about -220 ms to sidebar and WS start; about -270-290 ms on every first open of settings, projects, statistics, PRs and the new-thread draft

What happens today

Every route component and RootAppShell is a React.lazy() inside <Suspense>; the thread routes use fallback={null}, which still counts. React 19.2.8 (react-dom-client.production.js:10793) defers any commit made only of retry lanes until globalMostRecentFallbackTime + 300 ms. The timestamp is global, so any fallback anywhere restarts the clock.

Measured on loopback:

  • RootAppShell content was ready at ~71 ms but committed at 352 ms; react-dom scheduleTimeout was observed with delays 299/298/282 ms.
  • The thread route was ready ~230 ms before it committed; timers of 294-221 ms fired at 743, composer appeared at 749.
  • The CPU profile is idle in both windows.

A/B test (patching the minified constant 300→0 in the served main chunk):

  • Composer 803→412 ms (-49%), LCP 852→440 ms, sidebar 438→220 ms, WS open 460→239 ms (the WS only starts after RootAppShell commits).
  • Settings 326→40, projects 324→41, statistics shell 313→36, PRs 391→125.

Effect on prefetching: Settings is prefetched at idle (0 chunk requests) yet still takes 336 ms. A preloaded import() still suspends a lazy() on first render, so the prefetch buys nothing for time-to-content.

Proposal

Stop committing fallbacks for code that is already loading or loaded:

1. Root: in resolveRootBeforeLoadContextAsync, start import('../components/RootAppShell') in parallel with the auth fetches (non-hosted, non-/pair) and await it. Store the module in a variable and render <RootAppShellModule.RootAppShell/> directly; keep lazy()/Suspense only as a fallback when the module is not yet resolved.

2. Routes: replace component-level lazy()+<Suspense> with TanStack Router route-level code splitting (createLazyFileRoute / lazyRouteComponent, or autoCodeSplitting). The router then awaits the chunk inside router.load() before committing the match, so no Suspense fallback ever commits and the throttle never applies.

3. Add defaultPreload: 'intent' (and preload on pointerdown) in router.ts. Turn the idle preloadSettingsPage into router.preloadRoute({to:'/settings'}).

4. Add a perf guard test asserting route components are not wrapped in a Suspense whose fallback commits during warm navigation (e.g. count react-dom scheduleTimeout calls of 200-300 ms in a browser test).

Verifier (Confirmed)

Checked react-dom 19.2.8 react-dom-client.production.js:10791-10794: (lanes & 62914560) === lanes (retry lanes only) and globalMostRecentFallbackTime + 300 - now(), then scheduleTimeout(commitRootWhenReady, …). The A/B and timer evidence is in .perf-research/browser-measure/measurements-summary.json.

All six route files wrap React.lazy in <Suspense>:

  • thread route 7-24, draft 6-21
  • statistics 11-30, projects 8-34, settings 9-38, pull-requests 11-38

RootAppShell is at __root.tsx:29-31 and 244-246. router.ts:7-14 has no defaultPreload and no route code splitting. preloadSettingsPage (settingsRoute.ts:13-15) only warms the module; React.lazy still suspends on first render because the factory returns a fresh .then() promise. That explains settings at 336 ms despite the prefetch.

The proposal holds: in TanStack Router 1.170.33, Match.js MatchInner returns renderPending() for status 'pending' instead of throwing. Route-level lazyRouteComponent/autoCodeSplitting therefore commits without a Suspense fallback, and the 300 ms throttle never arms.

Caveats:

  • The A/B patched the constant globally, which also removed nested lazy boundaries (AppSidebarLayout, CommandPalette, ChatRightPanel, ThreadWorkspacePanel …). Treat -390 ms as an upper bound for this proposal; audit nested boundaries on the boot path too.
  • HostedHubRoot (__root.tsx:32-36, 230-232) uses the same lazy+Suspense pattern, so the hosted-hub connect flow pays the same toll. It was not measured, but the code is identical.
Prior work

None. The Aug hardening pass added these lazy route boundaries (statistics/diagnostics/pairing) and docs/research does not mention the React fallback throttle. This is a side effect of that work, not a re-proposal.

Part of Priority 9: Statistics: memoize, aggregate incrementally, never block the server

Expected gain

Statistics data visible on reopen: 2.5-8 s → <100 ms with a memo hit; first open about -40% from concurrent sources; lower server CPU and possibly memory

What happens today

Four opens of the 30-day view took 8,155 / 5,355 / 2,495 / 5,952 ms from request to Exit. That is with 1,298 of 1,343 Claude and 265 of 265 Codex files already reused from the in-memory scan cache, 96.5k Claude responses.

scanStartedAt/FinishedAt show the providers processed one after another (Claude 1,014 ms, then Codex 1,222 ms). The for (const source of sources) loop and the per-file yield* readFileRecords loop are sequential. Every request rebuilds a fresh UsageAggregator over all cached records and prices each record again.

The client caches nothing between opens: every navigation to /statistics re-runs the scan and shows skeletons for seconds. The page is unusable for about 5 s on a heavy user's machine.

Server RSS was 643 MiB after ~30 min with 4 scans (EVIDENCE: 360 MiB at boot). Unattributed, but consistent with the scan cache holding raw records in memory.

Proposal

1. Memoize the finished summary per (range, timeZone, sources, scan-cache generation, rates revision). Return it immediately on a hit; on change, use stale-while-revalidate with a 'refreshing' flag. The client already has refreshing.

2. Store per-file daily aggregates (per day × model × provider) in the scan cache instead of raw records, so a summary costs O(files × days), not O(records). Re-price lazily per (model, day) bucket.

3. Scan independent sources concurrently (bounded, e.g. 2).

4. Client: keep the last summary per range in memory and show it immediately on reopen.

5. Kick off the summary request when hovering the statistics link.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Verified in UsageService.ts:

  • readSummaryUnlocked starts at 453.
  • for (const source of sources) at 473 is sequential.
  • A fresh UsageAggregator is built per source on every request (498-505), pricing each record again via priceUsageRecord.
  • The per-file loop at 599-620 is sequential.
  • listUsageTranscriptFiles re-walks every root on every request (585-590).
  • No summary memo exists.
  • useUsageSummary.ts:76-116 holds results only in component state, so every remount re-requests.

Additional specifics:

  • scanSemaphore = Semaphore.make(1) (166, 806-808) serializes all summary requests, so a range change while one is in flight queues behind it.
  • SOURCE_SCAN_RECORDS = 100,000 (line 67). The measured 96.5k Claude records are near the cap, so heavy users will soon get 'partial' results.
  • The scan cache on disk is 15.2 MB (/tmp/ryco-perf-home-browser/userdata/usage/scan-cache.json, 1,608 file entries). I measured ~35 ms JSON.parse on the first open per process, and ~33 ms JSON.stringify in persistScanCache (201-212, called at 769) whenever any transcript changed. Both block the server event loop.
  • ensureRates (455) can also block the request on an outbound fetch; see the additional finding.

The proposal is sound. Memoization and per-day aggregates also shrink the cache. Risk is medium because of the pricing-revision and time-zone keys.

Prior work

None in the prior perf docs (the usage scan cache exists; summary memoization and aggregate caching do not).

Part of Priority 9: Statistics: memoize, aggregate incrementally, never block the server

Expected gain

Fixes a permanently broken Statistics view on reload, deep link and desktop restore to /statistics

What happens today

useConnectedEnvironments reads listEnvironmentConnections() during render (useMemo on a revision counter) and only subscribes in a later useEffect. EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap is an earlier sibling of the route outlet in RootAppShell. Because the Suspense throttle makes RootAppShell and the statistics route commit in the same pass, its effect runs first: connectPrimary → register → emit() fires before the statistics listener exists. The emit is lost; the page rendered with 0 connections and never re-renders.

Reproduced in a clean context: direct navigation to /statistics shows the empty state from 592 ms and stays there for 20 s+. Only server.getConfig is sent; getUsageSummary never is. The sidebar on the same page is connected. In-app navigation works because the connection already exists by then.

Proposal

1. Replace the useState/useMemo/useEffect pattern with useSyncExternalStore(subscribeEnvironmentConnections, getSnapshot). Have the supervisor expose a version counter or a cached immutable array snapshot so getSnapshot is stable.

2. Show a 'connecting' state, not the empty state, while the primary connection is pending.

3. Audit the other hand-rolled subscribers listed by grep (useAutomationCentre, useWorktreeNotes, AiFocusSettings, scheduleProposalHistory); they bind on subscribe + bind() and look safe, but should use the same primitive.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Verified the race in code:

  • useConnectedEnvironments (useUsageSummary.ts:22-29) reads listEnvironmentConnections() in render and subscribes only in a later useEffect.
  • supervisor.start() (supervision.ts:858-875) synchronously calls connectPrimary() (609-621) → register() (537-549) → emit() (274-277).
  • EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap (RootAppShell.tsx:80, effect at 182-193) is an earlier sibling of {appShell}/Outlet (line 99). When RootAppShell and the statistics page commit in the same pass, its passive effect runs first and the emit is lost.
  • With 0 connections, the effect at 76-116 resolves Promise.all([]) and sets loading=false, giving a permanent empty state.
  • emit only fires on register/remove, so nothing re-renders the page later.

The reproduction screenshot exists (.perf-research/browser-measure/statistics-direct-load.png). Fixing the Suspense throttle would not reliably fix this; it only changes commit timing.

Note for the fix: supervisor.list() returns a fresh array on every call (supervision.ts:914), so useSyncExternalStore needs a cached snapshot or version counter, as the investigator says.

Category: Process spawnsRisk: lowInvestigator confidence: highbrowser-measure:project-icon-node-spawn

Part of Priority 10: Sidebar and projects: stop running the full VCS pipeline per row

Expected gain

-2N node spawns per load (N = projects; 6 for 3 projects, about 40 for 20); about -130-180 ms per icon; lower server CPU and RSS spikes at boot

What happens today

readProjectFavicon runs execFile(process.execPath, ['--eval', WORKER_SCRIPT, '--', cwd]) for every lookup. The resolver has a 2-permit semaphore and no result cache.

ProjectFavicon renders the /api/project-favicon <img> while the server config is still unknown (rpcSupported false before the WS connects). After the connection it switches to projects.readIcon, which resolves the same favicon again.

With 3 tiny scratch projects, one cold load did 3 HTTP favicons (127/170/182 ms) plus 3 readIcon RPCs (56-134 ms): 6 node processes per page load. The cost scales linearly with project count, and the 2-permit semaphore queues them. The client LRU only lasts 5 min per connection.

Proposal

1. Server: add a resolver-level LRU keyed by realpath(cwd) plus the mtimes of the candidate icon files (or a 10-min TTL), shared by the HTTP route and the RPC, with single-flight.

2. Replace spawn-per-lookup with one long-lived worker_thread or child that serves lookups over a message channel, if isolation is needed.

3. Client: until config and connection are known, render the monogram placeholder instead of starting the HTTP fallback, so an icon is fetched once per project.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed:

  • readProjectFavicon.ts:41-57 runs execFile(process.execPath, ['--eval', WORKER_SCRIPT, '--', cwd]) per lookup.
  • ProjectFaviconResolver.ts:10-19 has a Semaphore(2), a 5 s timeout and no result cache.
  • The HTTP route (http.ts:629-661) and readProjectIcon (readProjectIcon.ts:21-36) both go through it.
  • ProjectFavicon.tsx:33-38 and 68-93 use the HTTP URL while config/connection are unknown, then switch to the RPC.

Corrections:

  • The child process is deliberate (projectFaviconWorker.ts:1-6: cloud-backed files can block in the kernel; the parent must be able to kill a stalled read). Proposal #2 must keep kill-ability, e.g. a long-lived child with per-request timeout and respawn, not a worker_thread.
  • The HTTP favicon is served with Cache-Control 'private, max-age=3600' (http.ts:41, 197-205). On normal warm reloads the <img> usually comes from the browser cache. The '6 spawns per load' figure applies to cold or cache-disabled loads.
  • Warm reloads still pay N RPC spawns: the client LRU (projectIconSource.ts:5-46) is memory-only and keyed per connection generation, so it resets on every reload and reconnect.

The server-side LRU + single-flight is the high-value, low-risk part.

Prior work

The prior docs cover static favicon.svg size only; per-request process spawn and double resolution are new.

Part of Priority 9: Statistics: memoize, aggregate incrementally, never block the server

Expected gain

-0.2-0.3 s on the first statistics open each day on a fast link (measured download), several seconds on slow links. Removes up to 10 s of added latency per open while offline or firewalled with stale rates.

What happens today

readSummaryUnlocked calls yield* ensureRates() (line 455) before any scanning, inside scanSemaphore.withPermits(1) (166, 806-808).

ensureRates (243-283) works like this:

  • After loadRatesFromDisk, if ratesFetchedAtMs is null or older than RATES_TTL_MS (24 h), it synchronously awaits httpClient.get(LITELLM_USAGE_RATES_URL) with a 10 s timeout.
  • It then parses the document and rewrites pricing-cache.json.
  • Measured: the document is 2,750,280 bytes, and curl takes 0.20-0.26 s on a fast link. That is added to the first statistics open of every day, before any transcript work.
  • On failure (document === null) ratesFetchedAtMs is not advanced. Every later statistics open re-attempts the fetch.
  • With a stale on-disk cache (>24 h, e.g. a laptop that was offline), each open waits for the failed attempt. Behind a packet-dropping firewall or captive portal that is up to 10 s. Because it holds the single scan permit, concurrent summary requests (range changes, multiple tabs) queue behind it.
Proposal

1. Make pricing stale-while-revalidate: price with the in-memory or disk rates immediately, and fork a background refresh (Effect.forkScoped, single-flight) when older than the TTL. Only block when no rates exist at all, and then with a short timeout (about 2 s).

2. Record lastAttemptAtMs and back off failed fetches (e.g. 1 h, exponential), so an offline node does not retry on every open.

3. Move the fetch outside scanSemaphore.

4. Bump a rates revision so a memoized summary (see statistics-usage-summary-latency) is re-priced when fresh rates arrive.

5. Optionally warm the rates once, shortly after server start, at idle.

This finding was added by the adversarial verifier while checking the investigator's report. It has not been verified a second time.

Part of Priority 13: Serve compressed assets and flatten chunk waterfalls (remote clients)

Expected gain

About -4.2 MB per cold load (-70%); on 1.6 Mbps about -21 s of transfer; about -1 RTT + CSS transfer time (3.2 s throttled) by removing the CSS→main.js serialization; negligible on loopback/desktop

What happens today

staticFileResponse streams HttpServerResponse.file with no Content-Encoding: curl with Accept-Encoding gzip,br got content-length 317,285 for main-*.js. A cold load moves 6,075 KiB of assets; gzip would be 1,852 KiB (-70%), brotli 1,684 KiB. On 150 ms / 1.6 Mbps that is 31.1 s vs 9.5 s of pure transfer, and the measured composer time was 38.7 s.

The built index-*.js loader wraps import('./main-*.js') in __vitePreload with deps ['assets/main-*.css']. It appends <link rel=stylesheet> and waits for its load event before issuing the main.js request. Throttled: CSS 413-3,581 ms, main.js requested at 3,623 ms (fully serialized). Locally the same chain shows as CSS 24-27 → main.js 32 ms.

The extra index-*.js (2.5 KB) costs one more round trip after the HTML. Remote access (LAN, Tailscale, phones via pairing, saved environments) is where users feel this.

Proposal

1. Precompress at build time: emit .br and .gz next to each hashed asset (vite-plugin-compression or a small post-build step in the server bundle stage). In staticFileResponse, negotiate Accept-Encoding: serve the precompressed file with Content-Encoding and Vary: Accept-Encoding, keep the existing ETag/immutable logic, and fall back to identity.

2. Emit <link rel=modulepreload href=/assets/main-*.js> plus <link rel=stylesheet href=main-*.css media=print onload="this.media='all'"> (or an equivalent early preload) into index.html. CSS and main.js then download in parallel; this also keeps the boot splash non-blocked.

3. Inline the 2.5 KB entry loader into index.html.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code claims hold:

  • staticFileResponse (http.ts:211-244) streams HttpServerResponse.file with Cache-Control/ETag only. Grep finds no Accept-Encoding/Content-Encoding/zlib anywhere in apps/server/src, and dist has no .br/.gz files.
  • Built dist/assets/index-Ca8qsKFg.js (2,189 B) has __vite__mapDeps=['assets/main-BKvXLkrW.css']. The preload helper appends the stylesheet link and awaits its load event before running import('./main-C8t65ccR.js'). That confirms the CSS→main.js serialization. Sizes: CSS 601,335 B, main.js 317,285 B.

Corrections:

  • The source loader is index.html:128-131 (not 125-130).
  • Desktop loads the UI from the loopback backend (apps/desktop/src/main.ts:1459 loadURL(backendHttpUrl)), so desktop and local web users gain ~0. Only LAN/Tailscale/pairing/saved-environment remote clients benefit.
  • On a bandwidth-bound link, parallelizing CSS and main.js does not save the 3.2 s CSS transfer, because both still share the 1.6 Mbps pipe. The realistic gain from removing the serialization is ~1-2 RTT. Compression is the real win (-70% bytes, ~-21 s on 1.6 Mbps for a cold load).

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

About -113-240 KB of JSON (and its main-thread decode) per load; about -2.3 s to shell snapshot on 1.6 Mbps; -1 RTT + 113 KB on statistics/new-thread/projects opens (about -1 s each on 1.6 Mbps, -30-40 ms locally)

What happens today

Boot: startServerStateSync subscribes to config and, because getServerConfig() is still null, also calls client.getConfig() in parallel. Both answer with the full config (113-130 KB; providers 119 KB of it), i.e. 2 copies at 447 and 460 ms. Each subscription also forks providerRegistry.revalidateStale (providerRpc.ts:696), which then pushes 1-2 more full 'providerStatuses' lists of about 119 KB. Across loads I saw 2-4 config chunks plus 1 getConfig in the first 1.2 s; 371 KB of config JSON in a 60 s idle window.

Throttled (1.6 Mbps): the 4 KB shell snapshot, requested at 25,328 ms, arrived at 28,371 ms behind the 113 KB config chunk (27,002) and the 113 KB getConfig Exit (28,330): about 2.3 s of head-of-line blocking.

Page-level re-fetches:

  • getUsageSummary does a sequential getConfig (113 KB) just to read usageContractVersion: +32 ms locally, +1.03 s throttled (3,155→4,185).
  • useHandleNewThread does getConfig then getProjectPreferences sequentially before navigating: 0→77 ms locally.
  • useAutomationCentre (Projects page) refetches it for config.providers: 1,817→2,910 ms throttled.
Proposal

1. serverState.ts: drop the parallel getConfig, or only issue it if the subscription has not delivered a snapshot within ~1-2 s. The stream's first element is defined to be a snapshot.

2. Replace page-level getConfig calls with the live serverConfigAtom (getServerConfig()) for the primary environment, and a per-connection cached config for saved/hosted ones. getUsageSummary already re-validates summary.contractVersion in useUsageSummary.ts:84, so its pre-flight can go.

3. Server: make providerStatuses carry only changed provider instances (or a hash + delta), and split the static model catalogs (about 100 KB) into a versioned resource fetched lazily by pickers.

4. Run revalidateStale once per TTL, not once per subscription.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed:

  • serverState.ts:155-186: subscribeConfig plus a parallel client.getConfig() whenever getServerConfig() is null, i.e. two full configs on every boot.
  • wsRpcClient.ts:804-806: getUsageSummary does a sequential getConfig preflight just for usageContractVersion.
  • useHandleNewThread.ts:146-151: getConfig, then readEffectiveProjectPreferences, in sequence. The comment at 143-145 says this is intentional, because a hosted node's descriptor and primary cache can be stale. A replacement must be a per-connection cache, not the primary serverConfigAtom.
  • useAutomationCentre.ts:116-121: getConfig only for config.providers.
  • providerRpc.ts:665-713: each subscription emits the full snapshot, and providerStatuses carries the full provider list.

Proposal #4 is already done:

  • providerRegistry.revalidateStale → source.revalidate → revalidateSnapshot (makeManagedServerProvider.ts:244-257) is gated by isProviderSnapshotFresh with DEFAULT_SNAPSHOT_FRESHNESS = 5 min (line 27).
  • upsertProviders only publishes when haveProvidersChanged (ProviderRegistry.ts:391-398).
  • So per-subscription revalidation is a cheap no-op within 5 min. The extra providerStatuses pushes seen at boot come from the initial provider refresh, not from the subscription itself. On reloads after more than 5 min they do re-probe the provider CLIs.

Impact: large on slow links (head-of-line blocking measured at ~2.3 s), ~30-40 ms locally.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

-1 WebSocket, -1 ws-token HTTP, -2 RPCs, about -400 ms of server-side simctl process work per page load; fewer reconnect paths to supervise

What happens today

createEnvironmentConnection always calls bindDeviceConnection when client.device exists. That subscribes device.subscribeEvents and immediately calls refreshInventory() → device.read{type:'list', includeShutdown:true}.

The device client uses its own DeviceWsTransport on /ws/device. That means a second /api/auth/ws-token fetch, a second handshake (41-45 ms locally), and its own 8 s ping loop for the life of the page.

Server side, listDevices runs xcrun simctl list devices --json (plus the devicetype catalogue) with no cache: device.read took 400-470 ms per load and returned 10 KB. This happens for every user on every reload, on top of other boot work.

Proposal

1. Bind the device connection lazily on first use: SimulatorPanel mount, an open-device request, or an agent device event. Multiplex device control RPCs over the main /ws and keep a dedicated socket only for the frame stream (/ws/device-frames).

2. Server: cache the inventory with a short TTL, invalidated by the existing simctl/lifecycle event stream, and push changes over device.subscribeEvents instead of re-listing per connection.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Confirmed eager wiring:

  • connection.ts:281-283 binds the device connection unconditionally.
  • device/runtime.ts:54-75 subscribes events and immediately runs refreshInventory → list({includeShutdown:true}).
  • The non-hosted client builds a separate DeviceWsTransport on '/ws/device' with its own issuePrimaryWebSocketToken (service.ts:906-912, 923-926).
  • Hosted mode already shares the main transport (service.ts:902, manageTransport:false), which is a precedent for multiplexing.

The server cost is understated. DeviceManager.list (DeviceManager.ts:338-345) first calls backend.availability() (IosSimulatorBackend.ts:349-390), which runs:

  • xcode-select -p
  • xcodebuild -version (license check; toolchainEnv spawns another xcode-select)
  • listDevicesUnchecked (xcode-select via simctl()/toolchainEnv at ~1000, then xcrun simctl list devices --json)

Then discover() → listDevices → listDevicesUnchecked runs again (another xcode-select plus simctl list). That is about 7 child processes per device.list, mostly sequential, which fits the 400-470 ms measured.

Correction: the devicetype catalogue is memoized (this.deviceTypes ??=), so it is not re-read per call. Non-darwin returns early. The work runs on a separate socket, so it does not block the shell snapshot directly. It is boot-time CPU/process churn plus an extra socket, token and ping loop.

The proposal is also worth extending: drop the duplicate simctl call between availability() and discover(), and cache xcodeSelectPath / license state.

Part of Priority 13: Serve compressed assets and flatten chunk waterfalls (remote clients)

Expected gain

Locally about -20-60 ms per route; at 150 ms RTT about -300-600 ms per first open (statistics about -2 s throttled), and the thread route about 300 ms locally / about 13 s throttled earlier, because the 1.14 MB chunk overlaps the WS handshake

What happens today

With modulePreload:false a dynamic import() fetches only the entry chunk; its static deps are discovered level by level.

Measured import depth (start times, ms):

  • Boot graph: 32 → 40 → 49 → 59/73 → 76/79 (4 levels).
  • RootAppShell: 113 → 119 → 128 → 150 (3 levels).
  • Thread route: 514 → 517 → 532 → 542 (3 levels).
  • Settings prefetch: 436 → 447 → 485 → 492 → 516 (4 levels).
  • Statistics: StatisticsPage → useStatistics (367 KB) → 7 d3 chunks. Throttled: 112-551, then 554-2,597, then 2,614-3,086.
  • Projects throttled: 111-1,339, then 1,345-1,722.

The thread route chunk (31 KB) and ChatRightPanel (1.14 MB) are requested only after the WS snapshot arrives and NoActiveThreadState redirects (514 ms locally, 28.6 s throttled). The network sits idle between ~152 and ~405 ms. The last thread id is knowable from the URL or local storage much earlier.

Proposal

1. Enable build.modulePreload with a resolveDependencies filter: keep boot preloading for main's closure and let each dynamic import preload its own static closure (Vite then passes deps to __vitePreload), which flattens each lazy graph to one level.

2. In root beforeLoad, when the path is '/' or a thread URL, start import() of ChatThreadRouteView (and ChatRightPanel) in parallel with the auth fetch, keyed on the last-visited thread already stored client-side.

3. Statically co-locate useStatistics with StatisticsPage (or preload both together) so the 367 KB chunk is not one level deeper.

4. Keep webBundleSplitting.test.ts guarding boot size, and add a max-import-depth assertion per route.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

modulePreload:false is confirmed (vite.config.ts:187). The built loader lists only CSS deps, so each lazy graph's static closure is discovered level by level.

This is a documented residual (docs/research/performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md:97, 252, 268: 'retest modulePreload'). The new value here is the measured depths.

StatisticsPage statically imports UsageView/ActivityView (StatisticsPage.tsx:15-17). The separate 367 KB useStatistics chunk is a rolldown shared-chunk artifact, so enabling modulePreload deps fixes its depth without code moves.

The late thread-route start is confirmed: the redirect comes from EventRouter.handleWelcome (RootAppShell.tsx:210-260), which awaits ensureEnvironmentConnectionBootstrapped. _chat.index.tsx:41 renders NoActiveThreadState.

The impact is inflated:

  • The 152-405 ms local network idle gap is the Suspense throttle (finding 1), not chunk depth.
  • On the throttled link the pipe is busy (settings prefetch, configs), so starting the 1.14 MB chunk earlier mostly reorders bytes. '~13 s earlier' is not credible; the gain is bounded by link idle time.
  • Realistic: ~1-3 RTT per first route open remotely (~300-450 ms at 150 ms RTT), and tens of ms locally.
Prior work

docs/research/performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md item 8 says 'modulePreload is disabled and should be retested'. This adds measured depths and timings. ChatRightPanel splitting is Aug residual #1 (not re-proposed); the prefetch-at-boot idea is new.

Part of Priority 1: Remove the 300 ms React Suspense reveal delay from every navigation

Expected gain

About -200 KB of boot-time downloads; about -1 s of contention on 1.6 Mbps; no change locally

What happens today

requestIdleCallback(preloadSettingsPage, {timeout: 4000}) fires during the Suspense-throttle idle gap (about 436 ms) on every boot. It pulls SettingsPage, SettingsPanels (91 KB), lifecycleSuggestionPolicy, TraitsPicker and others: 4 import levels, about 200 KB raw.

Throttled, it downloaded from 25,065-27,994 ms, exactly while the WS snapshot and the thread route chunk were waiting on the same 1.6 Mbps link.

With the chunks already prefetched, the settings first open still took 336 ms, because lazy() suspends and the 300 ms reveal delay applies, so the prefetch saves 0 ms today.

Proposal

Prefetch on intent instead: pointerenter/focus of the Settings button via router.preloadRoute, which avoids the Suspense fallback once routes use route-level splitting. Or defer the idle prefetch until after primary-shell-usable plus the first thread render. Skip it when navigator.connection.saveData is set or effectiveType is not '4g'.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed: the requestIdleCallback(preloadSettingsPage, {timeout:4000}) runs on every non-phone boot (SettingsRouteBridge.tsx:33-43; settingsRoute.ts:13-15).

On loopback it buys nothing measurable, because React.lazy still suspends and the 300 ms throttle applies (finding 1).

It is not pure waste on slow links: it moves the ~200 KB download from first open to boot. It is a contention trade-off, not 0 benefit. Once routes use router.preloadRoute and route-level splitting, the intent-based prefetch proposal is the right shape.

Expected gain

About -110 ms main thread at 4x CPU (about -28 ms at 1x) during first thread render; fewer forced layouts at steady state

What happens today

Profiled during cold boot at 4x CPU:

  • getAnimations 83 ms self time in useFlipLayout recordResting/t1 (commitHookEffectListMount).
  • getClientRects 31 ms in useInboxListMotion's per-commit useLayoutEffect.

Both run after every commit of their host. useFlipLayout reads getAnimations() and getBoundingClientRect() for every [data-flip-id] item even when the trigger did not change. useInboxListMotion reads every row's offset per commit.

Related: ContextWindowMeter re-renders the composer footer every 1 s via useRelativeTimeTick(1000), so per-commit layout effects in that subtree recur continuously.

Proposal

1. In useFlipLayout, record resting rects only from the ResizeObserver callback and when the trigger changes. Skip getAnimations unless an animation was started by this hook (track it in a WeakSet).

2. In useInboxListMotion, read layout only when orderSignature changed.

3. Make ContextWindowMeter tick only when a relative label actually changes (minute granularity), or move the tick into a leaf that renders only the text.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed:

  • Additional detail: its useEffect (73-82) also has no deps, so it disconnects and recreates a ResizeObserver on every commit. The new observer's initial callback triggers recordResting again.

  • The ContextWindowMeter link is wrong. useRelativeTimeTick's state is local to ContextWindowMeter (settingsLayout.tsx:35-50), so the 1 s tick re-renders only that leaf, not the NewThreadWorkLocation or inbox subtrees.
  • useInboxListMotion's per-commit read is deliberate (comment at 120-121) and limited to inbox commits.
  • On first render, getAnimations self-time includes a style recalc that would happen before paint anyway, so the -110 ms at 4x is inflated. The real saving is on repeated commits.

Both go through retainAgentControlProposalSync (useAutomationProposalSync.ts:88-112) into bindEnvironmentProposalSync (40-68).

The failure is non-retryable, so it is exactly one failing stream RPC per load plus a console.warn (wsTransport.ts:270-283), not a loop.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

WS and shell snapshot about -150-300 ms earlier on loopback (more with the throttle still present); thread messages about 1 RTT + render earlier on open

What happens today

startEnvironmentConnectionService runs in a useEffect of EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap, so /api/auth/ws-token is only requested once RootAppShell has downloaded and committed: 405 ms cold / 365 ms warm, vs root-before-load-ready at 47-113 ms. Throttled: 24,970 ms vs 15,204 ms.

retainThreadDetailSubscription (→ orchestration.subscribeThreadWindow) runs in a ChatView effect: request sent at 875 ms, after the composer is already visible at 869 ms. For a thread with history, messages arrive one RTT plus decode after the view mounts.

The auth state needed for both is known when beforeLoad resolves; the thread id is in the URL.

Proposal

1. Kick off ensurePrimaryEnvironmentReady → token issue → connectPrimary (and subscribeShell) from the root beforeLoad, in parallel with the RootAppShell import. Keep RootAppShell's effect as the idempotent owner (connectPrimary already returns an existing connection).

2. Add a loader/beforeLoad on /_chat/$environmentId/$threadId that calls retainThreadDetailSubscription (released on route leave, or with a short TTL). Call the same retain on sidebar row pointerdown, extending useSidebarThreadPrewarm.

Connection and state sync 19 findings · 2 high · 10 medium · 7 low

The connection starts only after the 533 KiB-gzip shell chunk has mounted, ServerConfig is sent twice, every stream event costs a Chunk+Ack round trip, and every connect opens a device socket that spawns simctl.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

Cold boot (local web/desktop, primary environment): main boot graph → root beforeLoad (GET session + primary descriptor in parallel) → the lazy RootAppShell graph (59 files / 533 KiB gzip) downloads, evaluates and commits. Only then does EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap call startEnvironmentConnectionService (RootAppShell.tsx:182-190). The connection code itself (service.ts, supervision.ts, store.ts, serverState.ts) is already in the boot-graph runtime-*.js chunk. The client then POSTs /api/auth/ws-token twice, once for /ws and once for /ws/device, and opens two WebSockets. Over /ws it pipelines subscribeShell, subscribeTerminalEvents, subscribeServerLifecycle, subscribeServerConfig, a duplicate serverGetConfig, subscribeProposals, threadPriority.ensureCurrent, vcs status and thread-window subscriptions. Over /ws/device it sends device.subscribeEvents and device.list. Transport-level requests are pipelined, not awaited one after another. The sequential waterfall is elsewhere: RootAppShell chunk → ws-token RTT → WS upgrade RTT → server snapshot → client decode. Saved environments add GET session → POST ws-token → WS → a 150 ms race followed by a fallback getConfig → register, and only after that can thread subscriptions attach.

Server side, each WS connection builds its own handler context, and some layers (SourceControlDiscovery, ProviderMaintenanceRunner, ContextHandoffInspection) are rebuilt per connection. subscribeShell forks reconcileAllWorktrees, which on first run loads the full shell snapshot 1+2P times and runs git per project. It then builds the shell snapshot: synchronous node:sqlite reads (7.7 ms on the user's real DB, 63% of thread rows read and then discarded), git repo-identity probes (2 per project, 1-min TTL), a redundant Schema re-decode, Schema encode and JSON. The whole snapshot goes out as ONE JSON message: about 1.6 KiB per thread, 3.2 MiB at 2,000 threads, no permessage-deflate, and a hard 4 MiB limit on the hosted relay. The client JSON.parses it and Schema-decodes it on the main thread (15 ms at 2k threads on desktop V8). device.list spawns roughly 4–10 child processes per connect.

Steady state and reconnect cost more than they should, for two reasons. First, every orchestration stream sends one RPC Chunk per event and waits for a client Ack round trip, because Stream.tap/mapEffect de-chunk the stream. Second, every thread event (about 52k/day measured, 94% activity-appended; assistant deltas every 32 ms) becomes a full thread-upserted: 3 synchronous SQL reads per subscriber, about 1.6 KiB on the wire, and an O(N) client store update. Together these make replay/resume take one RTT per event, can overflow live queues on remote or hosted links, and burn CPU on both ends. Thread-priority rankings re-send the whole shell snapshot to every subscriber.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

Replay of N events goes from N RTTs to ~1–2 RTTs (a 1,000-event resume at 50 ms RTT: ~50 s → <0.2 s); about half as many WS frames during streaming; removes the overflow → forced-resync loop on remote/hosted links

What happens today

effect/rpc over WebSocket has supportsAck=true. RpcServer runs Stream.runForEachArray and, for each array, writes one Chunk and then waits on latch.await until the client Ack arrives. Arrays are the unit of batching, but per-element Stream.mapEffect and Stream.tap emit single-element arrays. Measured with stream-chunking.mjs: 1,000 events produce 1,000 writes through mapEffect, fromQueue→tap→tap (the live feed at :550-551) and the replay tap (:548/:640), versus 1 write through filter/map. The handlers add a further per-item Stream.tap for perf payloads. Results: (a) a resumed subscription replays up to ORCHESTRATION_REPLAY_PAGE_MAX_LIMIT=1000 events as 1,000 sequential Chunk+Ack RTTs; (b) live bursts on a remote or hosted link (RTT 50–150 ms → 7–20 events/s per stream) fall behind 31 assistant deltas/s plus tool activity, so the bounded live queue (1,000 events / 4 MiB) fills and the stream fails with 'reconnect to resynchronize', forcing a full re-snapshot; (c) even on loopback every event costs 2 WS frames, a client fiber decode and an Ack.

Proposal

Make the shell and thread pipelines chunk-preserving. Replace Stream.mapEffect(toShellStreamEvent) with Stream.mapArrayEffect that maps a whole batch. Fold the replay/dequeue metric and byte-ledger taps into one batch-level effect (mapArrayEffect returning the same array). Apply the same change to the recordServerPerfPayload taps in orchestrationRpc.ts. Keep a per-chunk byte cap (e.g. split arrays at ~256 KiB) so batches stay well under the 4 MiB relay message cap. On the client, consume arrays with Stream.runForEachArray in wsTransport.subscribe and hand the store one batch per commit. Add a regression test asserting that N queued events produce ≤ ceil(bytes/cap) Chunk writes.

Verifier (Confirmed)

I re-ran .perf-research/client-runtime-sync/stream-chunking.mjs against effect 4.0.2. Pipelines using mapEffect or fromQueue→tap→tap produce 1,000 writes per 1,000 events; filter→map produces 1. The mechanism holds. RpcServer.ts:446-457 waits on latch.await after each array. RpcClient.ts:591-614 sends the Ack only after Queue.offerAll. supportsAck is true for both the WS protocol (RpcServer.ts:1627, used by toHttpEffectWebsocket in ws.ts:76/109) and the relay (RpcByteSession.ts:328). The cited lines are correct: orchestrationStreams.ts:427, :548, :550-551, :640, :642-643 and orchestrationRpc.ts:512-516, 580-584, 615-619. Stream.mapArrayEffect exists in effect 4.0.2 (Stream.ts:2319), so the fix is feasible.

The rate claim needs tempering. On the user's real DB (last 24 h): peak minute 864 events (14.4/s), peak second 48. 54% of activity events are task.progress, which the live path coalesces before enqueue. Only 440 streaming assistant deltas were recorded, so 31 deltas/s is a per-message ceiling, not observed load. Overflow is therefore plausible only under sustained peaks on 100-150 ms links. Lag on those links is certain.

Resume replay at one RTT per event applies only to direct connections (saved environments, or a LAN/remote-served primary). Hosted connections never resume. On loopback the cost is CPU and frames only.

Prior work

Aug hardening added bounded live queues, coalescing and replay metrics (docs/research/2026-08-12-performance-hardening-results.md residual #7). The per-event chunk/Ack interaction is new and not covered there.
