Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

Removes one codex app-server spawn plus a full-history thread/read per opened, prewarmed or retained Codex thread per 30 s. Also removes 100-400 ms of event-loop blocking (estimate: 105 ms measured SQL+parse plus Schema decode) per large-thread poll from the serial ingestion worker that also carries live deltas.

What happens today

Polling: withHistoryRecovery wraps both subscribeThread and subscribeThreadWindow. For the stream's lifetime it forks Effect.forever(reconcile(threadId) then sleep 30 s). Reads are deduped per thread through the historyReads set, a 30 s historyLastRead cache and Semaphore(2).

Per read: for any thread with a session and a stored binding that has a resumeCursor, providerService.readThreadHistory runs. For Codex threads without a live runtime, readStoredCodexThread spawns a fresh codex app-server process, sends initialize, and calls thread/read with includeTurns:true, i.e. the whole history. The result goes onto the serial ProviderRuntimeIngestion worker, the same queue that ingests live runtime events and assistant-delta flushes. There, processHistory first calls resolveThreadDetail → getThreadDetailById, which loads ALL messages and ALL activities with no limit. Only after that does it check the cheap preconditions (updatedAt and session id), and it returns early when nothing changed.

Real DB (read-only): 178 live Codex threads and 491 Codex bindings with resume cursors. The largest live Codex thread has 2,693 activities and 50 MB of payload_json. Loading its activities took 49 ms of synchronous SQL plus 56 ms of JSON.parse (measured), before Effect Schema decode.

Triggers: opening a thread, 3 prewarmed sidebar rows (SIDEBAR_THREAD_PREWARM_LIMIT), and up to 32 retained idle subscriptions kept for 5 min. Each repeats the cycle every 30 s.

Proposal

(1) In processHistory, check the preconditions with getThreadShellById plus the binding before loading anything. Replace getThreadDetailById with bounded queries: messages and activities by the ids the history mentions, and the turns of completed history turns only. (2) Make recovery event-driven rather than polling per subscription. Run it once per thread per runtime-session generation, and only when a gap is possible: the session is running or connecting without a live runtime, or the latest turn is unsettled. Back off exponentially when a read restores nothing. (3) Never trigger it from prewarm or retained idle subscriptions; only an actively viewed thread qualifies. (4) Reuse one pooled read-only codex app-server with an idle timeout instead of spawning one per read.

This finding was added by the adversarial verifier while checking the investigator's report. It has not been verified a second time.

Prior work

None in the perf docs. The feature was added in commit 0e3c78cb4 ('Recover missed Codex history and retire failed runtimes').

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

Overlaps network and server snapshot time with RootAppShell download/eval; estimated 50–200 ms off time-to-sidebar on desktop, more on slow web or remote links, and one extra RTT saved through the ws-token prefetch

What happens today

startEnvironmentConnectionService() and startServerStateSync() run in useEffect hooks inside RootAppShell, which __root renders through Suspense/lazy after beforeLoad resolves. The connection code is not in that lazy graph: the sourcemaps show apps/web/src/environments/runtime/service.ts, connection/supervision.ts, rpc/serverState.ts and state/threads/store.ts all live in the boot-graph runtime-*.js chunk. So the ws-token POST, WS upgrade, server snapshot build and wire transfer wait behind 59 files / 1,681 KiB raw of JS that have nothing to do with them. ServerStateBootstrap's effect also needs an extra commit, because it reads the connection through useSyncExternalStore after the sibling effect registers it.

Proposal

Kick off the primary connection as soon as auth is known. In resolveRootBeforeLoadContextAsync, after authGateState is 'authenticated', call startEnvironmentConnectionService() and startServerStateSync(getPrimaryEnvironmentConnection().client.server) without awaiting, from a module-level singleton that the React bootstraps adopt (both are ref-counted or idempotent today). Also start the POST /api/auth/ws-token in parallel with resolveInitialServerAuthGateState and hand the token to the first socket attempt. A ws token from a still-valid cookie session saves one RTT; a 401 is harmless.

Verifier (Confirmed)

I checked the sourcemaps. environments/runtime/service.ts, connection/supervision.ts, rpc/serverState.ts and state/threads/store.ts are all in runtime-Ccb5EWxk.js (boot graph) and none are in RootAppShell-KkbzvhlV.js. The connection starts only in EnvironmentConnectionManagerBootstrap's effect (RootAppShell.tsx:182-193). RootAppShell itself is lazy (__root.tsx:29-30, 241-246). getServerConfig is not needed earlier. issuePrimaryWebSocketToken has no prefetch (primaryAuth.ts:139-150).

Measured in browser-measure/measurements-summary.json, cold loopback load: boot shell gone at ~90 ms, sidebar ~400 ms, wsOpen ~425 ms, shellUsable 426-499 ms. web-bootstrap shows /ws opening at 302 ms, right after the shell mounts. Locally this saves about 25-90 ms of shellUsable; much of the remaining gap is the separately measured React Suspense throttle. On the throttled profile (4x CPU, 150 ms RTT) wsOpen trails boot-shell-gone by about 10 s, so the gain is large on slow links.

The early start must be restricted to non-hosted mode, because AGENTS.md assigns a single owner to hosted lifecycle recovery.

Prior work

Aug hardening moved the main graph behind the boot shell and lazy-loaded RootAppShell. Starting the connection before that chunk is new.

Part of Priority 5: Cut database work at boot (it scales with DB size)

Expected gain

Removes ~2P full shell snapshot loads at first connect (58 for this user, est. ~0.45–0.9 s of server CPU, mostly synchronous) and the contention with the first client's snapshot

What happens today

subscribeShell runs reconcileAllWorktrees.pipe(Effect.forkDetach), with a process-wide 5-min throttle, on the first subscription after boot. That is exactly when the first client's own snapshot is being built. reconcileAllWorktrees loads getShellSnapshot once. Then for every available project, with concurrency 4, ensureProjectMainWorktree loads the full shell snapshot again (:259) and reconcileProjectWorktrees loads it once more (:862). It also runs git worktree list and, for projects without a main worktree, git status. All SQL runs on one synchronous node:sqlite connection that blocks the event loop. With the user's real DB (29 projects): 59 full snapshot loads × 7.7 ms measured SQL ≈ 450 ms of event-loop blocking from SQL alone, plus row decode for 753 rows and git processes on each load. Each load only needs the worktrees of a single project.

Proposal

Load the snapshot once in reconcileAllWorktrees and pass snapshot.worktrees filtered by project into ensureProjectMainWorktree and reconcileProjectWorktrees. Expected gain

−1 full config load (~100+ KiB plus ~6 ms synchronous server probe) per connect and per environment; −1 RTT and −1 config load per usage-range change per environment; −5.9 ms of event-loop blocking per config build

What happens today

startServerStateSync subscribes to subscribeServerConfig, whose first item is a full config snapshot (providerRpc.ts:701-713). It also calls getConfig whenever getServerConfig() is null, which is always the case at cold boot. Saved environments race the config subscription against a 150 ms timer and fall back to getConfig; on any link whose ws-token, upgrade and first item take more than 150 ms, the config is fetched twice. getUsageSummary calls serverGetConfig before every usage request for every environment, only to check usageContractVersion. Each loadServerConfig runs resolveAvailableEditors(): synchronous statSync/accessSync over every PATH entry × ~28 editors plus app-bundle candidates. Measured 5.85 ms median with 41 PATH entries. It also re-serializes the provider list (~100 KiB, 116 models measured).

Proposal

Drop the getConfig call in startServerStateSync, since the subscription snapshot is authoritative. Saved environments should await the subscription's first snapshot under the existing 20 s SAVED_ENVIRONMENT_INITIAL_CONFIG_TIMEOUT_MS instead of a 150 ms race. getUsageSummary should read usageContractVersion from the cached config (serverConfigAtom or savedRuntime.serverConfig) and rely on the existing decode-error mapping. Server: compute availableEditors once at startup (or with a TTL of minutes, refreshed on an explicit 'refresh editors' action) and reuse it in loadServerConfig.

Saved environments race 150 ms (service.ts:125, 1467-1474) and otherwise fall back to getConfig (service.ts:1140-1146). getUsageSummary preflights getConfig (wsRpcClient.ts:804-819). loadServerConfig calls resolveAvailableEditors synchronously (context.ts:884-918, open.ts:267-295, shell.ts:365-372).

Expected gain

Up to ~170 ms off the first snapshot (estimated, 29 projects) and −2P git processes per snapshot after cache expiry

What happens today

getShellSnapshot calls resolveRepositoryIdentitiesForProjects with timeoutMs 1000. For each workspace root, with concurrency 4, that runs git rev-parse --show-toplevel then git remote -v (11.2 ms and 11.7 ms measured), cached for only 1 minute (positive and negative). For 29 projects that is ~58 process spawns and an estimated ~170 ms on the first snapshot, and again on any snapshot more than a minute after the last one: priority re-sends, reconnects, reconciliation loads, other tabs. Git remotes almost never change.

Proposal

Cache identities for much longer (hours) and invalidate cheaply via fs.stat of <root>/.git/config (and HEAD for worktrees) mtime. Alternatively persist the identity in projection_projects when a project is created or meta-updated. Never block the snapshot on cold git: return the last known (or null) identity immediately and push a project-upserted when resolution finishes.

The 'first snapshot' framing is overstated. The server boot traces (.perf-research/server-boot/trace-*.json) show resolveRepositoryIdentityCacheKey/FromCacheKey running at boot, so the first desktop snapshot within 60 s of server start usually hits a warm cache. The cost lands on web reloads, other tabs, reconnects and reconciliation loads more than 60 s later. With 29 unique roots at concurrency 4, the ~170 ms wall time is a plausible estimate, capped at 1 s.

Part of Priority 11: Sidebar render cost at large thread counts

Expected gain

~8–30× fewer shell upserts during streaming (32 ms deltas → ≤4/s per thread); removes 3 synchronous SQL reads per event per subscriber; client saves 0.5–2.4 ms per event at 2k–5k threads (≈15–75 ms/s of main thread while one thread streams)

What happens today

For every domain event with aggregateKind 'thread', toShellStreamEvent's default branch runs getThreadShellById (3 SQL queries plus row decode through synchronous node:sqlite behind a Semaphore(1)) and emits a full thread-upserted of ~1.6 KiB. This happens once per shell subscriber, with no check that the shell changed. The projector bumps projection_threads.updated_at on every thread.message-sent, and assistant deltas flush every 32 ms, so the shell always differs during streaming. Real DB: 52,038 events in 24 h, 94.5% thread.activity-appended, each turned into a shell upsert. Client: writeThreadShellState spreads up to 4 dictionary-mode records keyed by every thread. Measured 0.52–0.77 ms per upsert at 2k threads and 1.8–2.4 ms at 5k (0.27 ms even when nothing changed).

Proposal

(1) Server: since the upsert always re-reads the row, it is safe to coalesce latest-wins per threadId. Within each drained batch (see the chunking finding), or a 250 ms window, collapse thread events to one getThreadShellById per thread. Batch-read the shells with WHERE thread_id IN (...). (2) Share the read across subscribers: memoize shell rows by (threadId, sequence) in a small LRU so N tabs/clients do one read. (3) Skip the upsert when the derived shell fields are unchanged; event types such as progress activities do not change them. Better still, stop bumping updated_at on streaming deltas and bump only on the final message. (4) Client: build per-environment indexes with structural sharing (Map/immutable map or persistent records) so an upsert is O(1), and short-circuit before ensureThreadRegistered when the thread is already registered under the same project.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code matches the claim. toShellStreamEvent's default branch (orchestrationStreams.ts:254-267) calls getThreadShellById (ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:2939-3008, three queries) per event per subscriber. The client spreads the whole record maps (store.ts:1067-1141). The projector bumps updated_at on every message-sent and activity-appended (ProjectionPipeline.ts:1105-1121, 1146-1162).

The costs are smaller than stated at this user's scale. The 3 prepared statements take 0.017 ms per call on the real DB (my measurement, decode excluded), so server SQL is not the issue. At this user's 282 live threads, the investigator's own bench shows 0.005-0.024 ms per client upsert; the 0.5-2.4 ms figures only apply to 2k-5k-thread fixtures. The live path already coalesces task.progress, context-window and streaming agent.message activities before toShellStreamEvent runs.

The proposal to skip unchanged upserts conflicts with updated_at being bumped by every activity, so updatedAt semantics would have to change first. The real value is fewer events on the wire, which pairs with the chunking finding, and large-N clients.

Prior work

Aug hardening made thread shell summaries incremental on the projector side. Shell-stream coalescing exists only for progress-grade activities before enqueue (orchestrationEventCoalescing.ts), not for shell upserts. New.

Expected gain

−1 WebSocket and −1 ws-token RTT per environment at boot; −4 to −10 child processes (~340 ms+ of process time) per connect, reconnect and environment; reconnect latency no longer includes xcodebuild (20 s timeout worst case)

What happens today

createPrimaryEnvironmentClient and createSavedEnvironmentClient always construct a DeviceWsTransport, which builds its session eagerly in the RpcTransport constructor. That costs a second ws-token POST and a second WebSocket per environment. bindDeviceConnection immediately subscribes to device events and calls refreshInventory → device.list. On the server, list() calls availability(): for iOS, with no cache, xcode-select -p, xcodebuild -version and simctl list; Android has a 5 s cache but runs adb version, emulator -version, emulator -list-avds and adb devices -l, which can start the adb daemon. discover() then lists again, running simctl list a second time. Measured here: xcode-select 6 ms, xcodebuild -version 63–80 ms, simctl list 122–196 ms per run, so ~340 ms of process wall time per list for iOS. This repeats on every reconnect and resubscribe. EnvironmentConnection.reconnect() awaits refreshInventory before refreshMetadata and bootstrap (connection.ts:322-325), so the user-visible 'Reconnect' waits for the simulator probes.

Proposal

Make the device channel lazy. Construct DeviceWsTransport and bindDeviceConnection on first use of a device surface, or when the shell or a thread reports device state. Server: cache iOS availability (xcode-select/xcodebuild results for minutes, invalidated by DEVELOPER_DIR or Xcode path mtime); reuse the simctl output from availability() in discover() (one simctl per list); keep a short TTL (2–5 s) on discovery. In connection.reconnect(), refresh inventory in parallel and do not await it (void deviceBinding?.refreshInventory()).

Verifier (Confirmed)

The code matches. createPrimaryEnvironmentClient and createSavedEnvironmentClient build a DeviceWsTransport with its own authenticatedSocketUrl, so each makes its own ws-token POST (service.ts:906-936, 1075-1089). bindDeviceConnection subscribes and calls refreshInventory immediately (runtime.ts:54-75). reconnect() awaits refreshInventory before refreshMetadata and bootstrap (connection.ts:317-329). Hosted primary shares the main transport (service.ts:901-902), so it does not open a second socket.

Per iOS list() (IosSimulatorBackend.ts:349-400, 989-1089): xcode-select runs about 4 times (availability plus toolchainEnv for xcodebuild and for each simctl), xcodebuild -version once, and simctl list twice; deviceTypeCatalogue is cached. Android has a 5 s availability cache (AndroidEmulatorBackend.ts:216-222).

Measured in web-bootstrap/browser-boot-local-nothrottle.json: /ws/device opened at 303 ms and its first message arrived at 785 ms (~480 ms for device.list), while /ws's first message arrived at 313 ms. It runs in parallel and does not block the first sidebar; it does serialize reconnect.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

Removes ~2×1,000 event reads/decodes per resumed subscription (up to ~66 pages on a reconnect with 32 thread subs); stops full window re-snapshots of idle retained threads after reconnect (each 100 KB–MBs)

What happens today

canResumeAfter fetches an anchor page and then readEventsPage(fromSequence, 1000). That reads up to 1,001 rows and Schema-decodes every payload just to learn hasMore, after which the replay stream reads the same page again. On reconnect this runs for the shell plus every retained thread subscription (up to 32). Thread subscriptions resume from a global sequence: appliedSequence only advances on that thread's events, while canResume counts all global events. A retained idle thread therefore cannot resume after a reconnect if more than 1,000 events happened anywhere since its last event. That is ~32 s of one thread streaming at 31 deltas/s, or minutes at the measured 52k/day. The client then reloads a full 150-message window snapshot for each such thread. Thread replay also scans global pages and filters, even though idx_orch_events_stream_sequence (aggregate_kind, stream_id, sequence) exists on the real DB.

Proposal

(1) Implement the resume check as an index probe with no payload decode, e.g. SELECT sequence FROM orchestration_events WHERE sequence > ? ORDER BY sequence LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1000. (2) For thread streams, decide and replay using the per-stream index: WHERE aggregate_kind='thread' AND stream_id=? AND sequence > ? LIMIT n, so resume depends on the thread's own backlog. (3) Optionally send a periodic {kind:'watermark', sequence} on thread streams so the client's resume point keeps advancing while the thread is idle.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The double read is real: canResumeAfter (orchestrationStreams.ts:494-504) calls readEventsPage(fromSequence, 1000), and the replay then reads the same page again (:362-421). But readPage reads only limit+1 rows of what exists (OrchestrationEventStore.ts:401-443), so the cost scales with the actual backlog. The '2x1,000' case only occurs when the backlog is at least 1,000, and then resume is refused anyway. On the real DB, a 1,001-row read plus JSON.parse took 3.45 ms, versus 0.02 ms for an OFFSET-1000 index probe.

The idle-thread gap is confirmed and is the important part. appliedSequence advances only on a snapshot or a matching thread event (supervision.ts:379-381, 400-401, 445-446), while canResumeAfter counts global events. With the real DB's peak of 864 events/min, an idle retained thread fails to resume after about 1-2 busy minutes and reloads a full window. Resume applies only to direct, non-hosted connections (supervision.ts:380). The idx_orch_events_stream_sequence index exists on the real DB.

Prior work

Docs propose making the 1,000-event replay cap explicit and deprecating legacy replayEvents. Resume via resumeFromSequence already exists. The double read and the global-versus-thread resume gap are new.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

−1 to −2 RTTs per saved environment connect (e.g. −100–300 ms over Tailscale/WAN), thread panes on remote environments start streaming earlier, −1 duplicate config transfer

What happens today

connectSavedEnvironment runs in sequence: read the bearer (secret store) → prepare (SSH) → GET session (readSavedEnvironmentSession) → optional rotate + GET → create the client, whose URL provider reads the bearer again and POSTs ws-token → WS upgrade → wait up to 150 ms for the config snapshot, else a getConfig RPC → only then registerConnection. Thread-detail subscriptions for that environment attach only once the connection is registered (attach → read(environmentId)). That is at least 4 sequential RTTs plus the device socket's own ws-token and socket. The supervisor also waits up to 2.5 s for the primary snapshot before starting saved connects (deliberate prioritisation).

Proposal

Add a server endpoint that validates the bearer and issues a ws-token in one response (e.g. POST /api/auth/ws-token returning session state), saving 1 RTT. Register the connection as soon as the socket opens; config and metadata can stream in later because the UI already treats serverConfig as optional. Let thread subscriptions attach immediately. Remove the 150 ms race (see the duplicate-config finding).

Verifier (Confirmed)

The chain is confirmed (service.ts:1343-1474). It reads the session (GET), runs savedSessionRenewal.renew (possibly a rotate plus GET), and creates the client. The socket URL provider then POSTs a ws-token (resolveSavedEnvironmentSocketUrl, service.ts:940-968) and the WS upgrades. Next comes waitForConfigSnapshot(150 ms) or getConfig, then registerConnection.

Thread attaches return false until register (supervision.ts:358-369, 537-549). The shell subscription is started inside createEnvironmentConnection before registration, so the shell itself is not blocked; thread panes are. waitForPrimaryShellSnapshotApplied(2,500 ms) (supervision.ts:33, 767) is deliberate. Registering before config or metadata needs care around role and credential-rejection handling, so the medium risk rating stands.

Category: ReliabilityRisk: lowInvestigator confidence: mediumclient-runtime-sync:thread-window-full-activity-payloads

Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

Fixes threads that cannot be opened over the hosted relay; at least one live thread on this user's DB is already over the cap. Cuts window snapshots for heavy threads from 3-5 MiB to ≤1 MiB (3-5x less decode and transfer). Removes the path that can ship a 50 MB legacy detail.

What happens today

Window size: the client always requests 150 messages and 150 activities (supervision.ts:421-433). listNewestThreadActivityRows selects the full payload_json of each activity. On the real DB (read-only), the last 150 activities of the top live threads hold 4.99, 3.85, 3.32, 3.03 and 3.01 MiB of payload, before messages. The hosted relay caps a reassembled RPC message at 4 MiB, and RpcByteSession fails an over-cap response with 'The response exceeded the largest message this connection can carry.'

Fallback: that error is not in isRetryableSubscriptionError, so the window subscription's onError fires requestLegacy. The entry then switches permanently to protocol 'legacy', i.e. subscribeThread. That RPC loads getThreadDetailById with every message and activity, with no limit; the largest live Codex thread is 50 MB of activity payload. Over the relay it fails again, so the thread never opens. On direct connections it ships tens of MB.

Direct connections also pay for these windows: client JSON.parse plus Schema decode, plus estimateRetainedBytes re-stringifying the whole snapshot on the main thread. The 12 MiB retained-bytes budget evicts other cached threads after 2-3 such windows.

Proposal

(1) Bound the window by bytes as well as count. In getThreadWindow, stop adding activities once ~1 MiB is reached, set hasMore, and let the existing history pagination fetch older ones. (2) Send activity payloads trimmed or previewed (e.g. a 16-32 KiB cap with a truncated flag), with a getActivityPayload RPC for full content on demand. (3) Restrict the legacy fallback to 'method not found' or unsupported-server errors, and never fall back on size or SQL errors. On too_large, retry the window with smaller limits. (4) Have the client estimate retained bytes from the frame length instead of re-stringifying.

This finding was added by the adversarial verifier while checking the investigator's report. It has not been verified a second time.

Prior work

Overlaps the residual 'Make thread detail snapshots selective or paged' (docs/research/performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md:43) and the Aug bounded 150-item windows. New here: per-activity payload size makes count-bounded windows 3-5 MiB on real data, the relay cliff for thread windows, and the sticky unbounded legacy fallback.

Part of Priority 12: Start the connection earlier and stop duplicate work on connect

Expected gain

Fixes a hard failure for hosted users above ~2.6k threads; −10 ms server CPU per snapshot @2k (re-decode); excluding archived threads cuts the payload roughly in proportion to the archived share (90% in the fixture → 3.2 MiB → ~0.33 MiB, client decode 15 ms → ~1.5 ms)

What happens today

Every non-deleted thread, archived included, goes into one stream item with full session, latestTurn, modelSelection (with options), worktree paths and lineage. The fixture measures ~1.6 KiB/thread: 3.2 MiB at 2k threads, 8 MiB at 5k. Rows are already Schema-decoded per row by SqlSchema (ProjectionThreadDbRowSchema with fromJsonString columns). The assembled snapshot is then decoded again with decodeShellSnapshot (10.2 ms @2k, measured) and Schema-encoded by RPC (10.4 ms @2k) before JSON.stringify (4.0 ms). The client spends 15 ms decoding @2k on V8, an estimated 5–10× that on Hermes. The hosted/relay path caps a message at min(4 MiB, maxQueued−maxControl). A larger snapshot makes the sink return 'too_large', RpcByteSession fails that request with 'The response exceeded the largest message this connection can carry.', and the hosted session can never accept its required fresh snapshot. At 1.6 KiB/thread that cliff is ≈2,600 threads.

Proposal

(1) Remove the redundant decodeShellSnapshot (ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:2742). Rows are already validated, and the RPC encode is a second guard; keep it in tests or debug builds only. (2) Stream the snapshot in pages: {kind:'snapshot-begin', sequence, projects, worktrees}, {kind:'snapshot-threads', threads:[≤500 or ≤256 KiB]}… {kind:'snapshot-end'}, applied atomically client-side at 'end'. This bounds message size for the relay and lets JSON/decode work interleave with frames. (3) Leave archived threads out of the boot shell. Send counts per project and page archived threads through a new RPC when the archive or settings views open. (4) Trim per-thread wire fields: session.threadId duplicates the parent; runtimeSessionId and lastError can be fetched with thread detail. (5) Optionally move JSON.parse+decode of large chunks into a Worker on web.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The mechanics are confirmed. getShellSnapshot (ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:2556-2750) decodes per row via SqlSchema, then calls decodeShellSnapshot at :2742 (defined at :98), and RPC encodes again. RELAY_MAX_RPC_MESSAGE_BYTES is 4 MiB (relay.ts:49) and is enforced at RelayChannelRegistry.ts:724-730. RpcByteSession.ts:301-321 fails an over-cap request with 'The response exceeded the largest message…'.

The scale is overstated for this user. Real data (hub-connection/shell-size.txt): 282 threads produce 363 KiB at 1,317 B/thread, so the cliff sits near 3,200 threads, about 9x headroom. Archived live threads in the real DB are 4 of 282 (1.4%), not 90%, so excluding archived threads barely helps here; deleted rows are already filtered out. The redundant decode costs about 1.4 ms at 282 threads (scaled from 10.2 ms at 2k). The decode also applies withDecodingDefault normalizations, so it should only be removed with a test proving the assembled object is already normalized.

Expected gain

~60% less SQL and row decode for this user's shell snapshot (≈4–5 ms synchronous per snapshot, multiplied by snapshots per connect, reconciliation loads and priority re-sends)

What happens today

listThreadRows has no WHERE clause; rows are filtered with deleted_at === null in JS after SqlSchema has decoded every row, including the fromJsonString columns. The latestCompletedTurnAt correlated subquery runs for every row, deleted ones included. listThreadSessionRows reads all sessions. Real DB: 753 thread rows read and decoded, 282 kept (63% discarded). The threads query takes 5.33 ms of the 7.7 ms total (synchronous), and 702 sessions are read for 282 live threads.

Proposal

Add WHERE deleted_at IS NULL to listThreadRows in the shell variant, plus a partial index ON projection_threads(created_at, thread_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. Join sessions to live threads (WHERE thread_id IN (SELECT thread_id FROM projection_threads WHERE deleted_at IS NULL)). Consider materializing latest_completed_turn_at as a projected column, updated by the projector, instead of a per-row subquery.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Confirmed: listThreadRows has no WHERE clause (ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:625-666), the correlated subquery is at :514-527, sessions are unfiltered at :941-962, and deleted threads are filtered in JS at :2698.

Measured on the real DB (node:sqlite, read-only): threads query 5.47 ms for 753 rows versus 1.52 ms with WHERE deleted_at IS NULL (282 rows); sessions 0.85 ms for 702 rows versus 0.52 ms for 280 rows. That saves about 4.3 ms of synchronous work per snapshot, plus decoding 471 rows. listThreadRows is shared with getSnapshot (:1961) and getCommandReadModel (:2285), which may need deleted rows, so the fix must be a shell-specific query. The saving compounds with the 53 reconciliation loads (≈0.2 s).

Category: CPURisk: lowInvestigator confidence: mediumclient-runtime-sync:per-event-size-accounting-and-metrics
Expected gain

Removes 2–5 JSON.stringify+encode passes per event per subscription on the server and 1 per event on the client; replay-metric overhead goes from O(S) per event to O(1)

What happens today

Server, per live event per subscription: approximateJsonBytes (JSON.stringify plus TextEncoder.encode) runs at offer, again at release on dequeue, and 1–3 more times in the coalescer for progress frames. Streaming agent-message activities carry the full text so far, so these strings grow. Every recordReplayEvent, recordLiveEnqueued and recordLiveDequeued calls publishAggregate, which reads 5 Refs for every active subscription and updates 4 gauges, so per-event cost is O(S). Client, per thread-detail event: estimateRetainedBytes allocates a new TextEncoder and JSON.stringify of the event (and of whole window snapshots); evictToCapacity maps and plans over all entries; and reconcileThreadDetailSubscriptionEvictionForEnvironment clears and re-arms a setTimeout for every retained subscription, once per event.

Proposal

Compute an event's size once: the same event object is shared by all PubSub subscribers, so a WeakMap cache works, or carry the size in the queue entry. Use a cheap estimate (e.g. sum of string lengths) instead of encoding. Release with the stored size. Publish replay gauges on a 1 s schedule (or only when values change) instead of per event. Client: use the WebSocket frame length (or server-provided size) for retained-bytes estimates, a shared TextEncoder, and run eviction reconciliation at most once per frame or batch.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Confirmed. approximateJsonBytes runs at offer (orchestrationStreams.ts:60-62), again at release (:119-122), and up to 2 more times in the coalescer (:103, :124, :130, :136). It does JSON.stringify plus TextEncoder (perf.ts:55-66). publishAggregate reads 5 Refs for each active subscription of the same kind and updates 4 gauges, on every enqueue, dequeue and replay event (wsReplayMetrics.ts:114-190).

On the client, estimateRetainedBytes allocates a new TextEncoder and stringifies every event and every whole window snapshot (supervision.ts:280-295). evictToCapacity runs per event, and reconcileForEnvironment re-arms timers for all entries (supervision.ts:483-513, service.ts:761). Each item is cheap: at most 32 entries, ~1.2 KB average events. Whole-window stringification costs more for multi-MiB windows (see additional finding). Low impact.

Part of Priority 13: Serve compressed assets and flatten chunk waterfalls (remote clients)

Expected gain

Large payloads 6–8× smaller on remote links (3.2 MiB → ~0.4 MiB, roughly 2.5 s → 0.3 s at 10 Mbit/s); small CPU cost at level 1

What happens today

NodeHttpServer.layer is called without a websocket option, and ws defaults to perMessageDeflate:false. Shell snapshot JSON deflates 8× (3,210 KiB → 397 KiB at 2k threads, measured). The provider-heavy ServerConfig (~100 KiB) and thread windows compress similarly. Over loopback compression is pure CPU cost, but over LAN or Tailscale for saved environments, and over mobile cellular, bytes dominate.

Proposal

Enable websocket: { perMessageDeflate: { threshold: 16 * 1024, zlibDeflateOptions: { level: 1 }, serverNoContextTakeover: true, clientNoContextTakeover: true } } on the NodeHttpServer layer, ideally only for non-loopback listeners or remote-exposed servers (a second WebSocketServer instance, or decide by bind host). For the hosted relay, consider compressing large RPC messages (above a threshold) before E2EE encryption, since the relay payload is opaque. That also reduces the 13 ms ChaCha cost per 3.2 MiB.

Verifier (Confirmed)

NodeHttpServer.layer is called with only host and port (server.ts:193-196). The platform-node Options.websocket field, which would allow permessage-deflate, is unused (NodeHttpServer.ts:78-90, 150). Under Bun, BunHttpServer is used instead (server.ts:180-187).

Real shell: 363 KiB → 41 KiB with deflate-raw (8.9x, hub-connection/shell-size.txt). The protocol.ts:470-473 citation is just layer composition and has nothing to do with compression. Browsers negotiate deflate natively, but the React Native iOS WebSocket may not. The gain is for remote links only; on loopback it is pure CPU.

Expected gain

Each ranking sends KBs instead of N_subscribers × full snapshot (3.2 MiB / ~35 ms server + 15 ms client decode @2k threads); removes a full sidebar re-render per ranking; fixes priority flicker and loss

What happens today

prioritySnapshotStream maps every ThreadPriorityCoordinator change to Stream.mapEffect(() => snapshot), which is a full getShellSnapshot per subscriber with no sharing (SQL, repo-identity git, re-decode, encode; 3.2 MiB at 2k threads). The client then fully re-syncs the environment, and syncEnvironmentShellSnapshot creates new objects for every thread, so the whole sidebar re-renders. Rankings can happen as often as once per minute (THREAD_PRIORITY_AUTOMATIC_MIN_INTERVAL_MS) while threads change. Correctness side issues: getThreadShellById omits priority, so any thread event erases that thread's priority on the client (store.ts:456 maps priority: thread.priority) until the next full snapshot. And snapshot updatedAt ignores priority rows, so a forced re-rank with no other events comes back with the same sequence and updatedAt, is classified 'current', and is ignored.

Proposal

Add a shell stream item such as {kind:'thread-priorities', sequence, entries:[{threadId, priority|null}]} built from the ranking batch (dozens of rows) and apply it as a patch on the client. Include the projected priority in getThreadShellById, using the same SQL join as listThreadPriorityRows filtered by thread_id, so upserts preserve it. If a full re-snapshot is ever needed, single-flight it per server and share the result across subscribers.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The mechanism is real. prioritySnapshotStream maps each change to a full snapshot (orchestrationStreams.ts:558-564), and the coordinator publishes after each ranking (ThreadPriorityCoordinator.ts:207-208). However, this path only fires when the user opts in: aiFocusEnabled defaults to false (contracts/src/settings.ts:88), rankings are LLM-bound, and automatic rankings run at most once per minute (THREAD_PRIORITY_AUTOMATIC_MIN_INTERVAL_MS=60_000).

The correctness side issues are confirmed for opted-in users. getThreadShellById (ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:2939-3008) omits priority, while getShellSnapshot adds it (:2734-2735). The client maps summary.priority = thread.priority (store.ts:456), and sidebarThreadSummariesEqual compares priority (store.ts:610), so any thread upsert erases the priority. The snapshot updatedAt ignores priority rows, so a re-rank with no intervening events is classified 'current' (projectionTracker.ts:8-29) and dropped (supervision.ts:735-742).

Expected gain

Avoids full sidebar re-renders on every re-snapshot (reconnect or priority); cuts store commits during streaming from one per event (~31+/s per thread) to ≤60/s total

What happens today

syncEnvironmentShellSnapshot rebuilds threadShellById, threadSessionById, threadTurnStateById and sidebarThreadSummaryById from scratch with new objects for every thread. Store cost is low (2–9 ms measured), but every selector over these records sees new identities, so a reconnect, resubscribe or priority re-snapshot re-renders the whole sidebar and inbox. Thread-detail events go through applyEnvironmentThreadDetailEvent → applyRecoveredEventBatch([event]) → one useStore set per event with no frame batching, unlike the shell path, which has a rate-based coalescer. Each set notifies every store subscriber.

Proposal

In syncEnvironmentShellSnapshot, reuse the previous shell, summary, session and turn objects when they are equal (the equality helpers threadShellsEqual and sidebarThreadSummariesEqual already exist). Route thread-detail events through a per-frame batcher, like createShellEventCoalescer, and apply arrays in one commit, which pairs with the server chunking fix. (Note: createOrchestrationRecoveryCoordinator in state/orchestration/orchestrationRecovery.ts is unused in production and could be deleted.)

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Confirmed: syncEnvironmentShellSnapshot builds fresh objects for every thread (store.ts:1947-2014). The detail path is applyEnvironmentThreadDetailEvent → applyRecoveredEventBatch([event]) → one useStore set per event (service.ts:707-769, store.ts:3835-3838). createOrchestrationRecoveryCoordinator is defined only and never used in production (orchestrationRecovery.ts:88).

The impact is limited. The primary direct connection resumes the shell after a reconnect when it can (resumeShell: true), priority re-snapshots are off by default, and one streaming thread produces at most ~31 commits/s, which is below 60 fps. Per-frame batching therefore only helps with several concurrent streams or replay bursts.

Prior work

React compiler scoping and render work landed in Aug. Snapshot structural sharing and detail-event batching are new.

Part of Priority 14: Trim the JS on the boot and thread paths

Expected gain

Estimated −60–80 KiB raw / ~5–10 ms eval from the boot graph; removes per-connection layer construction and duplicated discovery probes across tabs and clients

What happens today

wsTransport-*.js is 431.8 KiB: 196 KiB effect core (needed at boot) and ~210 KiB of contracts schema definitions evaluated eagerly at import, because RpcClient.make(WsRpcGroup) references every RPC. That includes rarely used groups: agentControl 25.5 KiB, hostedIdentity 11.2, computer 6.7, device 6.8, relay 5.5, nativeE2ee 4.7, nativeHandoff 4.1, changeRequestReview 3.8. Evaluating the full contracts graph takes ~30 ms in Node. On the server, makeServerWsRpcLayer(principal) is called per connection. SourceControlDiscovery.layer, ProviderMaintenanceRunner.layer and ContextHandoffInspectionLive are not part of the main server graph, so they are rebuilt per WS connection, and their caches (e.g. the 5 s discovery cache) are per-connection. serverDiscoverSourceControl always calls .refresh, which re-spawns git/jj/gh probes.

Proposal

Client: move cold feature groups (agent-control admin, native E2EE, native handoff, computer, hosted identity) into separately imported RpcGroups exposed through lazily created clients, either sharing the socket via the hosted-style merged group or via a separate lazy socket like device. Contract modules then evaluate on first use. Server: provide SourceControlDiscovery, ProviderMaintenanceRunner and ContextHandoffInspection once in the main runtime graph (server.ts), and make discoverSourceControl use discover (TTL) unless the user explicitly asks for a refresh.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The attribution is confirmed in client-runtime-sync/wsTransport-attribution.txt. However, the cold contract modules (hostedIdentity, relay, nativeE2ee and others) are also reachable from other boot-graph importers; EVIDENCE.md notes relay/E2EE code is in the eager graph. Splitting the RPC groups alone would not remove them, so the −60-80 KiB estimate is optimistic.

Server side: makeServerWsRpcLayer is provided per upgrade (ws.ts:30-64, 82). Effect.provide builds with a forked CurrentMemoMap (effect Layer.ts:600-604, 993-1003), so layers that also appear in the main graph are likely reused. SqlitePersistenceLayerLive and SourceControlProviderRegistry.layer are referenced in server.ts:44/256/313. SourceControlDiscovery.layer, ProviderMaintenanceRunner.layer, ContextHandoffInspectionLive and ChatAttachmentUploadsLive are genuinely rebuilt per connection. Since serverDiscoverSourceControl always calls refresh (providerRpc.ts:373), the per-connection 5 s cache is moot anyway. Construction cost was not measured.

What happens today

Mobile, the hosted web read cache and desktop hub workspaces already hydrate an environment from a persisted CachedEnvironmentShellSnapshot (hydrateEnvironmentStateFromCache, which also marks rows as last-known state). The direct primary environment on web and desktop, the most common path, has nothing to show until boot graph → beforeLoad → RootAppShell chunk → ws-token → WS → server snapshot (SQL + git + encode) → decode. Even mobile always downloads a full snapshot after hydrating, because resume is attempted only from a baseline the live connection established itself.

Proposal

Reuse projectThreadReadCacheShell and hydrateEnvironmentStateFromCache for the primary environment. Persist the applied shell (debounced) to IndexedDB in web/desktop and hydrate it in beforeLoad. Phase 2: persist the projection sequence with it and allow the first subscription to send resumeFromSequence from the cached baseline, after the server's canResumeAfter anchor check. Cold boot after a short absence then becomes a delta replay (one chunk once the chunking fix lands) instead of a full snapshot.

Confirmed: hydrateEnvironmentStateFromCache is used only by mobile (environmentSnapshotPersistence.ts:294), hosted (readCache.ts:252, threadReadCache.ts:115, hostedConnectionCoordinator.ts:781) and desktop hub workspaces (desktopWorkspace.ts:178). The primary direct environment never hydrates. Resume requires a baseline the live connection established itself (connection.ts:215-219, 253-258).

The benefit is small for the main local scenario: measured sidebar-to-shellUsable gaps on cold loopback were only 25-87 ms (412→499, 401→426, 403→428). It grows for a primary served over LAN or WAN, and was 3.4 s on the throttled profile. Effort and risk are high: last-known-state marking, mutation readiness, and invalidation when the server DB changes.

B. New thread and working in a thread

New thread, open, switch 16 findings · 1 high · 9 medium · 6 low

The first 'New thread' takes 401 ms (~300 ms of it the idle throttle). Every thread switch remounts ChatView (a regression from split panes), and history is requested only after mount, so existing threads briefly show the new-thread hero.

How it works today (investigator's summary)

How it works today. Both chat routes (/_chat/$environmentId/$threadId and /_chat/draft/$draftId) render a React.lazy route view inside <Suspense fallback={null}>. Nothing prefetches the chat code: only the Settings page is preloaded at idle. After RootAppShell loads, the thread/draft route still needs 40–42 more chunks, 1.57–1.60 MiB raw / 505–515 KiB gzip. Most of that is one chunk named "ChatRightPanel" (1,115 KiB). It is really ChatView plus everything ChatView imports statically: Lexical, MessagesTimeline, the composer, the overview "crown", GitActionsControl and side panels. Another 269 KiB chunk holds shiki and @pierre/diffs, pulled in by a static import in ChatMarkdown and by DiffWorkerPoolProvider. With modulePreload:false these chunks load as a 5-level import waterfall.

Where the time goes. "New thread" waits on two RPCs in a row (server.getConfig at 85–131 KB, then getProjectPreferences) before it even navigates. The thread view asks for its 150-message window only from a passive effect after ChatView has mounted and painted. Measured in headless Chromium against the production server with a scratch home:

  • First "New thread" in a document: 401 ms from click to composer at 1x CPU, 592–1,714 ms at 4x.
  • About 300 ms of that is idle time. React 19 holds back showing a Suspense boundary's content until 300 ms after its fallback appeared (FALLBACK_THROTTLE_MS). Because the route uses React.lazy under a sync navigation, the empty fallback is committed even when the chunk is already in the HTTP cache. Measured: fallback at +20 ms, content at +321 ms.
  • Every thread switch remounts the whole ChatView, including Lexical and LegendList. Split panes, added in commit 141d441c7, key each pane by thread, which also disables the older useDeferredValue timeline deferral. Busy time for an empty thread: 48–90 ms at 1x, 242–331 ms at 4x.
  • An unloaded thread's snapshot request goes out 227 ms after the click at 1x and 913 ms at 4x.

Server and side costs. Each ChatView mount re-runs vcs.listRefs: twice on first mount, about 7 git processes per call, about 52 ms on this 590-branch repo. The first composer mount in each document triggers source-control discovery, and the server handler throws away its cache first. That re-runs gh/glab auth status (network calls), about 0.8–1.5 s. Thread-window snapshots are 80–95 % activity payload (full tool output and diffs): up to 463 KB for recent threads in the user's real DB and 1.1 MB for older threads saved before PR #481. The client then re-serialises every snapshot and event just to estimate its size. Code blocks are highlighted synchronously during render; the first use of a language costs 50–70 ms. Typing is fine on an empty draft (about 1 frame; key handling up to 21 ms at 4x). But the composer store re-serialises its whole saved state on every keystroke, including image data, which costs 2–6 ms per key once MB-sized images are attached.

Part of Priority 1: Remove the 300 ms React Suspense reveal delay from every navigation

Expected gain

-300 ms (measured idle gap) on the first open of each lazy route per document: first 'New thread' 401 → ~100 ms at 1x, first thread open similar; up to -600 ms per session when both the draft and thread routes are opened

What happens today

Each route component is lazy(() => import(...)) wrapped in <Suspense fallback={null}>, and TanStack navigation applies as a synchronous update. React.lazy's initializer always throws on its first render, even when the module is already loaded, because it resolves through .then (react.production.js lazyInitializer). So the empty fallback is committed. The retry then runs in a RetryLane, and React 19.2.8 delays that commit to globalMostRecentFallbackTime + 300 - now(). Measured: on draft→thread navigation the old composer is removed at +20 ms and the new one appears at +321 ms. On 'New thread' from /statistics the chunks are ready at +100 ms but the composer appears at +401 ms. The main thread is idle for that gap (profile: 210 ms busy vs 557 ms idle). The Settings idle preload (import() only) does not avoid this either, because the React.lazy wrapper itself is still uninitialised. The same pattern sits on RootAppShell, statistics, settings, projects and ThreadWorkspacePanel ('Loading workspace...').

Proposal

Define route components with TanStack's lazyRouteComponent(() => import('../components/routeViews/ChatThreadRouteView'), 'ChatThreadRouteView'), and read params/search inside via getRouteApi. The router then calls .preload() in loadMatches before it commits the match, and once loaded the component renders without suspending, so no fallback is committed and the 300 ms delay never starts. Export preloadChatThreadRoute() / preloadDraftRoute() that call .preload(). Do the same for ThreadWorkspacePanel: keep a module-level loaded flag and render the real component directly once loaded. Update webBundleSplitting.test.ts, which asserts lazy(, so it also accepts lazyRouteComponent(. Apply the same change to settings, statistics and projects, which other dimensions own.

Verifier (Confirmed)

I reproduced it by re-running measure4.mjs on port 13874 (output in .perf-research/verifier-thread-and-draft/measure4-run.txt). Draft→thread: old composer removed at +12 ms, new composer at +313 ms, while the ChatThreadRouteView chunk arrived at +13–14 ms. 'New thread' from a fresh /statistics document: chunks came from the HTTP cache at +93–98 ms, composer at +399 ms. The same gap shows on boot: replaceState to the bootstrap thread at 707 ms, composer at 1,029 ms (+322). Checked react 19.2.8 lazyInitializer (react.production.js:264-282): an already-imported module still throws on first render. The retry-only throttle is at react-dom-client.production.js:10791-10794 ((lanes & 62914560) === lanes, globalMostRecentFallbackTime + 300). One correction: TanStack does not apply navigation as a sync update; it commits through React.startTransition (Transitioner.js:16-20). A newly mounted Suspense boundary still commits its fallback inside a transition, so the effect is the same. The proposal is valid: lazyRouteComponent's preload is awaited by loadRouteChunk (router-core load-client.js:11,21), and once comp is set the component never suspends. As a bonus, the old route stays visible instead of a blank pane. Saving is roughly 300 ms minus chunk-load time, so about 200–300 ms locally and little when a cold remote chunk takes longer than 300 ms. The Settings idle preload (settingsRoute.ts:13-15) only calls import() and does not initialise the lazy wrapper, as claimed.

Prior work

Aug report made these routes lazy (statistics/diagnostics/pairing/native-auth); the 300 ms reveal delay this introduced is not documented anywhere. New.

Part of Priority 14: Trim the JS on the boot and thread paths

Expected gain

Desktop boot: the thread view is ready ~200–550 ms earlier (route chunk fetch overlaps the 530–880 ms shell wait; waterfall 221 ms → ~1 round). Hosted / remote: saves ~4 RTTs on first thread or draft open. Cold first click without bootstrap: the whole chunk load moves off the click

What happens today

Only SettingsPage is preloaded at idle; the router has no defaultPreload, and sidebar rows navigate with router.navigate on click, so nothing preloads on hover. On desktop the app loads '/', and EventRouter first awaits ensureEnvironmentConnectionBootstrapped (welcome → shell snapshot) before it redirects to the bootstrap thread. Measured: the RootAppShell chunk loads at 301–322 ms, but the thread route chunk is first requested at 855 ms (run 1) and 1,208 ms (run 2). With modulePreload:false the 42 new chunks arrive in 4–5 sequential rounds: 1,208→1,429 ms = 221 ms on a local server, and SettingsPage was fetched ahead of it. When there is no bootstrap thread, the first click on a thread or 'New thread' pays the full cold load: 505–515 KiB gzip, depth 5.

Proposal

(1) After the RootAppShell first paint, call scheduleIdleTask(() => { preloadChatThreadRoute(); preloadDraftRoute(); }), at higher priority than the settings preload. In handleWelcome, start preloadChatThreadRoute() and retainThreadDetailSubscription(bootstrapThread) before awaiting ensureEnvironmentConnectionBootstrapped. (2) Preload on intent: call preload() from sidebar rows and the 'New thread' button on pointerenter/pointerdown, and/or switch rows to <Link> with defaultPreload: 'intent'. (3) Re-enable modulepreload only for dynamic-import dependencies with build.modulePreload: { polyfill: false, resolveDependencies: (_f, deps, { hostType }) => hostType === 'js' ? deps : [] }. The route's whole static closure is then fetched in parallel, while index.html keeps no eager preloads (the reason it was turned off).

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The code facts hold. router.ts:7-14 has no defaultPreload. useSidebarThreadActions.ts:98-112 calls router.navigate on click. vite.config.ts:188 sets modulePreload:false. EventRouter awaits ensureEnvironmentConnectionBootstrapped before navigating (RootAppShell.tsx:224-266). My boot run: RootAppShell chunk at 274 ms, SettingsPage idle preload at 636 ms, ChatThreadRouteView first requested at 718 ms (right after replaceState at 707). Its dependencies arrived in 4–5 rounds until 856 ms (about 140 ms locally), and the composer appeared at 1,029 ms. Key correction: while the routes use React.lazy, prefetching alone does not move the composer earlier when the chunk lands within 300 ms of the fallback. The 300 ms throttle sets the floor: chunks were done at 856 ms but content could not show before ~1,007 ms. So most of the claimed 200–550 ms depends on the previous finding (lazyRouteComponent .preload). Waterfall cost is ~140–220 ms on a cold local load and ~5 ms when HTTP-cached (later documents); the larger win is on hosted or remote RTTs. The modulePreload resolveDependencies idea overlaps the documented 'retest modulePreload' residual.

Prior work

Partial overlap with the Aug residual 'retest modulePreload after chunk splitting' (performance-efficiency-size-improvements.md §8). The idle preload of the chat route and the boot ordering are new.

Part of Priority 8: New thread and the first turn

Expected gain

-85 ms at 1x locally and -150–250 ms at 4x per fresh 'New thread'; on hosted relay -2 RTTs (~100–400 ms); saves ~100 KB of WS decode per click and 6 ms of server event-loop blocking per getConfig

What happens today

createAndOpenDraft awaits api.server.getConfig() and then readEffectiveProjectPreferences before router.navigate, so the route chunk load and render cannot start until both RPCs return. The config is already kept live by the subscribeServerConfig stream. Server-side, loadServerConfig rebuilds providers, settings, keybindings and diagnostics, and runs resolveAvailableEditors(): 6.2 ms of synchronous statSync on the event loop per call. Measured: getConfig 84,855 B / 45 ms and 130,999 B / 23 ms, prefs 57 ms and 2 ms; pushState at +85 ms after the click. At 4x CPU, decoding getConfig was a 72 ms long frame (wsTransport onmessage). At boot the client also calls getConfig (45 KB) on top of the subscription, which pushed 6 frames / 413 KB in 12 s.

Proposal

Navigate first and fill in defaults afterwards: register the draft from the environment's cached ServerConfig (per-environment atom fed by subscribeServerConfig), then navigate immediately. Fetch project preferences in parallel and apply them with store.setModelSelection / envMode when they arrive; only force a fresh fetch for hosted nodes whose config generation or lease changed. If a fresh read is kept, run both RPCs with Promise.all and start preloadDraftRoute() at click time. On the server, cache resolveAvailableEditors(), invalidated on PATH change or a settings/editor refresh, and add a light getProjectDefaults RPC instead of the full config.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The sequential awaits are real: useHandleNewThread.ts:146 (getConfig), 147-151 (prefs), 176-179 (navigate). It only happens for a fresh draft. A warm 'New thread' that reuses the stored draft skips both RPCs (pushState at +33 ms in my run). The cost is overstated at 1x locally. In my run getConfig was sent at +51 ms and returned at +76 ms (113,814 B), prefs returned at +79 ms and pushState fired at +85 ms. So the RPC part is ~30 ms; the first ~50 ms is Playwright click overhead, not the waterfall. resolveAvailableEditors re-measured at 4.0 ms median (claimed 6.2). The fresh read is deliberate: the comment at useHandleNewThread.ts:143-145 explains the primary cache can hold the previous hosted node's settings, so 'navigate first' must keep hosted lease and target correctness, and may make the model selector flicker. Confirmed side issue: at boot the client also calls getConfig (serverState.ts:168-178) right after subscribeServerConfig, so the same ~95.6 KB config arrives twice within 20 ms. Worth it at 4x CPU and on hosted relays (2 RTTs); small locally.

Part of Priority 8: New thread and the first turn

Expected gain

Removes ~5–7 child processes and 2 network auth checks (0.8–1.5 s of server work, measured) per chat entry after 30 s; fewer competing processes during boot

What happens today

useSourceControlDiscovery() in ChatComposer mounts an Atom.swr({ staleTime: 30s, revalidateOnMount: true }) that calls server.discoverSourceControl. The server handler maps that RPC to sourceControlDiscovery.refresh, which first does Cache.invalidate on its 5 s cache and then re-probes git/jj/gh/glab/az --version plus gh auth status --json hosts, glab auth status and az account show. Measured: the RPC took 1,557 ms at boot and ~810 ms on draft open in a fresh document; on this machine glab auth status takes 799 ms and gh auth status 379 ms (both network); all probes together 762 ms. Not triggered on in-document thread switches (atom stays mounted), but it runs on each new document (desktop reload, hosted tab) and whenever chat remounts after more than 30 s away (settings, statistics, projects).

Proposal

Split the RPC: discoverSourceControl serves the cached discover (raise the server TTL to minutes and refresh in the background); only an explicit user 'refresh' in settings calls refresh. On the client, use a staleTime of several minutes, revalidate on window focus/online, and don't fetch from the composer at all until the UI needs auth state (GitActionsControl / PR actions).

Verifier (Confirmed)

sourceControlDiscoveryState.ts:64-75 uses Atom.swr with a 30 s staleTime and revalidateOnMount, and calls the manager's refresh. providerRpc.ts:370-377 maps discoverSourceControl to sourceControlDiscovery.refresh, which does Cache.invalidate and then Cache.get (SourceControlDiscovery.ts:155-159), defeating the 5 s TTL (line 58). The probes include gh auth status --json hosts, glab auth status and az account show (Catalog 169-196). Measured in my run: 1,161 ms at boot (906→2,067) and 776 ms on 'New thread' in a fresh document; nothing on in-document switches. It is off the paint path, but ChatComposer.tsx:513-522 gates hasSourceControlRemote on the result, so those affordances appear ~1 s late, plus the server process and network cost on each document and on chat re-entry after 30 s.

Prior work

Aug report bounded the discovery cache; that the RPC path bypasses it is new.

Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

Active thread snapshot not queued behind up to 6 × 80–500 KB sibling snapshots; fewer store commits during thread open (estimate)

What happens today

useChatSessionTabsPrefetch retains up to MAX_SPECULATIVE_SIBLING_TAB_PREFETCH = 6 sibling windows straight from the mount effect (not idle-scheduled), on the same WebSocket and the same main-thread decode path as the active thread's snapshot. Sidebar prewarm is idle-scheduled and limited to 3 threads (SIDEBAR_THREAD_PREWARM_LIMIT = 3; the Aug doc says 10). With real window sizes of 80–500 KB, up to ~3 MB can arrive in the same second as the active snapshot, each with parse, decode, the size estimate and a separate store commit that re-runs every useStore selector.

Proposal

Schedule sibling retains with scheduleIdleTask after the active thread's window has been applied (gate on selectThreadDetailLoaded(activeRef)), and stagger them (1 every ~100 ms). Prefer intent-based warming (hover/pointerdown, see finding detail-subscription-after-mount-hero-flash) and consider a smaller prewarm window (e.g. 30 messages, no activities) that upgrades on open.

Verifier (Confirmed)

useChatSessionTabsPrefetch (useChatSessionTabsPrefetch.ts:69-83) retains up to 6 sibling windows straight from a mount effect. Worse than described: the hook is called at ChatView.tsx:1095, before the active thread's retain effect at 2462. In the same passive-effect flush, all sibling subscribeThreadWindow requests therefore go out ahead of the active thread's own request. It is on the hot path for typical users: sessionTabs.selectors.ts:59-71 treats every main-worktree thread (worktreePath null) of the project as a sibling. Because ChatView remounts on each switch, the effect re-runs every switch, though already-cached windows are not refetched. Sidebar prewarm is idle-scheduled with SIDEBAR_THREAD_PREWARM_LIMIT = 3 (Sidebar.logic.ts:21), as stated. The evidence is code-only: the scratch repo had a single thread, so there was no measurement.

Prior work

Aug report bounded sidebar prewarming; sibling prefetch timing and its competition with the active snapshot are new.

Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

For heavy users after long streaming sessions: switching back to a recent thread hits the cache instead of a fresh 80–460 KB snapshot plus 200–900 ms re-open (estimate based on measured window sizes and the investigator's open timings); eviction no longer runs on every event

What happens today

recordRetainedEvent adds the full JSON size of every live event to entry.estimatedRetainedBytes, and also every history page (line ~329). That includes streaming deltas and in-place tool updates whose effect on store state is bounded, since the window holds 150 messages and deltas merge into one row. The value is capped only at MAX_CACHED_THREAD_DETAIL_ESTIMATED_BYTES (12 MiB) and reset only when a new snapshot arrives. Measured read-only in the user's real state.sqlite: thread b2714955… persisted 24,541 orchestration events, 28.8 MB of event JSON, between 14:27 and 17:12 today (084484ed…: 620 events / 1.55 MB; cf005c9e…: 1,803 / 3.2 MB). A client watching such a thread therefore reaches the 12 MiB cap in about an hour. planEvictionsToCapacity sums the bytes of every entry, including pinned ones, and evicts idle entries until the total fits. Once one pinned entry (retained or non-idle) sits at 12 MiB, every idle cached thread window is evicted on the next event. That includes the thread the user just switched away from, so switching back pays a cold subscribeThreadWindow snapshot (80–460 KB measured window sizes), the 'new thread' hero flash, and the remount side effects. Code reading plus real event volumes; the eviction itself was not reproduced in a browser.

Proposal

Make the estimate track retained state, not traffic. Set it on snapshot; for events, add bytes only for row-creating events (new message, new activity, new plan) and not for in-place updates or deltas. Or re-baseline every N events from the store's window (messages and activities by id), or clamp each entry to max(2 × snapshot estimate, 1 MiB) until the next snapshot. In planEvictionsToCapacity, budget idle entries separately from pinned ones (e.g. pinned bytes do not count against the idle budget), so a pinned hot thread cannot starve the cache. Add a unit test: a pinned entry receiving 20 MiB of events must not evict an idle 200 KB entry. The CPU fix in retained-bytes-json-stringify (approximate size from frame length) fits naturally in the same change.

This finding was added by the adversarial verifier while checking the investigator's report. It has not been verified a second time.

Prior work

The Aug report added the 32-entry / 12 MiB caps (evictionPolicy.ts). Finding retained-bytes-json-stringify covers only the CPU cost of measuring. The drift in the accounting, and the resulting eviction of every idle entry, is new.

Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

An estimated 40–70 % less main-thread work per thread switch (measured baseline 48–90 ms at 1x, 242–331 ms at 4x for empty threads; more with transcripts); with the deferred timeline, composer/header appear 1 frame after the click

What happens today

In single-pane mode ChatPanes builds { kind: 'thread', ref: threadRef } and renders the pane as <section key={paneKey(ref)}>. Changing thread changes the key, so the entire ChatView unmounts and mounts again: LexicalComposer editor, LegendList, header/crown, dozens of store subscriptions and effects. Before commit 141d441c7 (split panes, 2026-09-15) ChatView was rendered without a key. The useDeferredValue(activeThreadIdRaw) gate from 406334a4d ('urgent render paints the placeholder, then the timeline in a transition') never triggers on a fresh mount, because the deferred value starts equal to the current one. Measured on empty threads (measure5): new composer element every switch, commit after 30–45 ms, busy 48–90 ms at 1x and 163–204 ms / 242–331 ms at 4x; a 152 ms blocking long frame at 4x. Every remount also re-runs mount side effects (listRefs, vcs status, overview queries).

Proposal

Quick win (S, low risk): useDeferredValue(activeThreadIdRaw, null) so a fresh mount paints chrome and composer first and mounts MessagesTimeline in a transition. Structural fix (M): when the layout is not split, give the single pane a stable key (e.g. 'primary') so ChatView, Lexical and composer instances survive navigation. Thread-scoped useState then needs resetting on threadId change, as before 141d441c7 (some resets already exist, e.g. the setInspectedContextHandoff effect). Keep keyed sections only for real splits.

Verifier (Confirmed)

ChatPanes.tsx:286-292 builds {kind:'thread', ref: threadRef} when not split, and ChatPanes.tsx:595-596 renders <section key={key}> keyed by paneKey(ref). The thread route view always wraps ChatView in ChatPanes (ChatThreadRouteView.tsx:284-303, 326-345). I checked with git show 141d441c7^: before split panes, ChatView was rendered without a key. ChatView.tsx:808 calls useDeferredValue(activeThreadIdRaw) with no initial value, so the deferral is a no-op on a fresh mount. Caveat on impact: MessagesTimeline is itself keyed by thread id (ChatView.tsx:5066), so a stable pane key saves only the composer, Lexical, header and effect remounts, not the timeline mount. Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

The snapshot request goes out 200–900 ms earlier (measured effect delay), overlapping server query and RTT with chunk load and mount; removes a visible wrong-surface flash and one or two listRefs calls (~7–14 git procs) per first open of a non-prewarmed thread

What happens today

retainThreadDetailSubscription runs inside a passive useEffect. Measured: subscribeThreadWindow left the client 227 ms (1x) / 913 ms (4x) after the click for a thread that had not been prewarmed, after composer commit and paint. Meanwhile the shell already knows the thread (shell has latestTurn and latestUserMessageAt), so ChatView renders. shouldShowNewThreadSurface only checks messages, optimistic messages and timeline entries, and nothing in ChatView uses selectThreadDetailLoaded. An existing thread with unloaded detail therefore renders NewThreadHero, mounting NewThreadWorkLocation and its BranchToolbarBranchSelector (listRefs, git status), until the window arrives. Only the hosted read cache seeds old messages.

Proposal

(1) Call retainThreadDetailSubscription at navigation intent: pointerdown/hover on sidebar rows with an auto-release after ~10 s unless the route takes over, plus a route beforeLoad/loader for /_chat/$environmentId/$threadId that retains synchronously. ChatView's effect then only adds its ref. (2) Gate the hero: show it only when selectThreadDetailLoaded is true or the shell says the thread never started (latestTurn === null && latestUserMessageAt === null); otherwise render a light transcript skeleton. (3) Consider a non-hosted read cache (last 20 messages) so revisits after eviction paint at once.

Verifier (Confirmed)

retainThreadDetailSubscription runs in a passive effect (ChatView.tsx:2462-2476). getThreadFromEnvironmentState (threadDerivation.ts:102-117) returns a Thread from the shell alone, with empty messages. shouldShowNewThreadSurface (ChatView.logic.ts:416-430, used at ChatView.tsx:1978-1985) never checks selectThreadDetailLoaded, so an existing thread whose detail is not loaded renders NewThreadHero and its NewThreadWorkLocation and branch selector. That is a real UX/correctness bug. On timing, in my boot run subscribeThreadWindow left 340 ms after replaceState, and most of that is the 300 ms Suspense throttle. Once the throttle finding is fixed, the effect fires ~50–150 ms after the click at 1x, so the extra gain from retaining at intent time is smaller than '200–900 ms' (still meaningful at 4x and on hosted relays). Hero gating is the more valuable half of the proposal.

Part of Priority 8: New thread and the first turn

Expected gain

-7 to -14 git child processes (~50–100 ms of server CPU/IO on large repos) per draft/thread open and switch; fewer WS round trips

What happens today

BranchToolbarBranchSelector runs useEffect(prefetchBranches) before useGitBranches → watchBranches. The prefetch tracks in-flight requests in branchesPrefetchInFlight and the controller uses controller.inFlightPromise, and they do not share them; the new controller's poller then runs immediately (runImmediately ?? true). Result: two identical vcs.listRefs within 2 ms. When the last subscriber unmounts the controller is deleted, so each ChatView remount creates a fresh one with lastFetchedAt=0 and refetches regardless of the 15 s stale time. Server listRefs has no cache: repo detection + git branch, then symbolic-ref, worktree list, branch --remotes, remote and branch recency run concurrently. Measured in the browser: 2x listRefs on first mount; 1x listRefs + subscribeVcsStatus on every thread switch, including revisits. ~52 ms median per listRefs on a 590-branch / 32-worktree repo.

Proposal

Have prefetchBranchesByKey and the controller share one in-flight promise per key, or drop the explicit prefetch since watchBranches already loads immediately. Keep controllers alive for an idle TTL (e.g. 60 s, like the thread-detail idle eviction) and on (re)watch only refetch when Date.now() - lastFetchedAt >= GIT_BRANCHES_STALE_TIME_MS. Optionally add a short server-side TTL cache for listRefs keyed by cwd, invalidated by the vcs status broadcaster's ref-change events.

Verifier (Confirmed)

Reproduced: two vcs.listRefs within 3 ms at boot (#11/#13) and on 'New thread' (#13/#15), then one listRefs plus subscribeVcsStatus on every draft↔thread switch. In the code, the prefetch effect at BranchToolbarBranchSelector.tsx:240-243 runs before useGitBranches subscribes. prefetchBranchesByKey (gitAtoms.ts:487-524) keeps its own in-flight set and throws its result away once a controller exists. The new controller's poller refreshes immediately (visibilityPolling.ts:74). unwatchBranches deletes the controller (gitAtoms.ts:465-485), so every remount refetches regardless of GIT_BRANCHES_STALE_TIME_MS (line 103). Measured listRefs took 26–120 ms. The work is off the paint path (the branch selector simply shows pending), so it is mostly wasted server git processes, hence the downgrade.

What happens today

estimateRetainedBytes runs new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(value)).byteLength on each thread snapshot and on every live event (streaming deltas) on the main thread, followed by evictToCapacity(), which rebuilds an entries array each time. The code matches the claim. useFlipLayout.ts:23-70 is a useLayoutEffect with no deps that calls getAnimations and getBoundingClientRect per item each commit. The impact is overstated, though. Inside a mount commit, the forced style and layout covers the freshly mounted ChatView, which the browser must lay out before paint anyway. The 17–61 ms 'getAnimations' self-time at 4x is mostly that layout being moved earlier, not removed. Expected gain

Removes 50–70 ms per language (measured) plus ~0.04 ms/line from the thread-open commit; avoids 100+ ms long tasks for large code blocks

What happens today

For settled messages, UncachedShikiCodeBlock calls use(getHighlighterPromise(language)) and then highlighter.codeToHtml inside useMemo during render, using the shiki-js engine (oniguruma-to-es). Measured: init 4 ms; the first tsx block costs 52–70 ms whatever its size (grammar regex compile); warm cost ~0.04 ms/line (8.6 ms for 200 lines); a synthetic 400-line TS block took 296 ms cold. Opening a thread whose last 150 messages contain blocks in several languages pays this per language inside the mount commit, plus per-block cost for every row LegendList renders. The LRU result cache (500 entries / 50 MB) only helps on revisits.

Proposal

Render the plain <pre> immediately and highlight off the critical path: queue highlight jobs in startTransition / scheduleIdleTask, visible blocks first, and swap the HTML in when ready. Better still, run highlighting in a worker (the @pierre/diffs WorkerPoolManager already exists) or in a small dedicated worker using shiki/core with the JS engine. Warm the highlighter and the top grammars (ts/tsx/js/json/bash/diff) at idle after the first thread paint.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

The mechanism differs from the claim. The first time a language is used, use(getHighlighterPromise(language)) suspends (ChatMarkdown.tsx:385), the Suspense fallback (plain <pre>, 945-953) shows, and the expensive first codeToHtml runs in the later Suspense retry render, not in the thread-open mount commit. Blocks in languages already loaded are highlighted synchronously in render (useMemo at 386-398), and that part is on the mount path. I re-ran shiki-bench: tsx init 6.4 ms; the first 20-line block took 78.6 ms. The first call on new 60- and 200-line inputs still took 67.5 and 60.8 ms after warm-up, so cold cost recurs whenever new grammar rules are hit, not just once per language. Warm cost is ~10 ms per 200 lines. Each code block's fallback commit also resets the 300 ms reveal throttle for the highlighted swap. These are real long tasks just after open, but not before first paint. Moving the work to idle or a worker is a sound proposal.

Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

-2 to -6 ms per keystroke and multi-MB allocations when drafts hold images; removes a quota-related draft-loss risk

What happens today

setPrompt → zustand persist → setItem() runs partialize over all drafts and createJSONStorage → JSON.stringify synchronously on every set (zustand 5.0.15 middleware.mjs:300,358-368). createDebouncedStorage only debounces the final localStorage.setItem (300 ms). Saved attachments carry base64 dataUrl. Measured: 2.22 ms per keystroke with one 2 MiB image draft and 5.75 ms with 5 MiB (a 6.8 MB string allocated per key), and a multi-MB localStorage write every 300 ms while typing, which risks hitting the quota (an unhandled throw in the timer means silently lost drafts). Every set also re-runs ~70 useComposerDraftStore selectors, including one per sidebar project that iterates all draft threads. Empty-draft typing is otherwise fine (≤21 ms handlers at 4x).

Proposal

Write a PersistStorage that receives the state object and defers partialize + stringify into the debounced or idle flush (keeping the existing beforeunload flush). Move attachment bytes out of localStorage into IndexedDB or the existing upload pipeline, keyed by attachment id. Index draft threads by logical project once, so sidebar selectors don't scan all drafts per keystroke.

Verifier (Confirmed)

setPrompt (draftStore.ts:1501-1513) goes through zustand persist, whose createJSONStorage stringifies synchronously (draftStore.ts:2261-2268, partialize at draftPersistence.ts:1070-1095). createDebouncedStorage (storage.ts:42-66) only debounces the final setItem. I re-ran persist-bench: stringify alone is 0.00–0.02 ms without images, 1.19 ms with a 2 MiB image and 3.04 ms with 5 MiB (claimed 2.22 / 5.75 ms, which includes partialize and machine variance). syncPersistedAttachments (draftStore.ts:930-955) only marks an image persisted if the flushed write succeeded, so MB-sized dataUrls really do sit in the persisted state. Low impact; it only matters for drafts with images.
