Part of Priority 15: Opening and switching threads

Expected gain

Removes one projection SQL round per subscribed thread every 30 s (about 2 queries/s with 60 open subscriptions; estimated) and, for idle Codex threads, one codex app-server spawn per 30 s per open thread (estimated 0.3-1 s CPU and tens of MB RSS per spawn). Removes about 3.9 MB / 26k lines per 2 weeks from server-child.log (measured).

What happens today

withHistoryRecovery wraps subscribeThread streams (579, 614) and forks Effect.forever(reconcile(threadId).pipe(Effect.andThen(Effect.sleep('30 seconds')))) for the lifetime of the subscription. reconcileThread skips only while the 30 s TTL cache entry lives (3419-3423, 3429), and the cache is set at the end of each attempt (3470). In practice every subscribed thread therefore does a full attempt about every 30 s: resolveThreadShell (a heavy projection SELECT, visible in the trace), getProjectShellById, directory.getBinding, then adapter.readThreadHistory. For Codex threads without a live ready/running session this calls readStoredCodexThread. That spawns a new codex app-server child, sends initialize, then thread/read with includeTurns: true, re-reading and re-sending the full thread every time, even when nothing changed. Any failure is logged as 'Provider history recovery failed; preserving local thread' with only threadId; the cause is dropped (3466-3468). Measured on the user's install: 26,049 such WARNs in server-child.log.1 (37% / 3.88 MB of the file), about 40/min, on both UUID and agent-control threads. There is no backoff for persistently failing threads.

Proposal

(1) Run history recovery once on subscribe, then only on signals: provider session became idle or stopped, or reconnect. Do not poll forever. If polling stays, require that the thread's provider session is not live and use exponential backoff per thread on failure (30 s, 1 min, 2 min, up to 15 min) plus a stop after N consecutive failures until new activity. (2) For Codex, check cheaply before spawning: compare the rollout file mtime/size, or a stored updatedAt, with the last successful read. Reuse one pooled read-only app-server client with an idle timeout instead of a process per read. (3) Log the cause once per thread per failure streak (rate-limited), at Debug for expected cases (missing binding or instance).

Verifier (Confirmed)

Code checked. orchestrationRpc.ts:68-80 forks Effect.forever(reconcile, then sleep 30 s) for each subscribeThread (579) and subscribeThreadWindow (614). The TTL cache is set in ensuring at the end of each attempt (ProviderRuntimeIngestion.ts:3420-3424, 3470), so steady state is one full attempt per 30 s per thread. Failures are logged without the cause (3466-3468). Nuance: only CodexAdapter implements readThreadHistory (CodexAdapter.ts:2538, 2803). For Claude and other threads, each tick costs getThreadShellById, getProjectShellById and getBinding, then returns None. Every one of the 11 thread ids in the 26,049 server-child.log.1 WARNs is a stopped Codex binding (provider_session_runtime checked read-only). The current build's log shows a 30.4 s cadence, so about 400 ms per failed attempt, consistent with spawn + initialize + thread/read of codex app-server. The older log shows a 30.002 s cadence (fast pre-spawn failure). The 'about 40/min' rate cannot be verified because log timestamps carry no dates; the per-thread rate of 2/min is verified. The investigator missed some costs. On a successful read, processHistory (3286-3373) calls getThreadDetailById (ProjectionSnapshotQuery.ts:3025: all messages, plans, activities and checkpoints) and maps the whole history. This happens on the single shared ingestion worker (capacity 2,048, the same queue as live runtime events), every 30 s per open Codex thread. While a Codex session is live, it also runs thread/read with includeTurns over the live runtime every 30 s (CodexAdapter.ts:2549-2561). The first reconcile fires immediately on subscribe, so it competes with opening the thread.

Expected gain

Measured 36-50 us/event of redaction becomes about 1-3 us (one walk, no allocation; estimated) on every Claude runtime event; removes about 1.26 MB of allocation per worst-case workflow tick; worst-case queue memory falls about 2.5-16x

What happens today

redactAgentControlSecrets rebuilds every object with Object.fromEntries/Object.entries, maps every array, and runs replaceAll on every string, whether or not a secret is present. The Claude adapter calls it on every native message (2136) and on every runtime event (1986). Because raw.payload is the whole SDK message, one task_progress message is fully cloned 1 + fan-out times (2.5 on average, up to 16). Measured: 36-50 us per average canonical event (20-30 KB) and 1.6-2.0 us per native event. A worst-case tick copies about 1.26 MB (estimated 6-8 ms). Each queued event keeps its own clone. With runtimeEventQueue bounded at 2,048 records (ClaudeAdapter.ts:1933-1935) and the ProviderService PubSub at 4,096 (ProviderService.ts:374), a backlog during an ingestion stall could hold an estimated 130-400 MB of duplicated workflow_progress arrays. This cost exists even when logging is turned off.

Proposal

Make redaction copy-on-write: walk the value and return the same reference when no string matches SECRET_PATTERN. For strings, test with a non-global regex or includes('rycoac') before replaceAll, and allocate only along changed paths. Cache the redacted value per SDK message object in a WeakMap so fan-out events share one redacted raw by reference. Combined with canonical-raw-duplication, also stop carrying raw on derived events.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Code checked. ProviderInjection.ts:298-315 always rebuilds objects and arrays and runs replaceAll on every string. It is called on every runtime event (ClaudeAdapter.ts:1986), and on every native message only when a native logger exists (2136), so the raw SDK message is cloned once per fan-out event. The magnitude is overstated. The investigator's own bench (bench-58db.txt) gives 35.9 us per event only for 20 KB workflow events and 1.6 us for typical native-sized payloads. At the observed peak of about 7 canonical events/s on one thread, that is about 0.25 ms/s. The 130-400 MB memory figure is a speculative worst case: it needs the adapter queue (2,048, line 1933) and the PubSub (4,096, ProviderService.ts:374) both to back up behind a stalled ingestion worker, which was not observed. Copy-on-write plus WeakMap sharing is a reasonable cheap fix, but this is low impact. It mostly disappears once derived events stop carrying raw (canonical-raw-duplication).

Expected gain

Large-item log volume -90% or more (3 MB lines become a few KB); removes 2-6 ms stringify stalls per large item; bounds logger memory to a fixed budget; stops writing attachment payloads to disk

What happens today

Codex item/started and item/completed carry the whole item. On thread 421bac44 a userMessage with 1.5 MB of content (an attachment) appears in native item/started and item/completed (1.5 MB each) and in canonical item.started and item.completed, where it is present twice per line (raw.payload and payload.data), giving 3,015,702 B per line. A command item's 86 KB aggregatedOutput is likewise written 4 times. JSON.stringify of one 3 MB line takes 2.08 ms (measured), plus a Buffer.from copy and a byteLength scan. The persistence path already caps strings to 10,000 head + 5,000 tail characters (activityDataCap.ts:18-21), but the loggers write everything. The logger queue limit is a record count (2,048, lines 81 and 294), not bytes, so a backlog of large items has no memory bound (2,048 x 3 MB would be about 6 GB; estimated, worst case). Privacy: user attachments (base64) and command output stay in plaintext logs for 30 days.

Proposal

Serialize log records with a JSON.stringify replacer that caps strings (e.g. 4 KB head + 1 KB tail with a '...[N chars]' marker, reusing the capActivityData approach) and replaces data:/base64 blobs with {mime, bytes, sha256-prefix}. In canonical, drop raw when payload.data already holds the same object (Codex). Change the writer queue to a byte budget (e.g. 8 MiB per writer and 32 MiB global, measured with the already computed message length) and count drops in providerEventLogRecordsDroppedTotal.

Verifier (Confirmed)

activityDataCap.ts:18-22 caps only persisted activity data (16,000 chars, head 10k / tail 5k). The loggers stringify everything (EventNdjsonLogger.ts:150-173). The queue bound is a record count (81, 294). The investigator's analyze-codex.txt shows canonical item.started/item.completed max 3,015,703 B and native item/started and item/completed max about 1.5 MB on thread 421bac44. Large items are rare, though. On that same Codex thread, item.* lines are large but the file is still capped at 30 MiB. The 6 GB queue figure is a theoretical worst case with no observed backlog. Most of the savings overlap canonical-raw-duplication (dropping raw halves the canonical copy) and the logging default. The privacy point (attachments and command output in plaintext for 30 days) is valid and independent.

Part of Priority 21: Background I/O: logs and traces

Expected gain

No more lost tail records on quit or restart (today up to 200 ms plus one batch per active thread); writer map bounded by live sessions instead of every thread seen since boot; enables fd-holding sinks (appendfile-per-record) without fd leaks

What happens today

ProviderEventLoggersLive is a plain Layer.effect with no finalizer. Adapters close only managedNativeEventLogger, which is undefined whenever the shared logger is injected (CodexAdapter.ts:1921-1922 and 2784; AcpAdapter.ts:212; OpenCodeAdapter.ts:784-818), and that is the production path through the drivers. So EventNdjsonLogger.close (463-479) is never called. Flush timers are unref'd (284-286), so on graceful shutdown or crash the pending batch (up to 200 ms, or a full in-flight flush) is dropped, and those are the records most useful for debugging. The threadWriters map (434-441) only grows: one writer pair per thread touched since boot, never released when a session stops. Each in-memory buffer is bounded at 2,048 records, not bytes (81, 294). This contradicts the Aug report's claim that 'Shutdown drains accepted work within the existing lifecycle'.

Proposal

Make ProviderEventLoggersLive scoped and add Effect.addFinalizer(() => all(native.close(), canonical.close())), ordered after the provider adapters stop. Add release(threadId) to EventNdjsonLogger: flush and close one thread's writer when ProviderService stops or reaps that session, and evict idle writers after N minutes. Switch the queue bound to bytes (see uncapped-large-items).

Verifier (Confirmed)

ProviderEventLoggersLive (ProviderEventLoggers.ts:74-93) has no finalizer. Every driver (Claude, Codex, Copilot, OpenCode, Cursor, Grok, AcpRegistry) injects eventLoggers.native, so managedNativeEventLogger is undefined in production (CodexAdapter.ts:1921-1922; AcpAdapter.ts:212-213; OpenCodeAdapter.ts:784-785). Only ProviderService references the canonical logger, and it never closes it. EventNdjsonLogger.close (463-479) has no production caller. Flush timers are unref'd (284-286). This contradicts the Aug report's 'Shutdown drains accepted work' for these streams. Impact is low: these are best-effort debug logs, so at most the last ≤200 ms batch per active thread is lost. The never-evicted threadWriters map holds no fds (append opens and closes per write), only a small closure plus an empty buffer per thread, so memory growth is negligible today. Eviction only matters once a held-fd sink exists. Minor: resolveThreadWriter copies the whole Map on every new writer (434-435).

Prior work

The Aug hardening report claimed shutdown drains queued output. For the shared ProviderEventLoggers introduced with driver-constructed adapters, this no longer holds (regression).

Part of Priority 21: Background I/O: logs and traces

Expected gain

About 35x less synchronous Electron main-thread time per log chunk (measured 96 to 2.7 us); removes the server-to-Electron log copy entirely after readiness; about 140 MiB lower worst-case desktop log disk cap

What happens today

initializePackagedLogging builds two synchronous RotatingFileSinks (main.ts:1553-1562). Every backend stdout/stderr chunk is pushed through the pipe into Electron main and written with fs.appendFileSync (1579). Every console write in main is captured by writeDesktopStreamChunk as 3 separate appendFileSync calls: prefix, buffer, newline (1507-1511). Rotation uses existsSync/renameSync for up to 10 files (logging.ts:59-85, LOG_FILE_MAX_FILES = 10 at main.ts:291, a 200 MiB cap for the two files vs depth 3 for provider logs). Measured: 95.9 us per captured chunk vs 2.7 us for one writeSync on a held fd. The 'Listening on' detector is not a double-parse cost: it stops after settling (serverListeningDetector.ts:37-38). The backend output does cross a pipe and get written by the UI process, though, so server log bursts land on Electron main.

Proposal

Have the backend write its own rotating file (config.serverLogPath already exists and Diagnostics already tails it, Diagnostics.ts:741). Electron would then only feed the first chunks to ServerListeningDetector until it settles (or use the existing --bootstrap-fd readiness) and stop copying output afterwards. For desktop-main.log, use the async held-handle sink from appendfile-per-record, or at minimum concatenate prefix + chunk + newline into one write and keep an open fd. Reduce LOG_FILE_MAX_FILES to 3 for parity.

Verifier (Confirmed)

main.ts:290-291 (LOG_FILE_MAX_FILES = 10). writeDesktopStreamChunk at 1498-1512 makes 3 appendFileSync calls. initializePackagedLogging at 1550-1570 creates the two sync RotatingFileSinks. captureBackendOutput at 1572-1588 makes 1 appendFileSync per backend chunk. logging.ts:36-85 uses existsSync/renameSync for rotation. The detector stops after it settles (serverListeningDetector.ts:36-38). syncbench: 95.9 vs 2.7 us per chunk. Correction to the proposal: config.serverLogPath exists (config.ts:340), but nothing writes it. Diagnostics tails it (Diagnostics.ts:740-744) and silently gets ENOENT, so having the backend write its own server.log would also fix that dead Diagnostics source. Average backend output is about 0.8 MB/day (10.48 MB from Sep 27 to Oct 10), so outside failure storms the sync cost on Electron main is negligible. Packaged builds only.

Expected gain

About 1.15 KB less trace output per log record (about 17 KB/s at 15 writes/s measured), about 8.6% of current trace bytes counting SDK-path spans; estimated 5-15 us less CPU per write

What happens today

write (448), toLogMessage (150) and resolveThreadWriter (394) are Effect.fn with names, so each creates a span, and those spans are exported to server.trace.ndjson. Measured: 1,095 logger spans = 419 KB (4.0%) of a 24 s, 10 MB trace file, about 383 B per span, so about 1.15 KB of trace per log record. logNativeSdkMessage, writeNativeEvent and the surrounding handleSdkMessage chain add about 10 more spans per SDK message (1,046 spans / 483 KB, 4.6%). resolveThreadWriter runs SynchronizedRef.modifyEffect (397), a semaphore acquire on every write that serializes every thread's logging on one lock, even though the lookup is a synchronous Map.get in single-threaded JS.

Proposal

Implement the logger write path as plain functions: a Map lookup, a sync string build, and an enqueue. Expose write as a single Effect.sync, without Effect.fn or spans. Create writers lazily without a lock (JS is single-threaded; guard re-entrancy with a 'creating' marker). Drop Effect.fn naming from tiny per-event helpers (logNativeSdkMessage, writeNativeEvent, ensureThreadId, routeSteerFrame) or mark them untraced.

Verifier (Confirmed)

write (448), toLogMessage (150) and resolveThreadWriter (394) are named Effect.fn spans. resolveThreadWriter takes SynchronizedRef.modifyEffect (397), one lock per stream shared by all threads. Spans are exported. In the current server.trace.ndjson (10.16 MB), write, toLogMessage and resolveThreadWriter appear 836 times each and total 1.04 MB (10.3%). The per-SDK-message spans logNativeSdkMessage, handleSdkMessage, routeSdkMessage, routeSteerFrame and ensureThreadId appear 518 times each, about 1.19 MB (11.7%). Together that is about 22% of trace bytes, more than the investigator's 8.6% (sql.execute is 60%). Only a subset of log writes show up as spans in that window, so the per-record trace cost applies to traced records only. CPU impact is still small.

Prior work

Overlaps the already-covered trace volume finding (SQL spans, 280 KB/s). This finding adds the non-SQL logger and SDK spans and the per-write lock, which are not covered.

Category: Network / RTTRisk: lowInvestigator confidence: mediumgap-logging-io:client-tracing-always-on
Expected gain

Up to 1 authenticated HTTP POST per second less per open client while RPCs are active (about 10x fewer at a 10 s interval); removes an unbounded warning payload; small bundle saving from lazy OTLP (not measured)

What happens today

AuthenticatedTracingBootstrap always calls configureClientTracing (RootAppShell.tsx:174-178). That builds a ManagedRuntime with FetchHttpClient and an OtlpTracer exporting every 1,000 ms (clientTracing.ts:9, 81-85), whereas the server's own OTLP interval defaults to 10,000 ms (cli.ts:326). The server parses the JSON, decodes it, records it into the trace sink, and on decode failure logs the entire bodyJson as a warning (http.ts:293-297). Measured volume is small: 528 browser spans across about 5 minutes of trace files, 491 of them RpcClient.orchestration.getThreadHistoryPage.

Proposal

Enable client tracing only when the server reports a trace consumer (otlpTracesUrl set, or diagnostics tracing enabled), or behind the perf-profile flag. Raise the default export interval to 10 s to match the server. Log only the decode error and record count, never bodyJson. Lazy-import the OTLP modules so they leave the RootAppShell graph when tracing is off.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

clientTracing.ts:9 sets a 1,000 ms interval. RootAppShell.tsx:174-178 always configures tracing. http.ts:291-297 logs the full bodyJson on decode failure. The server default is 10,000 ms (cli.ts:326). Corrections: effect's OtlpExporter skips the export when the buffer is empty (node_modules effect/dist/observability/OtlpExporter.js:146), so a POST happens only when spans exist, not every second unconditionally. The lazy-import proposal targets the wrong graph: OTLP and FetchHttpClient code is in the boot runtime-*.js chunk through platform/index.ts:8, then platform/observability.ts:3, then ClientTracingLive. From the sourcemap, OtlpTracer, OtlpExporter, OtlpResource and OtlpSerialization plus clientTracing.ts total about 28 KB of unminified source, an estimated ~8-10 KiB minified boot saving if made lazy (effect/http is likely shared with other code). Low impact overall.

none. EVIDENCE lists the bundle graph but not client tracing.

Category: ReliabilityRisk: lowInvestigator confidence: highgap-logging-io:stale-missing-checkouts-reprobed

Part of Priority 21: Background I/O: logs and traces

Expected gain

Removes about 1.7k stack traces / 4.8 MB per 2 weeks from server-child.log on this install (measured), and one wasted DB read plus forked fiber per dead worktree per refresh fan-out (14 dead rows here). It also fixes stale 'live' workspaces in project and sidebar UI.

What happens today

refreshLinkedWorktreeSourceControlStates (ws/context.ts:333-338) filters only archivedAt and null worktreePath. refreshWorktreeSourceControlState (refreshWorktreeSourceControlState.ts:86-87) also skips checkoutRemovedAt rows. Nothing checks that the directory exists before registry.resolve({cwd}) (line 103). The only producer of worktree.checkoutRemoved is Ryco's own removal path (decider.ts:2225-2250, via WorkspaceLifecycle/StorageService), so checkouts deleted externally stay active forever. Measured read-only on the user's DB: 14 of 35 worktree rows with archived_at NULL and checkout_removed_at NULL point to directories that no longer exist. In server-child.log.1, all 1,735 'SourceControlProviderError ... detectProvider' INFO stacks (about 4.8 MB, roughly 46% of the file) share the cause chain VcsProcessSpawnError, then PlatformError NotFound from FileSystem.access, then ENOENT on such directories (e.g. 257× .../ryco-87dc6d1c__cihaw, 256× .../ryco-30c33595__cokob). They are triggered by ws.rpc.sourceControl.listChangeRequests and other refresh paths. The failure is cheap per call, but it never converges: the dead rows keep showing as live workspaces, and every refresh fan-out pays a DB read, a forkDetach and a pretty-printed stack each time.

Proposal

When resolve/detectProvider fails with NotFound/ENOENT on the worktree path (or a cheap fs.stat before resolve fails), dispatch the existing worktree.checkoutRemoved command with reason 'missing-on-disk' once, not on every refresh. Filter checkoutRemovedAt != null in refreshLinkedWorktreeSourceControlStates too, so these rows are never forked. Optionally run one boot-time sweep that stats active worktree paths (35 stats here, under 1 ms) and marks the missing ones. Log the transition once at Info instead of a stack on every refresh. Add a test: a deleted checkout dir yields exactly one checkoutRemoved event and zero further refresh attempts.

This finding was added by the adversarial verifier while checking the investigator's report. It has not been verified a second time.

Prior work

none. The investigator's retry-loop-log-storms finding attributes these stacks to an 'unknown source control provider' and proposes only demoting the log level, which would hide this bug.

Category: Blocking I/ORisk: lowInvestigator confidence: highRating changed by verifier: impact medium → low, effort M → Mgap-logging-io:appendfile-per-record

Part of Priority 21: Background I/O: logs and traces

Expected gain

Main-thread logging I/O cost drops 12-29x (measured 52.9 to 1.8 us/record native, 142 to 42 us/record canonical); threadpool ops per batch go from 3N to 1; about 1 ms/s less main thread on the busiest workflow thread

What happens today

flushBuffered splices the batch and then for (const message of messages) await sink.write(message) (246-256). sink.write does Buffer.from (a full copy of a string up to 3 MB) and then fs.promises.appendFile, which costs 3 libuv threadpool hops (open, write, close) and a FileHandle allocation per record. Each record also pays Buffer.byteLength and a recordResourceAttribution call that runs two regexes and builds a key string. Measured with real lines: 12,345 native records take 751 ms wall / 653 ms main-thread active (52.9 us/record) with the current approach, vs 23 ms / 22 ms with an fs.WriteStream (1.8 us/record) or 50 / 44 ms with FileHandle.writev per batch. Canonical: 142 vs 41.9 us/record. The default threadpool has 4 threads shared with dns.lookup, crypto and zlib, so 3 ops per log line compete with request work. Each new sink also does a readdir of the whole provider directory (689 entries) to prune backups (219-234), twice per thread.

Proposal

Hold one fs.WriteStream (or FileHandle) per sink. On flush, write the joined batch with a single writev and track size from the joined Buffer. On rotation, end the stream, rename, and reopen. Close idle handles through an LRU (e.g. at most 64 open, or idle for more than 5 minutes) so fd use stays bounded with many threads. Replace the readdir prune with stat/rm of the specific ${file}.${maxFiles+1..maxFiles+3} paths. Record attribution once per batch, not per line. The same sink should serve the trace file and the desktop logs.

Verifier (Partially confirmed)

Code checked. flushBuffered awaits sink.write once per message (EventNdjsonLogger.ts:246-256). AsyncRotatingFileSink.writeNow does fs.promises.appendFile per record (logging.ts:173-191). pruneOverflowBackups reads the whole directory per new sink (219-234). recordResourceAttribution runs 2 regexes per record (ResourceAttribution.ts:26-27). The '12-29x' claim does not match the investigator's own iobench.txt. Native small records: 52.9 vs 1.8 us (29x). Canonical large records: 142.3 vs 41.9 us (3.4x), where the write itself dominates. iobench measures sequential awaits with ELU 'active', so these are upper bounds. At real rates (2.7 native + 7 canonical records/s on the busiest thread) the saving is about 0.5-1 ms/s of main thread, and 3 threadpool ops per record at tens of records/s is not meaningful contention. sweepbench shows a readdir of 689 entries takes about 0.5 ms. Good hygiene and a prerequisite for a held-fd sink (which needs shared-loggers-never-closed fixed), but low impact.

Prior work

The Aug report moved these writers off sync fs ('asynchronous rotating writers'). Per-record open/close and the sequential awaits were not addressed. The trace-file SQL-span volume is covered elsewhere; this finding concerns the shared sink implementation.

Method and caveats

  • Coverage. 13 parallel investigations, one per scenario or subsystem, including a live browser measurement run and a root-cause investigation of the startup request hang. A completeness critic then chose 4 more: send → first token, logging I/O, side panels, and composer pickers. Every investigation was followed by an adversarial verifier that re-read the cited code, re-ran measurements where possible, corrected line numbers and adjusted ratings. That is 35 agents in total.
  • Builds and environment. Production builds of apps/web and apps/server at commit f1be4abc7; Chrome 155 via Playwright; Node 24.21; Apple M5 Max (18 cores). The machine was shared with the parallel agents (load average up to ~25), so absolute timings carry noise; verifiers saw up to 2× variance.
  • Your real data, read-only. Desktop and server logs (430 launches), state.sqlite (9.27 GB) via read-only queries and copies, the usage scan cache, and the size of the provider log directory. Nothing was modified and no data left the machine.
  • Not measured live. The hosted Hub connect flow (no hosted build was available; analysed from code and micro-benchmarks) and the mobile app on a device (analysed from the Metro import graph). Several mobile and Hub estimates are flagged as such in their findings.
  • Artifacts. Scripts, CPU profiles, raw JSON and per-agent scratch work are in .perf-research/ in this worktree. This includes the boot harness (boot-harness.mjs), bundle attribution (graph.mjs, attribute.mjs), the startup-gate prototype (startup-hang/fix-preload.mjs) and the desktop log parsers (desktop-boot/parse-*.mjs).
  • Policy-sensitive proposals. Several Hub and mobile proposals touch the hosted-lifecycle and service-worker boundaries in AGENTS.md (single lifecycle owner, accepting a current snapshot, offline gating). Those findings say so explicitly and need owner or security sign-off.
